docs.text: MBA diploma · Module 1 of 2 Business Analytics I From Python to nonlinear models. Learn to read data, build predictive models, and turn them into business decisions, without needing a technical background. Every example runs in your browser, and every idea comes with a simulator you can play with. 24 hours live · 12 hours self-paced See the program Start session 1 One company, six sessions The whole module follows Altamar Hotels , a Chilean hotel group with three properties: a business hotel in Santiago , a beach hotel in Viña del Mar , and a lake hotel in Puerto Varas . Its management team has two questions: Revenue management What rate can we charge? How much should a room-night cost, given the hotel, the season, the room, and how far ahead the guest books? A pricing question, answered with regression . Operations Which bookings will cancel? One booking in three is cancelled. Which ones, and how many rooms can we safely oversell? A risk question, answered with classification . Straight lines answer part of both questions. Seasons that differ by hotel, early-bird discounts, last-minute premiums, and bookings made months ahead do not follow straight lines, so the module ends with the models that capture them: decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting . How it works 01 A live session each week (4 hours). Concepts explained with interactive simulators, then the same idea applied to Altamar's data with ready-to-run code. The last part of each session is a clinic for your applied case. 02 A self-paced lab each week (2 hours). A notebook that runs as it is: you change the settings, run it, and interpret what comes out. It ends with a short graded quiz. 03 No programming from scratch. The code is written for you and explained line by line. Your job is to understand what it does, adjust it, and decide what the results mean for the business. 04 An applied case in teams. You use the course toolkit on a business dataset and present recommendations to a management audience. It is 70% of the grade; the six quizzes are the other 30%. Module 2: Business Analytics II This module is the first of two. Business Analytics II · Text, NLP and LLMs continues where this one ends: Altamar also has thousands of guest reviews, and the second module turns that text into insight with natural language processing and large language models. Instructor Sebastián Azócar Mathematical engineer with a master's degree in Data Science. Data scientist at LATAM Airlines and lecturer in machine learning, econometrics, and AI. Contact: hizocar@gmail.com · LinkedIn · hizocar.github.io

docs.text: Google Colab guide Google Colab is a Python notebook environment that runs in your browser. You don't need to install anything, just a Google account. The sessions also run directly on this site, but the applied case is done in Colab, where your work is saved and shared with your team. 1. Open a course notebook Open any session or the case toolkit and click Open in Colab at the top. The notebook opens in read-only mode . To edit it, go to File › Save a copy in Drive . Your copy is saved in the Colab Notebooks folder of your Google Drive. 2. Run code Action How Run the current cell and move to the next one Shift + Enter Run the whole notebook Runtime › Run all Start from scratch Runtime › Restart session and run all Add a code or text cell + Code and + Text buttons Order matters Colab remembers the variables from cells you already ran, even if you delete those cells. If something works "sometimes", restart the session and run everything from top to bottom. 3. Load data The recommended way in this course is to read the file directly from its URL . It works the same for everyone and doesn't depend on your Drive: import pandas as pd url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/altamar_bookings_clean.csv" df = pd . read_csv ( url ) df . head () The URL of each file is on the datasets page. Two other options: Upload a file Read from your Google Drive from google.colab import files uploaded = files . upload () # opens a file picker df = pd . read_csv ( "your_file.csv" ) The file is deleted when the Colab session ends. from google.colab import drive drive . mount ( "/content/drive" ) df = pd . read_csv ( "/content/drive/MyDrive/folder/file.csv" ) Every team member would need the file at the same path, so for the case the URL is a better choice. 4. Libraries Colab already includes pandas, NumPy, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, and statsmodels. If you need something else, install it in a cell: ! pip install xgboost 5. Teamwork and sharing the case notebook One team member opens the case toolkit in Colab, saves a copy (File › Save a copy in Drive), and shares it with the rest of the team as Editor (the Share button, top right). Also share it with hizocar@gmail.com as Commenter , so the instructor can follow your progress and leave comments during the case clinics. Several people can open the same notebook in Colab, but if two people edit at the same time they can overwrite each other's changes. Split the work by section and let the team know before you run everything. 6. Before you submit the case Runtime › Restart session and run all finishes without errors. The data is read from a URL, not from a path on your computer or your Drive. Each section has a heading and text explaining what was done and what you conclude. You downloaded the file with File › Download › Download .ipynb .

docs.text: Open any session or the case toolkit and click Open in Colab at the top. The notebook opens in read-only mode . To edit it, go to File › Save a copy in Drive . Your copy is saved in the Colab Notebooks folder of your Google Drive.
docs.title: 1. Open a course notebook

docs.text: Action How Run the current cell and move to the next one Shift + Enter Run the whole notebook Runtime › Run all Start from scratch Runtime › Restart session and run all Add a code or text cell + Code and + Text buttons Order matters Colab remembers the variables from cells you already ran, even if you delete those cells. If something works "sometimes", restart the session and run everything from top to bottom.
docs.title: 2. Run code

docs.text: The recommended way in this course is to read the file directly from its URL . It works the same for everyone and doesn't depend on your Drive: import pandas as pd url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/altamar_bookings_clean.csv" df = pd . read_csv ( url ) df . head () The URL of each file is on the datasets page. Two other options: Upload a file Read from your Google Drive from google.colab import files uploaded = files . upload () # opens a file picker df = pd . read_csv ( "your_file.csv" ) The file is deleted when the Colab session ends. from google.colab import drive drive . mount ( "/content/drive" ) df = pd . read_csv ( "/content/drive/MyDrive/folder/file.csv" ) Every team member would need the file at the same path, so for the case the URL is a better choice.
docs.title: 3. Load data

docs.text: Colab already includes pandas, NumPy, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, and statsmodels. If you need something else, install it in a cell: ! pip install xgboost
docs.title: 4. Libraries

docs.text: One team member opens the case toolkit in Colab, saves a copy (File › Save a copy in Drive), and shares it with the rest of the team as Editor (the Share button, top right). Also share it with hizocar@gmail.com as Commenter , so the instructor can follow your progress and leave comments during the case clinics. Several people can open the same notebook in Colab, but if two people edit at the same time they can overwrite each other's changes. Split the work by section and let the team know before you run everything.
docs.title: 5. Teamwork and sharing the case notebook

docs.text: Runtime › Restart session and run all finishes without errors. The data is read from a URL, not from a path on your computer or your Drive. Each section has a heading and text explaining what was done and what you conclude. You downloaded the file with File › Download › Download .ipynb .
docs.title: 6. Before you submit the case

docs.text: Program Business Analytics I · From Python to Nonlinear Models is the first of two modules on data and AI for managers. It runs over six weeks: each week has a live session of 4 hours and a self-paced lab of about 2 hours , for 24 hours live and 12 hours self-paced. Who it is for Managers and professionals who make decisions with data but do not program, or have not programmed in years. The module asks for no mathematics beyond percentages and averages. It explains every model with pictures and simulators first, and with code second; the code is always written for you. What you will be able to do By the end of the module you can: open, run, and adjust a Python notebook in Google Colab, and read code well enough to know what it does; clean a business dataset, summarize it with tables and charts, and turn what you see into findings; build and evaluate a regression model to estimate a number (a price, a cost, a sales figure) and explain its drivers; build and evaluate a classification model to estimate a risk (a cancellation, a default, a churn), and choose a decision threshold with business costs; recognize when straight lines are not enough and use decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting ; compare models fairly, explain what drives their predictions, and present a recommendation to a management audience. Sessions Week Live session (4 h) Self-paced lab (2 h) 1 Reading data like a manager : notebooks, the Python you need to read code, and Altamar's two questions First look at Altamar 2 From raw data to insight : cleaning, summary tables, and charts that answer questions Seasons by hotel 3 Pricing with regression : train and test, coefficients, and errors in dollars A rate simulator 4 Predicting cancellations : probabilities, the confusion matrix, and thresholds chosen with money An overbooking policy 5 When lines are not enough : curves, decision trees, overfitting, and cross-validation Tuning a tree 6 Forests, boosting, and decisions : ensembles, what drives a prediction, and from model to recommendation Choosing and explaining a model Each live session has two blocks of about 100 minutes with a break: the first explains the idea with simulators and live examples; the second applies it to Altamar's data and ends with a case clinic where teams take the same step with their own case. Each self-paced lab is a notebook that runs top to bottom as it is. You change the settings marked ✏️, rerun, and answer the questions in the notebook. It ends with a graded quiz of five questions, due before the next live session. Assessment Component Weight Details Quizzes 30% Six quizzes, one per lab (5% each). Your first submission counts. Applied case 70% In teams, using the course toolkit. Notebook and executive presentation. See the applied case . Tools Everything runs in the browser : each session page has its code ready to run (press ▶), with nothing to install. For the applied case you will use Google Colab , which saves your work and lets your team share it. The Colab guide explains how to start.

The model gives a probability; the business decides from which probability to act. The usual 0.5 is rarely the cheapest. docs.text: One notebook that runs the whole analysis once you tell it which data to use and what to predict: it audits and cleans the data, draws the patterns, trains five models, compares them, and explains the best one. Regression or classification Runs in your browser or Colab No coding from scratch How to use it. Open the notebook in Colab with the Open in Colab button and save a copy in your team's Drive ( Colab guide ). Then: Change only the cells marked ✏️ : the settings at the top, the cleaning decisions in section 03, and the number of charts in section 04. Run every cell from top to bottom (in Colab: Runtime → Run all ). Under each section, write what the result means for your business in the ✍️ Your interpretation cell. That text is your deliverable ( case brief and rubric ). The defaults run Case A, TalentCo salaries. Each section links to the week where the idea was taught. Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the tools and defines the helpers the sections below use. In [1]: Copied! # Setup: run this cell first. for {c}", "Skipped: there is no such column", 0) continue v = pd.to_numeric(df[c], errors="coerce") bad = pd.Series(False, index=df.index) if lo is not None: bad |= v < lo if hi is not None: bad |= v > hi say = lambda v: f"{v:,.0f}" if float(v).is_integer() else f"{v:,}" rule = f"{c} outside {say(lo) if lo is not None else 'no minimum'} to {say(hi) if hi is not None else 'no maximum'}" if c == TARGET or IMPOSSIBLE_ACTION == "drop": df = df[~bad] note(f"Impossible values: {rule}", "Rows dropped", int(bad.sum())) else: df.loc[bad, c] = np.nan note(f"Impossible values: {rule}", "Made missing, then filled like any gap", int(bad.sum())) n = int(df[TARGET].isna().sum()) df = df[df[TARGET].notna()] if n: note(f"Missing target ({TARGET})", "Rows dropped: a row without the answer cannot teach or values", f"Filled with the {how} of the training rows, inside each model", int(n)) note("Rows kept", f"{len(df):,} of {n0:,} ({len(df) / n0:.1%})", len(df)) return df.reset_index(drop=True), fact def make_prep(scale=False, drop_first=False): """Fill gaps, scale numbers (optional) and one-hot encode text (20 most frequent labels + 'other').""" fill = "median" if FILL_MISSING == "median" else "most_frequent" num = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy=fill), StandardScaler()) if scale else SimpleImputer(strategy=fill) enc = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", max_categories=21, sparse_output=False, drop="first" if drop_first else None) cat = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"), enc) return ColumnTransformer([("num", num, NUM_COLS), ("cat", cat, CAT_COLS)], verbose_feature_names_out=False) def nice_name(name): for c in CAT_COLS: if name.startswith(c + "_"): v = name[len(c) + 1:] return f"{c} = {'(other labels)' if v == 'infrequent_sklearn' else v}" return name def base_labels(prep): """For each text input, the label its 0/1 columns are compared with (the one left out).""" if not CAT_COLS: return {} enc = prep.named_transformers_["cat"][-1] names = [nice_name(n) for n in prep.get_feature_names_out()] infrequent = enc.infrequent_categories_ if getattr(enc, "infrequent_categories_", None) else [None] * len(CAT_COLS) out = {} for c, cats, inf in zip(CAT_COLS, enc.categories_, infrequent): kept = [k for k in cats if inf is None or k not in inf] + (["(other labels)"] if inf is not None and len(inf) else []) shown = {n.split(" = ", 1)[1] for n in names if n.startswith(c + " = ")} out[c] = next((k for k in kept if k not in shown), kept[0]) return out def predict_score(model, X): """Probability of 1 (classification) or the predicted number (regression).""" return model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] if CLASSIFICATION else model.predict(X) def scores(model, X, y): """The test metrics of one model, as a dictionary.""" p = predict_score(model, X) if not CLASSIFICATION: return {"MAE": skm.mean_absolute_error(y, p), "RMSE": skm.mean_squared_error(y, p) ** 0.5, "R²": skm.r2_score(y, p)} yhat = (p >= 0.5).astype("int64") return {"Accuracy": skm.accuracy_score(y, yhat), "Precision": skm.precision_score(y, yhat, zero_division=0), "Recall": skm.recall_score(y, yhat), "F1": skm.f1_score(y, yhat), "AUC": skm.roc_auc_score(y, p) if y.nunique() == 2 else np.nan} def score_table(model): t = pd.DataFrame([scores(model, X_train, y_train), scores(model, X_test, y_test)], index=["Train", "Test"]) return t.round(3 if CLASSIFICATION else 2) def cost_curve(p, y): """Cost of every threshold from 0.01 to 0.99 with the costs in the settings.""" rows = [] for t in np.round(np.arange(0.01, 1.0, 0.01), 2): yhat = p >= t fn, fp = int(((~yhat) & (y == 1)).sum()), int((yhat & (y == 0)).sum()) rows.append({"Threshold": t, "Missed 1s (FN)": fn, "False alarms (FP)": fp, "Cost": fn * COST_FALSE_NEGATIVE + fp * COST_FALSE_POSITIVE}) return pd.DataFrame(rows) print("Ready. docs.text: Tell the toolkit which file to read and which column to predict. With TASK = "auto" it decides by itself: a 0/1 (yes/no) column means classification , any other number means regression . The two costs matter only for classification: they turn mistakes into money so section 07 can pick the cheapest decision rule ( week 4 ). To switch case, remove the # at the start of the lines of the case you want, then run everything again. For your own data (Case C), put the file's link in DATA_URL (or, in Colab, upload the file and write its name, e.g. "my_data.csv" ). In [2]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings: which data, and what to predict DATA_URL = DATA + "employee_compensation.csv" # Case A · TalentCo TARGET = "Salary" # the column to predict TASK = "auto" # "auto", "regression" (a number) or "classification" (yes/no, 0/1) ID_COLUMNS = [] # identifiers: never used to predict DROP_COLUMNS = [] # leakage (only known after the fact) or irrelevant columns TEST_SIZE = 0.25 # share of rows kept aside to test the models RANDOM_STATE = 42 # fixes the random shuffle so the results repeat # Classification only: what each kind of mistake costs, in money COST_FALSE_NEGATIVE = 4000 # missing a real 1 (e.g. approving a loan that will default) COST_FALSE_POSITIVE = 400 # a false alarm on a 0 (e.g. rejecting a client who would repay) CURRENCY = "USD" # Case B · FinTrust Bank (classification): remove the # on the next three lines # DATA_URL = DATA + "loan_default.csv" # TARGET = "default" # ID_COLUMNS = ["loan_id"] # Altamar Hotels (the sessions' data): the first two lines, then ONE of the two questions # DATA_URL = DATA + "altamar_bookings.csv" # ID_COLUMNS = ["booking_id"] # TARGET, DROP_COLUMNS = "adr", ["canceled"] # the nightly rate (regression) # TARGET, DROP_COLUMNS = "canceled", [] # cancellations (classification) # COST_FALSE_NEGATIVE, COST_FALSE_POSITIVE = 400, 300 # an empty room vs a guest walked to another hotel (week 4) # ✏️ Change these settings: which data, and what to predict DATA_URL = DATA + "employee_compensation.csv" # Case A · TalentCo TARGET = "Salary" # the column to predict TASK = "auto" # "auto", "regression" (a number) or "classification" (yes/no, 0/1) ID_COLUMNS = [] # identifiers: never used to predict DROP_COLUMNS = [] # leakage (only known after the fact) or irrelevant columns TEST_SIZE = 0.25 # share of rows kept aside to test the models RANDOM_STATE = 42 # fixes the random shuffle so the results repeat # Classification only: what each kind of mistake costs, in money COST_FALSE_NEGATIVE = 4000 # missing a real 1 (e.g. approving a loan that will default) COST_FALSE_POSITIVE = 400 # a false alarm on a 0 (e.g. rejecting a client who would repay) CURRENCY = "USD" # Case B · FinTrust Bank (classification): remove the # on the next three lines # DATA_URL = DATA + "loan_default.csv" # TARGET = "default" # ID_COLUMNS = ["loan_id"] # Altamar Hotels (the sessions' data): the first two lines, then ONE of the two questions # DATA_URL = DATA + "altamar_bookings.csv" # ID_COLUMNS = ["booking_id"] # TARGET, DROP_COLUMNS = "adr", ["canceled"] # the nightly rate (regression) # TARGET, DROP_COLUMNS = "canceled", [] # cancellations (classification) # COST_FALSE_NEGATIVE, COST_FALSE_POSITIVE = 400, 300 # an empty room vs a guest walked to another hotel (week 4) What the two costs mean. A false negative is a real 1 the model missed: a loan approved that defaults, a cancellation nobody expected. A false positive is a false alarm: a good client rejected, a room oversold to a guest who does turn up. Put a rough amount on each; the ratio between them is what matters.

docs.text: Your decisions, written as settings. They are pre-filled for TalentCo; the commented blocks show the ones for FinTrust and Altamar. Every decision needs a reason you could defend in front of a manager. docs.text: A tree asks yes/no questions and can bend where a line cannot. Its depth decides how detailed it gets: too shallow misses patterns, too deep memorises the training rows. Cross-validation tries depths 2 to 10 on five different slices of the training rows and picks the depth that does best on rows it did not learn from ( week 5 ). ▶ Interactive simulator: open this page on the course website to use it. The next cell runs the cross-validation (45 small trees) and draws the training score against the validation score for each depth. In [20]: Copied! docs.text: Two ways to combine many trees ( week 6 ). A random forest averages a hundred trees, each grown on a different sample of rows. Gradient boosting grows trees one after another, each fixing the errors of the ones before. They are usually the most accurate, and harder to explain. The next cell trains the random forest and prints its metrics. A big gap between train and test is normal for forests; judge it by the test row. In [23]: Copied! docs.text: Two views of the best model ( week 6 ). Permutation importance shuffles one input at a time on the test rows and measures how much worse the model gets: the bigger the drop, the more the model relies on that input. Partial dependence shows how the prediction moves, on average, as one number changes. The next cell computes the permutation importance of the best model (three shuffles per input) and draws it. docs.text: Fill in this checklist before you build the slides. It follows the rubric of the case brief , so each item is worth points. Lead the presentation with the answer, then the arguments, then the evidence ( the pyramid, week 6 ). Business framing (15%) ☐ The business question, in two lines. Write it here. ☐ Who uses the answer, and which decision it changes. Write it here. Data and patterns (20%) ☐ The problems you fixed and why. Point to the cleaning log in section 03 and justify the two biggest decisions. ☐ Three findings, each with its chart from section 04. 1. … 2. … 3. … Models and evaluation (25%) ☐ The recommended model and why. Name it, give its test metric next to the baseline's, and say why that metric fits the decision (for classification: the threshold and its cost). Interpretation and recommendations (25%) ☐ What drives the predictions. The top drivers from section 11, in business words. ☐ Three recommendations. Concrete enough to act on: who does what, and what it is worth. ☐ Limitations. What the data cannot tell you, what could make the model wrong next year, and what you would check next. Communication (15%) ☐ The slides lead with the answer and use only the few charts that carry it (10 slides at most).

docs.text: Applied case 70% of the grade In teams of 3 or 4 , you apply what the module covers to a business dataset and present your recommendations to a management audience. You do not program from scratch: the case toolkit is a notebook that runs the whole analysis once you tell it which data to use and what to predict. Your work is the business thinking: choosing, checking, interpreting, and recommending. Choose a case A · TalentCo (regression) B · FinTrust Bank (classification) C · Your own data What drives an employee's salary? TalentCo suspects its pay structure is inconsistent: people with similar experience earn different amounts depending on their department, region, or education. The people team wants to know which variables explain salary and whether there are gaps to fix. Data: employee_compensation.csv , about 10,000 employees. What to predict: Salary (annual salary in USD). Questions for your presentation: which factors explain salary, how large each effect is, and where the pay structure looks inconsistent. Which applicants will not repay their loan? FinTrust's default rate keeps rising. The risk team wants to flag applicants likely to default before approving them. Data: loan_default.csv , about 10,000 loans. What to predict: default (1 = defaulted). Questions for your presentation: which applicants are riskier and why, what threshold to use given the cost of approving a defaulter versus rejecting a good customer, and what the bank gains with the model. A dataset from your own organization or a public source, if it has at least 1,000 rows , a clear number or yes/no outcome to predict, and a business question a model can answer. Send a one-paragraph proposal to the instructor by the end of week 2. Do not use confidential data unless it is anonymized and you are allowed to share it. The data is dirty on purpose, as real data is. Finding and fixing its problems is part of the work. How it moves forward The case advances with the sessions. The last part of each live session is a case clinic where teams take the same step with their own data, running the matching sections of the case toolkit . What you hand in One week after session 6 , each team submits: The notebook : the case toolkit run on your data, with your settings, and your written interpretation under each section. It must run from top to bottom without errors. An executive presentation : at most 10 slides , built with the pyramid principle (the recommendation first, then the arguments, then the evidence). docs.text: The whole module answers two management questions. Rewrite them as you would present them to Altamar's general manager: the decision, who takes it, how often, and which column of the file holds the answer (and so whether it is regression or classification). ✏️ Your version (double-click to edit in Colab): Revenue question: … Who decides, and how often: … Column that answers it: … → regression or classification? … Operations question: … Who decides, and how often: … Column that answers it: … → regression or classification? … Show the answer One good version: Revenue: For each new booking, what nightly rate can we charge given the hotel, season, room and how far ahead the guest books? The revenue manager, every morning, for each hotel and room type. Column adr , a number: regression . Operations: Which of tonight's bookings are likely to cancel, so how many extra rooms can each hotel safely sell? The operations manager of each hotel, every day. Column canceled , yes or no: classification . The test of a good question: someone could act on the answer tomorrow, and you could check afterwards whether it was right.

Ready: the Python tools are loaded. 01 Altamar's two questions ¶ Altamar Hotels has three properties: a business hotel in Santiago , a beach hotel in Viña del Mar , and a lake-and-volcano hotel in Puerto Varas . You are now part of its management team, and two questions land on your desk: Revenue management: What nightly rate can we charge for a booking? The industry calls it the ADR , average daily rate. Operations: Which bookings will cancel, and how many rooms can we safely oversell? Neither question is answered once a year. Rates are set every morning for every hotel and room type; overbooking limits are set for every night. Small, daily decisions: exactly where data pays off. Why data, and not only experience? Altamar already has the answer key for thousands of past bookings: the rate each guest paid and whether they cancelled. A good revenue manager carries a feel for these patterns in their head. Data lets you check that feel, find the patterns nobody noticed, and apply them to every booking, every day, consistently. That is what machine learning does, and it fits in one picture. Machine learning in one picture. A model studies past bookings whose answer is known, learns a recipe from the inputs to the answer, and applies it to new bookings. Almost every line you will see does one of three things: it gives a name to a value , it combines values, or it shows a result. adr = 180.5 reads “let adr be 180.5” . The = is not an equation; it attaches a label to a value. Values come in a few types : numbers (with or without decimals), text, and yes/no. The same booking, as a code cell. type() tells you what kind of value a name holds: str is text, float a number with decimals, int a whole number, bool yes/no. To turn values into a sentence, Python uses f-strings : an f before the quotes, and any name inside { } is replaced by its value. {revenue:,.2f} means two decimals and a thousands comma . F-strings are how a notebook talks to a manager. In [10]: Copied! def stay_revenue ( adr , nights , discount = 0 ): """Room revenue of one stay, after an optional discount (0.10 = 10% off).""" total = adr * nights if discount > 0 : total = total * ( 1 - discount ) return round ( total , 2 ) print ( stay_revenue ( 180.5 , 3 )) print ( stay_revenue ( 180.5 , 3 , discount = 0.10 )) def stay_revenue(adr, nights, discount=0): """Room revenue of one stay, after an optional discount (0.10 = 10% off).""" total = adr * nights if discount > 0: total = total * (1 - discount) return round(total, 2) print(stay_revenue(180.5, 3)) print(stay_revenue(180.5, 3, discount=0.10)) 541.5 487.35 ✏️ Predict, then run. First: how many bookings does each hotel have? value_counts() counts how often each label appears. Look at the bottom of the list. In [17]: Copied! df [ "hotel" ] . value_counts () df["hotel"].value_counts() Out[17]: hotel Santiago 2378 Viña del Mar 1987 Puerto Varas 1439 SANTIAGO 110 Pto. SANTIAGO , Vina del Mar , VIÑA DEL MAR and Pto. Varas are the same hotels typed differently by different systems. To Python, a different spelling is a different hotel, so 256 bookings are counted apart from their hotel. Fixing that is week 2's first job; for today, keep it in mind when you read the next numbers. Next question: what is the average rate in each hotel? groupby("hotel") splits the table by hotel; ["adr"].mean() averages the rate in each group. In [19]: Copied! df . groupby ( "hotel" )[ "adr" ] . mean () . round ( 1 ) . sort_values ( ascending = False ) df.groupby("hotel")["adr"].mean().round(1).sort_values(ascending=False) Out[19]: hotel Puerto Varas 158.0 Pto. Varas 148.5 Viña del Mar 140.4 VIÑA DEL MAR 138.3 Vina del Mar 137.4 SANTIAGO 101.9 Santiago 100.3 Name: adr, dtype: float64 Last question: how often do bookings cancel? canceled is 1 for a cancelled booking and 0 otherwise, so its average is the share cancelled . :.1% prints it as a percentage. Then the same groupby pattern gives it by hotel. In [20]: Copied! overall = df [ "canceled" ] . mean () print ( f " { overall : .1% } of all bookings were cancelled: about 1 in { 1 / overall : .0f } ." ) print ( "By hotel, % c ancelled:" ) by_hotel = df . groupby ( "hotel" )[ "canceled" ] . mean () . sort_values ( ascending = False ) print (( by_hotel * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) overall = df["canceled"].mean() print(f"{overall:.1%} of all bookings were cancelled: about 1 in {1 / overall:.0f}.") print("By hotel, % cancelled:") by_hotel = df.groupby("hotel")["canceled"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False) print((by_hotel * 100).round(1).to_string()) 33.7% of all bookings were cancelled: about 1 in 3. By hotel, % cancelled: hotel VIÑA DEL MAR 51.4 Vina del Mar 48.6 Viña del Mar 40.9 Puerto Varas 37.5 Pto. Varas 35.1 Santiago 25.7 SANTIAGO 17.3 What a manager takes from this: One booking in three is cancelled. That is the room inventory operations has to protect with overbooking. Viña del Mar cancels most (about 41% under its main label) and Santiago least (about 26%). One overbooking policy for the whole group would be wrong for both. Puerto Varas charges the highest average rate (about USD 158), Santiago the lowest (about USD 100). But every number above is slightly off : split labels, free rooms and typos are all inside these averages. Who uses the answer: the operations manager of each hotel, every morning, when setting the overbooking limit. Column to predict: canceled (yes/no → classification). docs.title: Reading data like a manager

docs.text: Altamar Hotels has three properties: a business hotel in Santiago , a beach hotel in Viña del Mar , and a lake-and-volcano hotel in Puerto Varas . You are now part of its management team, and two questions land on your desk: Revenue management: What nightly rate can we charge for a booking? The industry calls it the ADR , average daily rate. Operations: Which bookings will cancel, and how many rooms can we safely oversell? Neither question is answered once a year. Rates are set every morning for every hotel and room type; overbooking limits are set for every night. Small, daily decisions: exactly where data pays off. Why data, and not only experience? Altamar already has the answer key for thousands of past bookings: the rate each guest paid and whether they cancelled. A good revenue manager carries a feel for these patterns in their head. Data lets you check that feel, find the patterns nobody noticed, and apply them to every booking, every day, consistently. That is what machine learning does, and it fits in one picture. Machine learning in one picture. A model studies past bookings whose answer is known, learns a recipe from the inputs to the answer, and applies it to new bookings. Hotel Days ahead Channel Nights Rate (USD) Cancelled? Viña del Mar 92 Online agency 3 → 202.58 yes Santiago 5 Online agency 2 → 115.22 yes … 6,058 more … Puerto Varas 30 Direct 4 → ? ? Left: the inputs , known when the guest books. Right: what we want to predict . The two question marks are two different kinds of prediction: Regression Classification The answer is a number a category, often yes or no Altamar asks What rate can we charge? (column adr ) Will this booking cancel? (column canceled ) Other examples room-nights sold next month, revenue per guest will this guest come back? is this review a complaint? In this module weeks 3, 5 and 6 weeks 4, 5 and 6 The first question to ask of any business problem: is the answer a number or a category? {"q": "The general manager asks: “How many room-nights will Puerto Varas sell next July?” What kind of question is this for a model?", "options": ["Regression: the answer is a number", "Classification: the answer is yes or no", "Neither: a model cannot learn this from past bookings"], "answer": 0, "why": "The answer is a quantity (room-nights), so it is a regression question, just like predicting the rate. “Will this booking cancel?” would be classification.", "code": false}

docs.text: You are reading a notebook : a page that mixes text cells (like this one) with code cells you can run. Each code cell has a run button; its result appears right under it. A code cell is a calculator that remembers. The next one describes one booking and computes its revenue. Lines that start with # are notes for humans: Python ignores them. Run it. In [2]: Copied! # One booking at Santiago adr = 120.5 # the nightly rate, in USD nights = 3 # length of the stay print ( "This stay brings" , adr * nights , "USD" ) # One booking at Santiago adr = 120.5 # the nightly rate, in USD nights = 3 # length of the stay print("This stay brings", adr * nights, "USD") This stay brings 361.5 USD Python now remembers adr and nights , so any later cell can use them. That memory (the kernel ) only knows what has already run, in the order it ran . Run cells out of order, run one twice, or delete one, and the memory no longer matches what you read on screen. Play with it: run the three cells below in different orders, run cell 2 twice, delete cell 1 and restart. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Business takeaway: a notebook is a report that other people will rerun. Before you share one (or hand in your case), use Restart and run all : in Colab, Runtime → Restart session and run all ; on this site, Run all . If it runs top to bottom without errors, your team and your grader see exactly what you saw. {"q": "Cell 1 says adr = 120.5. Cell 2 says adr = adr + 10. You run cell 1, then cell 2 twice, then print(adr). What appears?", "options": ["120.5", "130.5", "140.5", "An error"], "answer": 2, "why": "Memory keeps results, not cells: cell 2 added 10 twice, so adr is 140.5. Restart and run all would give 130.5, the number the code on screen suggests.", "code": false}
docs.title: 02 What a notebook is

docs.text: You don't need to write Python from scratch, but you need to read it. Almost every line you will see does one of three things: it gives a name to a value , it combines values, or it shows a result. adr = 180.5 reads “let adr be 180.5” . The = is not an equation; it attaches a label to a value. Values come in a few types : numbers (with or without decimals), text, and yes/no. Step through a booking below. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The same booking, as a code cell. type() tells you what kind of value a name holds: str is text, float a number with decimals, int a whole number, bool yes/no. To turn values into a sentence, Python uses f-strings : an f before the quotes, and any name inside { } is replaced by its value. {revenue:,.2f} means two decimals and a thousands comma . F-strings are how a notebook talks to a manager. In [3]: Copied! hotel = "Viña del Mar" # text (str): always in quotes adr = 180.5 # number with decimals (float): USD per night nights = 3 # whole number (int) parking = True # yes/no (bool): True or False, no quotes print ( type ( hotel ), type ( adr ), type ( nights ), type ( parking )) revenue = adr * nights print ( f "A { nights } -night stay at { hotel } at USD { adr } a night brings USD { revenue : ,.2f } ." ) hotel = "Viña del Mar" # text (str): always in quotes adr = 180.5 # number with decimals (float): USD per night nights = 3 # whole number (int) parking = True # yes/no (bool): True or False, no quotes print(type(hotel), type(adr), type(nights), type(parking)) revenue = adr * nights print(f"A {nights}-night stay at {hotel} at USD {adr} a night brings USD {revenue:,.2f}.") <class 'str'> <class 'float'> <class 'int'> <class 'bool'> A 3-night stay at Viña del Mar at USD 180.5 a night brings USD 541.50. ✏️ Your turn. Cells marked ✏️ have settings at the top, in CAPITALS. Change them, run the cell again, and read the new sentence. Try a long stay at Puerto Varas, or a one-night stay in Santiago. In [4]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings HOTEL = "Puerto Varas" ADR = 210.0 NIGHTS = 5 print ( f " { NIGHTS } nights at { HOTEL } , USD { ADR } a night: USD { ADR * NIGHTS : ,.2f } of room revenue." ) # ✏️ Change these settings HOTEL = "Puerto Varas" ADR = 210.0 NIGHTS = 5 print(f"{NIGHTS} nights at {HOTEL}, USD {ADR} a night: USD {ADR * NIGHTS:,.2f} of room revenue.") 5 nights at Puerto Varas, USD 210.0 a night: USD 1,050.00 of room revenue. Watch out: numbers that are really text. Numbers often arrive from a file or a web form as text, in quotes. Python will not do arithmetic with text; it stops with an error message. Errors are normal and informative: read the last line, it says what went wrong. Here we catch the error so the notebook keeps running, then fix it with float() . In [5]: Copied! rate_from_form = "180.5" # text, not a number: note the quotes try : print ( rate_from_form + 20 ) except TypeError as error : print ( "Python refuses:" , error ) print ( "After float():" , float ( rate_from_form ) + 20 ) rate_from_form = "180.5" # text, not a number: note the quotes try: print(rate_from_form + 20) except TypeError as error: print("Python refuses:", error) print("After float():", float(rate_from_form) + 20) Python refuses: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str After float(): 200.5
docs.title: 03 Reading Python: values and names

docs.text: One booking is a handful of values. A business has many, so Python groups them. A list keeps values in order , inside square brackets: for example, Santiago's rates for the next five nights. You reach an item by its position , and positions start at 0 : rates[0] is the first night, rates[-1] the last. Try the expressions below. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Lists are useful because Python can summarize them in one word: len counts, sum adds, max finds the highest. In [6]: Copied! rates = [ 95.0 , 120.5 , 88.0 , 142.0 , 110.0 ] # Santiago, next five nights, USD print ( "First night:" , rates [ 0 ], "| last night:" , rates [ - 1 ]) print ( f " { len ( rates ) } nights, total USD { sum ( rates ) : ,.2f } , highest USD { max ( rates ) } " ) print ( f "Average rate: USD { sum ( rates ) / len ( rates ) : .2f } " ) rates = [95.0, 120.5, 88.0, 142.0, 110.0] # Santiago, next five nights, USD print("First night:", rates[0], "| last night:", rates[-1]) print(f"{len(rates)} nights, total USD {sum(rates):,.2f}, highest USD {max(rates)}") print(f"Average rate: USD {sum(rates) / len(rates):.2f}") First night: 95.0 | last night: 110.0 5 nights, total USD 555.50, highest USD 142.0 Average rate: USD 111.10 A dictionary stores values under names instead of positions, inside curly braces. It is the natural shape of one record : one booking, with its hotel, channel, rate… You ask for booking["hotel"] , not for “item number 2”. Asking for a name that is not there is an error; .get() asks politely and accepts a fallback. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Here is that booking in code. It is a real one: the first row of Altamar's file, which you will meet again in block 2. In [7]: Copied! booking = { "booking_id" : "AH-200974" , "hotel" : "Viña del Mar" , "channel" : "Online travel agency" , "lead_time_days" : 92 , "nights" : 3 , "adr" : 202.58 , "canceled" : True , } print ( booking [ "hotel" ], "|" , booking [ "nights" ], "nights at USD" , booking [ "adr" ]) print ( "Country:" , booking . get ( "country" , "not recorded" )) booking = { "booking_id": "AH-200974", "hotel": "Viña del Mar", "channel": "Online travel agency", "lead_time_days": 92, "nights": 3, "adr": 202.58, "canceled": True, } print(booking["hotel"], "|", booking["nights"], "nights at USD", booking["adr"]) print("Country:", booking.get("country", "not recorded")) Viña del Mar | 3 nights at USD 202.58 Country: not recorded Now the key step: a list of dictionaries is a table . Each dictionary is a row; each name is a column. The pandas library turns it into a DataFrame , a spreadsheet-like table. Altamar's booking file is exactly this, with 6,060 rows and 20 columns. In [8]: Copied! few_bookings = [ { "hotel" : "Santiago" , "nights" : 2 , "adr" : 115.22 , "canceled" : True }, { "hotel" : "Viña del Mar" , "nights" : 3 , "adr" : 202.58 , "canceled" : True }, { "hotel" : "Puerto Varas" , "nights" : 5 , "adr" : 148.0 , "canceled" : False }, { "hotel" : "Santiago" , "nights" : 1 , "adr" : 98.5 , "canceled" : False }, ] tiny = pd . DataFrame ( few_bookings ) tiny few_bookings = [ {"hotel": "Santiago", "nights": 2, "adr": 115.22, "canceled": True}, {"hotel": "Viña del Mar", "nights": 3, "adr": 202.58, "canceled": True}, {"hotel": "Puerto Varas", "nights": 5, "adr": 148.0, "canceled": False}, {"hotel": "Santiago", "nights": 1, "adr": 98.5, "canceled": False}, ] tiny = pd.DataFrame(few_bookings) tiny Out[8]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } hotel nights adr canceled 0 Santiago 2 115.22 True 1 Viña del Mar 3 202.58 True 2 Puerto Varas 5 148.00 False 3 Santiago 1 98.50 False
docs.title: 04 Collections: lists and dictionaries

docs.text: Managers work with rules of thumb . Operations at Altamar has one: “bookings made more than 90 days ahead through an online travel agency are high cancellation risk.” In Python a rule is an if : a test that is either True or False , followed by what to do in each case. elif (“else if”) adds a second test, else catches everything left. Change the booking below and follow the dot through the rule. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The same rule as a code cell. Three details to read in it: == compares (while = assigns), and needs both tests, or needs one. And the indentation (the spaces at the start of a line) says which lines belong to each branch. In [9]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings CHANNEL = "Online travel agency" # or "Direct", "Corporate", "Travel agent" LEAD_TIME_DAYS = 120 if CHANNEL == "Online travel agency" and LEAD_TIME_DAYS > 90 : risk = "high" elif CHANNEL == "Online travel agency" or LEAD_TIME_DAYS > 90 : risk = "watch" else : risk = "low" print ( f "Booked via { CHANNEL } , { LEAD_TIME_DAYS } days ahead: cancellation risk { risk } ." ) # ✏️ Change these settings CHANNEL = "Online travel agency" # or "Direct", "Corporate", "Travel agent" LEAD_TIME_DAYS = 120 if CHANNEL == "Online travel agency" and LEAD_TIME_DAYS > 90: risk = "high" elif CHANNEL == "Online travel agency" or LEAD_TIME_DAYS > 90: risk = "watch" else: risk = "low" print(f"Booked via {CHANNEL}, {LEAD_TIME_DAYS} days ahead: cancellation risk {risk}.") Booked via Online travel agency, 120 days ahead: cancellation risk high. A function packages a calculation so you can reuse it for any booking: write it once, call it a thousand times. def starts it, the names in brackets are its inputs , and return sends back its output . An input with = has a default : if you don't pass it, Python uses that value. Change the inputs and watch Altamar's revenue function work. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The function in code. Read it top to bottom: full price first, then the discount if there is one, then round to cents. The two print lines call it twice, without and with a 10% discount. In [10]: Copied! def stay_revenue ( adr , nights , discount = 0 ): """Room revenue of one stay, after an optional discount (0.10 = 10% off).""" total = adr * nights if discount > 0 : total = total * ( 1 - discount ) return round ( total , 2 ) print ( stay_revenue ( 180.5 , 3 )) print ( stay_revenue ( 180.5 , 3 , discount = 0.10 )) def stay_revenue(adr, nights, discount=0): """Room revenue of one stay, after an optional discount (0.10 = 10% off).""" total = adr * nights if discount > 0: total = total * (1 - discount) return round(total, 2) print(stay_revenue(180.5, 3)) print(stay_revenue(180.5, 3, discount=0.10)) 541.5 487.35 ✏️ Predict, then run. Before you press run, write down the revenue you expect. A long-stay discount of 12% on a 7-night stay at USD 150: is it more or less than USD 1,000? In [11]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings, predict the result, then run ADR = 150.0 NIGHTS = 7 DISCOUNT = 0.12 # a long-stay discount of 12% revenue = stay_revenue ( ADR , NIGHTS , DISCOUNT ) print ( f " { NIGHTS } nights at USD { ADR } with { DISCOUNT : .0% } off: USD { revenue : ,.2f } " ) # ✏️ Change these settings, predict the result, then run ADR = 150.0 NIGHTS = 7 DISCOUNT = 0.12 # a long-stay discount of 12% revenue = stay_revenue(ADR, NIGHTS, DISCOUNT) print(f"{NIGHTS} nights at USD {ADR} with {DISCOUNT:.0%} off: USD {revenue:,.2f}") 7 nights at USD 150.0 with 12% off: USD 924.00 {"q": "What does stay_revenue(100.0, 4, discount=0.25) return?", "options": ["400.0", "300.0", "375.0", "100.0"], "answer": 1, "why": "Full price is 100 × 4 = 400. A discount of 0.25 keeps 75% of it: 400 × 0.75 = 300.0.", "code": true}
docs.title: 05 Rules and functions

docs.text: Ten minutes. When we come back: the real data. Everything so far was one booking at a time; Altamar has thousands.
docs.title: ☕ Break

docs.text: The rule and the function above work on one booking. To apply them to 6,060 bookings, you could write a loop : for each booking, do this . It works, but it is slow and long to read. The libraries NumPy and pandas do it differently: you write the operation once, for the whole column , and they apply it to every row at once. Race the two below. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Both ways in code, on six rates. The loop needs three lines and visits each booking; the array version is one line. Same result. In [12]: Copied! rates_list = [ 95.0 , 120.5 , 88.0 , 142.0 , 110.0 , 185.0 ] new_rates = [] # the loop way: one booking at a time for r in rates_list : new_rates . append ( round ( r * 1.08 , 2 )) print ( "Loop: " , new_rates ) rates = np . array ( rates_list ) # the array way: the whole column at once print ( "Array:" , ( rates * 1.08 ) . round ( 2 )) rates_list = [95.0, 120.5, 88.0, 142.0, 110.0, 185.0] new_rates = [] # the loop way: one booking at a time for r in rates_list: new_rates.append(round(r * 1.08, 2)) print("Loop: ", new_rates) rates = np.array(rates_list) # the array way: the whole column at once print("Array:", (rates * 1.08).round(2)) Loop: [102.6, 130.14, 95.04, 153.36, 118.8, 199.8] Array: [102.6 130.14 95.04 153.36 118.8 199.8 ] Business takeaway: from now on, almost every line of code works on a whole column. df["adr"] * 1.08 raises every rate in the file by 8%; df["adr"].mean() averages all of them. One line, any number of bookings. You will rarely see a loop again in this module.

docs.title: 07 Meet the data

docs.text: Now the questions a manager would ask on day one, one line each. First: how many bookings does each hotel have? value_counts() counts how often each label appears. Look at the bottom of the list. In [17]: Copied! df [ "hotel" ] . value_counts () df["hotel"].value_counts() Out[17]: hotel Santiago 2378 Viña del Mar 1987 Puerto Varas 1439 SANTIAGO 110 Pto. Varas 74 VIÑA DEL MAR 37 Vina del Mar 35 Name: count, dtype: int64 A chart makes the problem impossible to miss. In [18]: Copied! counts = df [ "hotel" ] . value_counts () . sort_values () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) counts . plot . barh ( ax = ax , color = "#c85a24" ) ax . set_title ( "Altamar has three hotels, but the file lists seven" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Number of bookings" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "" ) plt . show () counts = df["hotel"].value_counts().sort_values() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5)) counts.plot.barh(ax=ax, color="#c85a24") ax.set_title("Altamar has three hotels, but the file lists seven") ax.set_xlabel("Number of bookings") ax.set_ylabel("") plt.show() Three hotels, seven labels. SANTIAGO , Vina del Mar , VIÑA DEL MAR and Pto. Varas are the same hotels typed differently by different systems. To Python, a different spelling is a different hotel, so 256 bookings are counted apart from their hotel. Fixing that is week 2's first job; for today, keep it in mind when you read the next numbers. Next question: what is the average rate in each hotel? groupby("hotel") splits the table by hotel; ["adr"].mean() averages the rate in each group. In [19]: Copied! df . groupby ( "hotel" )[ "adr" ] . mean () . round ( 1 ) . sort_values ( ascending = False ) df.groupby("hotel")["adr"].mean().round(1).sort_values(ascending=False) Out[19]: hotel Puerto Varas 158.0 Pto. Varas 148.5 Viña del Mar 140.4 VIÑA DEL MAR 138.3 Vina del Mar 137.4 SANTIAGO 101.9 Santiago 100.3 Name: adr, dtype: float64 Last question: how often do bookings cancel? canceled is 1 for a cancelled booking and 0 otherwise, so its average is the share cancelled . :.1% prints it as a percentage. Then the same groupby pattern gives it by hotel. In [20]: Copied! overall = df [ "canceled" ] . mean () print ( f " { overall : .1% } of all bookings were cancelled: about 1 in { 1 / overall : .0f } ." ) print ( "By hotel, % c ancelled:" ) by_hotel = df . groupby ( "hotel" )[ "canceled" ] . mean () . sort_values ( ascending = False ) print (( by_hotel * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) overall = df["canceled"].mean() print(f"{overall:.1%} of all bookings were cancelled: about 1 in {1 / overall:.0f}.") print("By hotel, % cancelled:") by_hotel = df.groupby("hotel")["canceled"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False) print((by_hotel * 100).round(1).to_string()) 33.7% of all bookings were cancelled: about 1 in 3. By hotel, % cancelled: hotel VIÑA DEL MAR 51.4 Vina del Mar 48.6 Viña del Mar 40.9 Puerto Varas 37.5 Pto. Varas 35.1 Santiago 25.7 SANTIAGO 17.3 What a manager takes from this: One booking in three is cancelled. That is the room inventory operations has to protect with overbooking. Viña del Mar cancels most (about 41% under its main label) and Santiago least (about 26%). One overbooking policy for the whole group would be wrong for both. Puerto Varas charges the highest average rate (about USD 158), Santiago the lowest (about USD 100). But every number above is slightly off : split labels, free rooms and typos are all inside these averages. Week 2 cleans the data first, then repeats these questions.

docs.text: Your applied case advances with the sessions. This week's step: the question . With your team: Form your team (3 or 4 people) and choose a case : A · TalentCo (what drives a salary: regression), B · FinTrust Bank (who will not repay: classification), or C · your own data. Write the business question in two lines , and who would use the answer , for which decision. Open the case toolkit in Colab (button at the top of the page; see the Colab guide ), choose your dataset in section 00 Settings , and run section 01 Load and first look : a first look at your data, like ours at Altamar. An example, written for Altamar. Notice it names a decision and a person, not a technique. Question: Which bookings are likely to cancel, so that each hotel can decide how many rooms to oversell every night? Who uses the answer: the operations manager of each hotel, every morning, when setting the overbooking limit. Column to predict: canceled (yes/no → classification). A weak version would be “analyse cancellations with machine learning” : no decision, no user, nothing to check at the end. ✏️ Your team's version (in Colab, double-click this cell to edit it): Question: … Who uses the answer, for which decision: … Column to predict: … (a number → regression; a category → classification) One thing we noticed in the first look at the data: … Before next week: do the lab, First look at Altamar , and its graded quiz. In week 2, From raw data to insight , we fix the seven hotel labels, the free rooms and the typos, and we find out that every hotel has its own seasons.

docs.text: The general manager wants to know how Altamar's three hotels really differ: when each one is expensive, when it is cheap, and which bookings are likely to cancel. In this lab you slice the clean file yourself, change the settings, and write three findings with numbers the code prints. ≈ 2 hours 5 tasks Runs in your browser Graded quiz From the live session: The raw file had duplicates, misspellings, impossible rates and gaps. Cleaning took it from 6,060 to 5,964 bookings, each decision written in a cleaning log. A mask ( df["hotel"] == "Santiago" ) keeps the rows you need; & means AND, | means OR. groupby and pivot tables answer "what is the average X for each Y?"; the mean of canceled is the cancellation rate. Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the clean file and adds the arrival month. In [1]: Copied! import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter sns . set_theme ( style = "whitegrid" ) pd . set_option ( "display.max_columns" , 20 ) pd . set_option ( "display.width" , 120 ) pd . set_option ( "display.max_colwidth" , 80 ) DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/" HOTELS = [ "Santiago" , "Viña del Mar" , "Puerto Varas" ] ROOMS = [ "Standard" , "Superior" , "Suite" ] MONTHS = [ "Jan" , "Feb" , "Mar" , "Apr" , "May" , "Jun" , "Jul" , "Aug" , "Sep" , "Oct" , "Nov" , "Dec" ] df = pd . read_csv ( DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv" ) df [ "arrival_month" ] = pd . to_datetime ( df [ "arrival_date" ]) . dt . month print ( f " { len ( df ) : , } bookings, cancellation rate { df [ 'canceled' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid") pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 20) pd.set_option("display.width", 120) pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 80) DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/" HOTELS = ["Santiago", "Viña del Mar", "Puerto Varas"] ROOMS = ["Standard", "Superior", "Suite"] MONTHS = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"] df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv") df["arrival_month"] = pd.to_datetime(df["arrival_date"]).dt.month print(f"{len(df):,} bookings, cancellation rate {df['canceled'].mean():.1%}") 5,964 bookings, cancellation rate 33.7%

docs.text: Pick a hotel and a range of arrival months, and compare those bookings with the same hotel's other months. The code builds two masks and combines them with & , as in the simulator. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Change the settings and run the cell. It prints the number of bookings, the average rate and the cancellation rate inside and outside your months. In [2]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings HOTEL = "Viña del Mar" # "Santiago", "Viña del Mar" or "Puerto Varas" FIRST_MONTH = 1 # 1 = January ... 12 = December LAST_MONTH = 2 at_hotel = df [ "hotel" ] == HOTEL in_months = df [ "arrival_month" ] . between ( FIRST_MONTH , LAST_MONTH ) season , rest = df [ at_hotel & in_months ], df [ at_hotel & ~ in_months ] period = f " { MONTHS [ FIRST_MONTH - 1 ] } – { MONTHS [ LAST_MONTH - 1 ] } " for label , part in [( period , season ), ( "other months" , rest )]: print ( f " { HOTEL } , { label : <12 } { len ( part ) : >5, } bookings · average rate USD { part [ 'adr' ] . mean () : >4.0f } · cancellation { part [ 'canceled' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) # ✏️ Change these settings HOTEL = "Viña del Mar" # "Santiago", "Viña del Mar" or "Puerto Varas" FIRST_MONTH = 1 # 1 = January ... 12 = December LAST_MONTH = 2 at_hotel = df["hotel"] == HOTEL in_months = df["arrival_month"].between(FIRST_MONTH, LAST_MONTH) season, rest = df[at_hotel & in_months], df[at_hotel & ~in_months] period = f"{MONTHS[FIRST_MONTH - 1]}–{MONTHS[LAST_MONTH - 1]}" for label, part in [(period, season), ("other months", rest)]: print(f"{HOTEL}, {label: < 12} {len(part):>5,} bookings · average rate USD {part['adr'].mean():>4.0f} · cancellation {part['canceled'].mean():.1%}") Viña del Mar, Jan–Feb 828 bookings · average rate USD 187 · cancellation 51.1% Viña del Mar, other months 1,194 bookings · average rate USD 107 · cancellation 34.3% Think about it. Run Viña del Mar for January–February, then for June–August. Then run Santiago for January–February. Which hotel is expensive in the summer, and which one is cheap? Do cancellations move with the rate? Show the answer Viña del Mar in January–February averages about 187 USD a night against about 107 in other months, and 51% of those bookings cancel against 34%. Summer at the beach is expensive and also uncertain: guests book early, shop around and cancel. Santiago is the opposite: January–February are its cheapest months (about 79 USD), because business travellers are on holiday. Same months, opposite seasons.
docs.title: 01 One hotel, one season

docs.text: One table answers the question for every hotel and month at once: average rate with hotels on the rows and months on the columns. The colours make the seasons visible at a glance. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Run the cell, then try VALUE = "canceled" to see the cancellation rate instead, and AGG = "median" to see the typical booking instead of the average. In [3]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings VALUE = "adr" # "adr" (nightly rate) or "canceled" (cancellation rate) AGG = "mean" # "mean" or "median" table = df . pivot_table ( index = "hotel" , columns = "arrival_month" , values = VALUE , aggfunc = AGG ) . loc [ HOTELS ] table . columns = MONTHS plt . figure ( figsize = ( 9 , 3.2 )) sns . heatmap ( table , annot = True , fmt = ".0f" if VALUE == "adr" else ".0%" , cmap = "YlOrRd" , cbar = False ) plt . title ( f " { AGG . capitalize () } of { VALUE } by hotel and arrival month" ) plt . xlabel ( "Arrival month" ) plt . ylabel ( "" ) plt . show () # ✏️ Change these settings VALUE = "adr" # "adr" (nightly rate) or "canceled" (cancellation rate) AGG = "mean" # "mean" or "median" table = df.pivot_table(index="hotel", columns="arrival_month", values=VALUE, aggfunc=AGG).loc[HOTELS] table.columns = MONTHS plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3.2)) sns.heatmap(table, annot=True, fmt=".0f" if VALUE == "adr" else ".0%", cmap="YlOrRd", cbar=False) plt.title(f"{AGG.capitalize()} of {VALUE} by hotel and arrival month") plt.xlabel("Arrival month") plt.ylabel("") plt.show() idxmax() and idxmin() give the column with the highest and lowest value in each row: each hotel's peak and low month. In [4]: Copied! for hotel in HOTELS : row = table . loc [ hotel ] print ( f " { hotel : <13 } peak { row . idxmax () } ( { row . max () : .2f } ) · low { row . idxmin () } ( { row . min () : .2f } ) · peak ÷ low { row . max () / row . min () : .1f } x" ) for hotel in HOTELS: row = table.loc[hotel] print(f"{hotel: < 13} peak {row.idxmax()} ({row.max():.2f}) · low {row.idxmin()} ({row.min():.2f}) · peak ÷ low {row.max() / row.min():.1f}x") Santiago peak Oct (113.87) · low Feb (76.35) · peak ÷ low 1.5x Viña del Mar peak Jan (192.78) · low Jun (84.56) · peak ÷ low 2.3x Puerto Varas peak Jan (198.28) · low May (99.21) · peak ÷ low 2.0x Think about it. With VALUE = "adr" , what are each hotel's peak and low months, and how many times more is a peak night worth than a low one? What would happen if Altamar used one price calendar for the whole group? Show the answer Viña del Mar peaks in January (about 193 USD) and bottoms out in June (85): 2.3 times. Puerto Varas peaks in January (198) with a second peak in July (175, winter holidays), and is lowest in May (99). Santiago peaks in October (114) and is lowest in February (76): only 1.5 times, and in the opposite direction. One group calendar would raise Santiago's prices exactly when its business guests are away, and leave money on the table at the beach in January.
docs.title: 02 A pivot table: hotel × month

docs.text: weekend_nights counts the Friday and Saturday nights of a stay. The cell labels every booking as Weekdays only , Weekend only , or Mixed , and compares the average rate by hotel. In [5]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings CUSTOMER = "All" # "All", "Business", "Leisure" or "Group" data = df if CUSTOMER == "All" else df [ df [ "customer_type" ] == CUSTOMER ] stay = np . select ([ data [ "weekend_nights" ] == data [ "nights" ], data [ "weekend_nights" ] == 0 ], [ "Weekend only" , "Weekdays only" ], "Mixed" ) by_stay = data . assign ( stay = stay ) . pivot_table ( index = "hotel" , columns = "stay" , values = "adr" , aggfunc = "mean" ) . loc [ HOTELS ] print ( by_stay [[ "Weekdays only" , "Mixed" , "Weekend only" ]] . round ( 1 ), " \n " ) for hotel in HOTELS : change = by_stay . loc [ hotel , "Weekend only" ] / by_stay . loc [ hotel , "Weekdays only" ] - 1 print ( f " { hotel : <13 } a weekend-only stay costs { change : +.0% } compared with a weekdays-only stay" ) # ✏️ Change these settings CUSTOMER = "All" # "All", "Business", "Leisure" or "Group" data = df if CUSTOMER == "All" else df[df["customer_type"] == CUSTOMER] stay = np.select([data["weekend_nights"] == data["nights"], data["weekend_nights"] == 0], ["Weekend only", "Weekdays only"], "Mixed") by_stay = data.assign(stay=stay).pivot_table(index="hotel", columns="stay", values="adr", aggfunc="mean").loc[HOTELS] print(by_stay[["Weekdays only", "Mixed", "Weekend only"]].round(1), "\n") for hotel in HOTELS: change = by_stay.loc[hotel, "Weekend only"] / by_stay.loc[hotel, "Weekdays only"] - 1 print(f"{hotel: < 13} a weekend-only stay costs {change:+.0%} compared with a weekdays-only stay") stay Weekdays only Mixed Weekend only hotel Santiago 109.2 99.7 84.9 Viña del Mar 124.3 141.2 155.9 Puerto Varas 152.1 155.8 172.6 Santiago a weekend-only stay costs -22% compared with a weekdays-only stay Viña del Mar a weekend-only stay costs +25% compared with a weekdays-only stay Puerto Varas a weekend-only stay costs +13% compared with a weekdays-only stay Think about it. Which hotel is cheaper on weekends, and which ones are pricier? Is it only because different customers stay on weekends? Try CUSTOMER = "Business" and CUSTOMER = "Leisure" . Explain the pattern from the business, not from the data. Show the answer Santiago's weekend-only stays cost about 22% less than weekday stays; Viña del Mar's cost about 25% more and Puerto Varas's about 13% more. The pattern holds for business and for leisure guests separately, so it is not just a different mix of customers. A city business hotel empties on Friday, when its corporate guests fly home, and discounts to fill rooms; beach and lake hotels fill on weekends, when leisure demand peaks. The same Saturday night is a low-demand night in Santiago and a high-demand night at the coast.
docs.title: 03 Weekends: who pays more?

docs.text: Operations wants to know whether bookings made far ahead are riskier. The cell cuts lead_time_days into buckets with pd.cut and computes the cancellation rate in each. EDGES are the upper limits of the buckets; the last bucket is "everything above". In [6]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings EDGES = [ 7 , 30 , 90 ] # buckets 0–7, 8–30, 31–90 and over 90 days. Try [7, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180] limits = [ - 1 ] + EDGES + [ np . inf ] labels = [ f " { a + 1 } – { b } " for a , b in zip ( limits [: - 2 ], limits [ 1 : - 1 ])] + [ f "over { EDGES [ - 1 ] } " ] labels [ 0 ] = f "0– { EDGES [ 0 ] } " bucket = pd . cut ( df [ "lead_time_days" ], bins = limits , labels = labels ) by_lead = df . groupby ( bucket , observed = True )[ "canceled" ] . agg ([ "count" , "mean" ]) ax = by_lead [ "mean" ] . plot . bar ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 ), rot = 0 ) ax . bar_label ( ax . containers [ 0 ], labels = [ f " { v : .0% } " for v in by_lead [ "mean" ]]) ax . yaxis . set_major_formatter ( PercentFormatter ( 1 )) plt . title ( "Do bookings made further ahead cancel more?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Days between booking and arrival" ) plt . ylabel ( "Cancellation rate" ) plt . show () # ✏️ Change these settings EDGES = [7, 30, 90] # buckets 0–7, 8–30, 31–90 and over 90 days. Try [7, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180] limits = [-1] + EDGES + [np.inf] labels = [f"{a + 1}–{b}" for a, b in zip(limits[:-2], limits[1:-1])] + [f"over {EDGES[-1]}"] labels[0] = f"0–{EDGES[0]}" bucket = pd.cut(df["lead_time_days"], bins=limits, labels=labels) by_lead = df.groupby(bucket, observed=True)["canceled"].agg(["count", "mean"]) ax = by_lead["mean"].plot.bar(figsize=(8, 4.5), rot=0) ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], labels=[f"{v:.0%}" for v in by_lead["mean"]]) ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1)) plt.title("Do bookings made further ahead cancel more?") plt.xlabel("Days between booking and arrival") plt.ylabel("Cancellation rate") plt.show() The same numbers as a table: count is how many bookings stand behind each rate. In [7]: Copied! by_lead . assign ( rate = by_lead [ "mean" ] . map ( " {:.1%} " . format )) . drop ( columns = "mean" ) by_lead.assign(rate=by_lead["mean"].map("{:.1%}".format)).drop(columns="mean") Out[7]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } count rate lead_time_days 0–7 1047 15.7% 8–30 1963 19.3% 31–90 1945 48.9% over 90 1009 51.3% Think about it. With the four starting buckets, the rate rises from 16% to about 50% and then flattens. Now try EDGES = [7, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180] . What happens after 90 days? If you drew a single straight line through these bars, what would it predict for a booking made 300 days ahead? Show the answer The risk is not "the earlier, the riskier". It climbs to about 70% for bookings made 61–90 days ahead and then falls back to about 40% for bookings made more than four months ahead: a peak around three months out. A straight line would keep rising forever and predict that the earliest bookings are the riskiest, which is wrong. **A straight line will struggle** with this shape; week 5 brings models that can bend. (Check the `count` column too: buckets with few bookings give noisy rates.)
docs.title: 04 Booking early, cancelling more?

1]} (USD {by_month.max():.0f}), low month {MONTHS[by_month.idxmin() - 1]} (USD {by_month.min():.0f})") print(f"Weekend-only stays USD {weekend:.0f} vs weekdays-only USD {weekday:.0f}") print(f"Cancellation: highest {by_channel.index[-1]} {by_channel.iloc[-1]:.1%}, lowest {by_channel.index[0]} {by_channel.iloc[0]:.1%}") Puerto Varas: 1,493 bookings, average rate USD 156, cancellation 37.5% Peak month Jan (USD 198), low month May (USD 99) Weekend-only stays USD 173 vs weekdays-only USD 152 Cancellation: highest Online travel agency 42.7%, lowest Corporate 12.9% Your three findings (double-click to edit this cell): What we see: … → What it means: … → Next: … What we see: … → What it means: … → Next: … What we see: … → What it means: … → Next: … Show an example for Puerto Varas **Two high seasons, not one.** Puerto Varas's average rate peaks in January (198 USD) and again in July (175 USD, winter holidays), against 99 USD in May. *For revenue management:* July deserves its own pricing and marketing plan, like the summer. *Next:* does July sell out, or is there room to raise the rate further? In [21]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . boxplot ( df , x = "room_type" , y = "adr" , order = ROOMS ) plt . title ( "Do rates differ by room type?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Room type" ) plt . ylabel ( "Nightly rate (USD)" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) sns.boxplot(df, x="room_type", y="adr", order=ROOMS) plt.title("Do rates differ by room type?") plt.xlabel("Room type") plt.ylabel("Nightly rate (USD)") plt.show() What it shows: the median climbs from about 98 USD for a standard room to 126 for a superior and 179 for a suite. The boxes overlap: a suite in Santiago's low season can cost less than a standard room at the beach in January. The room matters, but so do the hotel and the month. Which channel cancels most? A bar chart of the cancellation rate: the mean of canceled in each channel. In [22]: Copied! order = cancel_by_channel . index # sorted from lowest to highest rate plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax = sns . barplot ( df , x = "channel" , y = "canceled" , order = order , errorbar = None ) ax . bar_label ( ax . containers [ 0 ], fmt = " {:.1%} " ) ax . yaxis . set_major_formatter ( PercentFormatter ( 1 )) plt . title ( "Which channel cancels most?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Booking channel" ) plt . ylabel ( "Cancellation rate" ) plt . show () order = cancel_by_channel.index # sorted from lowest to highest rate plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) ax = sns.barplot(df, x="channel", y="canceled", order=order, errorbar=None) ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], fmt="{:.1%}") ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1)) plt.title("Which channel cancels most?") plt.xlabel("Booking channel") plt.ylabel("Cancellation rate") plt.show() What it shows: 42.2% of online travel agency bookings cancel, almost three times the 15.6% of corporate bookings. For operations, a room sold through an OTA is a much less certain room. Does each hotel have its own seasons? This is the key chart of the week: the average rate by arrival month, one line per hotel . In [23]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . lineplot ( df , x = "arrival_month" , y = "adr" , hue = "hotel" , hue_order = HOTELS , errorbar = None , marker = "o" ) plt . xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 ), MONTHS ) plt . title ( "Does each hotel have its own seasons?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Arrival month" ) plt . ylabel ( "Average nightly rate (USD)" ) plt . legend ( title = "Hotel" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) sns.lineplot(df, x="arrival_month", y="adr", hue="hotel", hue_order=HOTELS, errorbar=None, marker="o") plt.xticks(range(1, 13), MONTHS) plt.title("Does each hotel have its own seasons?") plt.xlabel("Arrival month") plt.ylabel("Average nightly rate (USD)") plt.legend(title="Hotel") plt.show() What it shows: three hotels, three calendars. Viña del Mar and Puerto Varas peak in January and February at about 190–200 USD; Puerto Varas peaks again in July, with the winter holidays. Santiago does the opposite: it dips in the summer (76 USD in February), when business travellers are on holiday, and peaks in October with conferences. Hold on to this chart. In weeks 3 and 4 we fit straight lines; in week 5 we will see why one straight line through "month" cannot draw three different curves. 08 From charts to findings ¶ A finding is not a number. It is a number plus what it means for someone : What we see (with the number) → what it means for the business → what to check next . First, the numbers we will quote, printed by the code, so nobody has to trust our memory: In [24]: Copied! monthly = df . pivot_table ( index = "arrival_month" , columns = "hotel" , values = "adr" , aggfunc = "mean" ) for hotel in HOTELS : peak , low = monthly [ hotel ] . idxmax (), monthly [ hotel ] . idxmin () print ( f " { hotel : <13 } peak { MONTHS [ peak - 1 ] } USD { monthly [ hotel ] . max () : .0f } , low { MONTHS [ low - 1 ] } USD { monthly [ hotel ] . min () : .0f } " ) print () print ( f "Cancellation: online travel agency { cancel_by_channel [ 'Online travel agency' ] : .1% } , corporate { cancel_by_channel [ 'Corporate' ] : .1% } " ) suite_premium = rate_table [ "Suite" ] / rate_table [ "Standard" ] print ( "Suite rate ÷ standard rate:" , ", " . join ( f " { h } { suite_premium [ h ] : .2f } x" for h in HOTELS )) monthly = df.pivot_table(index="arrival_month", columns="hotel", values="adr", aggfunc="mean") for hotel in HOTELS: peak, low = monthly[hotel].idxmax(), monthly[hotel].idxmin() print(f"{hotel: < 13} peak {MONTHS[peak - 1]} USD {monthly[hotel].max():.0f}, low {MONTHS[low - 1]} USD {monthly[hotel].min():.0f}") print() print(f"Cancellation: online travel agency {cancel_by_channel['Online travel agency']:.1%}, corporate {cancel_by_channel['Corporate']:.1%}") suite_premium = rate_table["Suite"] / rate_table["Standard"] print("Suite rate ÷ standard rate:", ", ".join(f"{h} {suite_premium[h]:.2f}x" for h in HOTELS)) Santiago peak Oct USD 114, low Feb USD 76 Viña del Mar peak Jan USD 193, low Jun USD 85 Puerto Varas peak Jan USD 198, low May USD 99 Cancellation: online travel agency 42.2%, corporate 15.6% Suite rate ÷ standard rate: Santiago 1.82x, Viña del Mar 1.98x, Puerto Varas 1.93x Finding 1 · Every hotel has its own season. Viña del Mar's average rate goes from 193 USD in January to 85 USD in June; Santiago moves the other way, from 76 USD in February to 114 in October. For revenue management: one price calendar for the group would undercharge the beach in summer and overcharge the city. Next: a rate model must let each hotel have its own months. Finding 2 · Online travel agency bookings cancel most. 42.2% of them cancel, against 15.6% of corporate bookings. For operations: how many rooms we can oversell depends on the channel mix of each night. Next: week 4 predicts cancellations booking by booking. Finding 3 · Suites earn about twice a standard room. The suite rate is 1.8 to 2.0 times the standard rate at every hotel. For sales: upgrading even a few bookings is worth testing. Next: how many suites go unsold? Correlation is not causation. Finding 2 says OTA bookings cancel more ; it does not say the OTA makes guests cancel. Look again at the cancellation table by channel and customer type from section 06: In [25]: Copied! print ( "Cancellation rate by channel, for each type of customer (%):" ) ( cancel_table * 100 ) . round ( 1 )[[ "Business" , "Leisure" ]] print("Cancellation rate by channel, for each type of customer (%):") (cancel_table * 100).round(1)[["Business", "Leisure"]] Cancellation rate by channel, for each type of customer (%): Out[25]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_type Business Leisure channel Corporate 15.6 NaN Direct 14.8 33.3 Online travel agency 17.4 44.6 Travel agent NaN 31.0 Among business travellers the channel barely matters: 15 to 17% cancel whichever channel they use. Most of the OTA gap comes from who books there (leisure guests, planning months ahead), not from the channel itself. Closing the OTA channel would not make leisure guests more reliable. Choose three charts from section 04 Exploration , one per pattern, with the question in the title and one sentence under each. docs.text: Altamar's booking file is full of copies, misspellings and impossible values, and every summary built on it is wrong. Today you find each problem, clean it with a decision you can defend, and turn the clean data into tables, charts and three findings a general manager can act on. 4 hours 9 ideas Runs in your browser Case: clean data and patterns Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the tools and a few lists the session uses. docs.text: Last week you joined Altamar's management team and opened the raw booking file: 6,060 bookings at three hotels. Two questions are waiting: Revenue management: what nightly rate ( adr ) can we charge? Operations: which bookings will cancel? Managers don't read 6,060 rows. They decide with summaries : an average rate per hotel, a cancellation rate per channel. So the summaries must be right. The cell below asks the raw file the first question any manager asks: what is our average rate at each hotel? In [2]: Copied! raw = pd . read_csv ( DATA + "altamar_bookings.csv" ) print ( f "Raw file: { len ( raw ) : , } bookings, { raw . shape [ 1 ] } columns \n " ) # The first summary a manager asks for: the average nightly rate by hotel raw . groupby ( "hotel" )[ "adr" ] . mean () . round ( 1 ) raw = pd.read_csv(DATA + "altamar_bookings.csv") print(f"Raw file: {len(raw):,} bookings, {raw.shape[1]} columns\n") # The first summary a manager asks for: the average nightly rate by hotel raw.groupby("hotel")["adr"].mean().round(1) Raw file: 6,060 bookings, 20 columns Out[2]: hotel Pto. Varas 148.5 Puerto Varas 158.0 SANTIAGO 101.9 Santiago 100.3 VIÑA DEL MAR 138.3 Vina del Mar 137.4 Viña del Mar 140.4 Name: adr, dtype: float64 Seven hotels, for a group that owns three. SANTIAGO , Vina del Mar and Pto. Varas are the same hotels typed differently by different systems, and pandas counts each spelling as a separate hotel. The averages are wrong too: hidden inside are free rooms and rates with an extra zero. Today, in order: look inside the table and pick exactly the rows you need, audit the file: find every problem with code, clean it, writing down each decision, summarize it with tables and charts that answer questions, write three findings for the general manager.

One column on its own is a Series : one fact for every booking. Click the parts of the table below to see where each lives and what pandas gives back. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. head() shows the first rows.
