docs.text: Most questions start by narrowing the table: only Viña del Mar , only suites , only bookings made 90 or more days ahead . A comparison on a column, like raw["hotel"] == "Viña del Mar" , gives a mask : one True or False per booking. Put the mask inside raw[...] and only the True rows survive. Combine masks with & (and) and | (or), with each condition in its own parentheses . ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Three masks, one at a time, then the revenue manager's real request: Viña del Mar bookings made 90+ days ahead , compared with the rest of Viña. len() counts the rows that survive. In [5]: Copied! is_vina = raw [ "hotel" ] == "Viña del Mar" is_suite = raw [ "room_type" ] == "Suite" is_early = raw [ "lead_time_days" ] >= 90 print ( f "Viña del Mar: { is_vina . sum () : , } Suites: { is_suite . sum () : , } Made 90+ days ahead: { is_early . sum () : , } \n " ) vina_early = raw [ is_vina & is_early ] vina_late = raw [ is_vina & ~ is_early ] # ~ means "not" print ( f "Viña del Mar, 90+ days ahead: { len ( vina_early ) : , } bookings, average rate USD { vina_early [ 'adr' ] . mean () : .0f } " ) print ( f "Viña del Mar, closer in: { len ( vina_late ) : , } bookings, average rate USD { vina_late [ 'adr' ] . mean () : .0f } " ) print ( f "Viña del Mar OR 90+ days: { ( is_vina | is_early ) . sum () : , } bookings" ) is_vina = raw["hotel"] == "Viña del Mar" is_suite = raw["room_type"] == "Suite" is_early = raw["lead_time_days"] >= 90 print(f"Viña del Mar: {is_vina.sum():,} Suites: {is_suite.sum():,} Made 90+ days ahead: {is_early.sum():,}\n") vina_early = raw[is_vina & is_early] vina_late = raw[is_vina & ~is_early] # ~ means "not" print(f"Viña del Mar, 90+ days ahead: {len(vina_early):,} bookings, average rate USD {vina_early['adr'].mean():.0f}") print(f"Viña del Mar, closer in: {len(vina_late):,} bookings, average rate USD {vina_late['adr'].mean():.0f}") print(f"Viña del Mar OR 90+ days: {(is_vina | is_early).sum():,} bookings") Viña del Mar: 1,987 Suites: 606 Made 90+ days ahead: 1,034 Viña del Mar, 90+ days ahead: 428 bookings, average rate USD 130 Viña del Mar, closer in: 1,559 bookings, average rate USD 143 Viña del Mar OR 90+ days: 2,593 bookings Early beach bookings pay about 13 USD less a night: early-bird discounts. Watch out: the filter only finds the exact text "Viña del Mar" . The cell below counts the bookings our filter missed because they were typed differently. The data is lying to our filters, which is why we audit next. In [6]: Copied! spellings = [ "Viña del Mar" , "Vina del Mar" , "VIÑA DEL MAR" ] all_vina = raw [ "hotel" ] . isin ( spellings ) # isin: "one of these values" print ( f "Exact spelling only: { is_vina . sum () : , } Any spelling: { all_vina . sum () : , } Missed: { all_vina . sum () - is_vina . sum () } " ) spellings = ["Viña del Mar", "Vina del Mar", "VIÑA DEL MAR"] all_vina = raw["hotel"].isin(spellings) # isin: "one of these values" print(f"Exact spelling only: {is_vina.sum():,} Any spelling: {all_vina.sum():,} Missed: {all_vina.sum() - is_vina.sum()}") Exact spelling only: 1,987 Any spelling: 2,059 Missed: 72 Sometimes you need one booking by its ID. Make booking_id the index, and .loc finds rows by their label ; .iloc counts positions 0, 1, 2… like a list. Most of the time you will filter with masks; the explainer shows the difference for when you meet .loc and .iloc in the toolkit. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The early beach bookings need &, AND, which keeps a row only when both are True.", "code": false}
docs.title: 03 Selecting and filtering
04 The data quality audit

docs.text: Every problem needs a decision , and every decision needs a reason a manager would accept: Problem Decision Why Duplicates Drop the copy One booking, counted once Spellings Map to the official names Same hotel, same label Rate of 0 or ≥ 1,000 USD Drop the booking Not a real price; guessing would invent one Negative lead time, 0 adults Drop the booking Impossible, and only 18 rows Missing children Fill with 0 Three in four bookings have none Missing country New label Unknown Honest: we don't invent a country Watch the pipeline first, then run it step by step. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Each step changes df (a copy of the raw file) and adds one line to log , the cleaning log . Step 1: duplicates. In [11]: Copied! df = raw . copy () log = [] # one line per decision: problem, decision, rows affected def record ( problem , decision , rows ): log . append ({ "problem" : problem , "decision" : decision , "rows affected" : int ( rows )}) print ( f " { problem } : { rows : , } rows → { decision } " ) before = len ( df ) df = df . drop_duplicates () . copy () record ( "Exact duplicate rows" , "Dropped the copy, kept the first" , before - len ( df )) df = raw.copy() log = [] # one line per decision: problem, decision, rows affected def record(problem, decision, rows): log.append({"problem": problem, "decision": decision, "rows affected": int(rows)}) print(f"{problem}: {rows:,} rows → {decision}") before = len(df) df = df.drop_duplicates().copy() record("Exact duplicate rows", "Dropped the copy, kept the first", before - len(df)) Exact duplicate rows: 60 rows → Dropped the copy, kept the first Step 2: labels. A dictionary says which spelling becomes which official name. For channels, lower case first, then ota becomes the full name, then a capital first letter. In [12]: Copied! HOTEL_FIX = { "SANTIAGO" : "Santiago" , "Vina del Mar" : "Viña del Mar" , "VIÑA DEL MAR" : "Viña del Mar" , "Pto. Varas" : "Puerto Varas" } fixed = df [ "hotel" ] . replace ( HOTEL_FIX ) record ( "Hotel written 4 other ways" , "Mapped to the 3 official names" , ( fixed != df [ "hotel" ]) . sum ()) df [ "hotel" ] = fixed fixed = df [ "channel" ] . str . lower () . replace ({ "ota" : "online travel agency" }) . str . capitalize () record ( "Channel written 3 other ways" , "Lower case, OTA to the full name" , ( fixed != df [ "channel" ]) . sum ()) df [ "channel" ] = fixed print ( f " \n Hotels now: { df [ 'hotel' ] . nunique () } Channels now: { df [ 'channel' ] . nunique () } " ) HOTEL_FIX = {"SANTIAGO": "Santiago", "Vina del Mar": "Viña del Mar", "VIÑA DEL MAR": "Viña del Mar", "Pto. Varas": "Puerto Varas"} fixed = df["hotel"].replace(HOTEL_FIX) record("Hotel written 4 other ways", "Mapped to the 3 official names", (fixed != df["hotel"]).sum()) df["hotel"] = fixed fixed = df["channel"].str.lower().replace({"ota": "online travel agency"}).str.capitalize() record("Channel written 3 other ways", "Lower case, OTA to the full name", (fixed != df["channel"]).sum()) df["channel"] = fixed print(f"\nHotels now: {df['hotel'].nunique()} Channels now: {df['channel'].nunique()}") Hotel written 4 other ways: 250 rows → Mapped to the 3 official names Channel written 3 other ways: 134 rows → Lower case, OTA to the full name Hotels now: 3 Channels now: 4 Steps 3 and 4: impossible values. We keep rates above 0 and below 1,000 USD, then drop the impossible bookings. (We could rebuild the 10 lead times from the two dates, but with 10 rows out of 6,000 the cleaner decision is to drop them and say so.) docs.title: 05 Cleaning with decisions you can defend
06 Summaries that answer questions

docs.text: A table convinces an analyst; a chart convinces a meeting. The rule: start from the question, then pick the chart. how one number spreads → histogram a number compared across categories → box plot a rate per category → bar chart a number across time → line chart , one line per group Every chart gets a title, axes in plain English, and one sentence under it saying what it shows . ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. How are our nightly rates spread out? A histogram counts the bookings in each price range. In [20]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . histplot ( df , x = "adr" , bins = 40 ) plt . axvline ( df [ "adr" ] . mean (), color = "black" , linestyle = "--" , label = f "average USD { df [ 'adr' ] . mean () : .0f } " ) plt . axvline ( df [ "adr" ] . median (), color = "grey" , label = f "median USD { df [ 'adr' ] . median () : .0f } " ) plt . title ( "How are our nightly rates spread out?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Nightly rate (USD)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Bookings" ) plt . legend () plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) sns.histplot(df, x="adr", bins=40) plt.axvline(df["adr"].mean(), color="black", linestyle="--", label=f"average USD {df['adr'].mean():.0f}") plt.axvline(df["adr"].median(), color="grey", label=f"median USD {df['adr'].median():.0f}") plt.title("How are our nightly rates spread out?") plt.xlabel("Nightly rate (USD)") plt.ylabel("Bookings") plt.legend() plt.show() What it shows: most nights sell between 80 and 160 USD, with a long tail to the right of expensive nights (suites, peak season at the beach). The tail pulls the average (127 USD) above the median (113 USD), the rate of the typical booking. Do rates differ by room type? A box plot per room type. In [21]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . boxplot ( df , x = "room_type" , y = "adr" , order = ROOMS ) plt . title ( "Do rates differ by room type?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Room type" ) plt . ylabel ( "Nightly rate (USD)" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) sns.boxplot(df, x="room_type", y="adr", order=ROOMS) plt.title("Do rates differ by room type?") plt.xlabel("Room type") plt.ylabel("Nightly rate (USD)") plt.show() What it shows: the median climbs from about 98 USD for a standard room to 126 for a superior and 179 for a suite. The boxes overlap: a suite in Santiago's low season can cost less than a standard room at the beach in January. The room matters, but so do the hotel and the month. Which channel cancels most? A bar chart of the cancellation rate: the mean of canceled in each channel. In [22]: Copied! order = cancel_by_channel . index # sorted from lowest to highest rate plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax = sns . barplot ( df , x = "channel" , y = "canceled" , order = order , errorbar = None ) ax . bar_label ( ax . containers [ 0 ], fmt = " {:.1%} " ) ax . yaxis . set_major_formatter ( PercentFormatter ( 1 )) plt . title ( "Which channel cancels most?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Booking channel" ) plt . ylabel ( "Cancellation rate" ) plt . show () order = cancel_by_channel.index # sorted from lowest to highest rate plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) ax = sns.barplot(df, x="channel", y="canceled", order=order, errorbar=None) ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], fmt="{:.1%}") ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1)) plt.title("Which channel cancels most?") plt.xlabel("Booking channel") plt.ylabel("Cancellation rate") plt.show() What it shows: 42.2% of online travel agency bookings cancel, almost three times the 15.6% of corporate bookings. For operations, a room sold through an OTA is a much less certain room. Does each hotel have its own seasons? This is the key chart of the week: the average rate by arrival month, one line per hotel . In [23]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . lineplot ( df , x = "arrival_month" , y = "adr" , hue = "hotel" , hue_order = HOTELS , errorbar = None , marker = "o" ) plt . xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 ), MONTHS ) plt . title ( "Does each hotel have its own seasons?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Arrival month" ) plt . ylabel ( "Average nightly rate (USD)" ) plt . legend ( title = "Hotel" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) sns.lineplot(df, x="arrival_month", y="adr", hue="hotel", hue_order=HOTELS, errorbar=None, marker="o") plt.xticks(range(1, 13), MONTHS) plt.title("Does each hotel have its own seasons?") plt.xlabel("Arrival month") plt.ylabel("Average nightly rate (USD)") plt.legend(title="Hotel") plt.show() What it shows: three hotels, three calendars. Viña del Mar and Puerto Varas peak in January and February at about 190–200 USD; Puerto Varas peaks again in July, with the winter holidays. Santiago does the opposite: it dips in the summer (76 USD in February), when business travellers are on holiday, and peaks in October with conferences. Hold on to this chart. In weeks 3 and 4 we fit straight lines; in week 5 we will see why one straight line through "month" cannot draw three different curves.
docs.title: 07 Charts that answer questions

docs.text: A finding is not a number. It is a number plus what it means for someone : What we see (with the number) → what it means for the business → what to check next . First, the numbers we will quote, printed by the code, so nobody has to trust our memory: In [24]: Copied! monthly = df . pivot_table ( index = "arrival_month" , columns = "hotel" , values = "adr" , aggfunc = "mean" ) for hotel in HOTELS : peak , low = monthly [ hotel ] . idxmax (), monthly [ hotel ] . idxmin () print ( f " { hotel : <13 } peak { MONTHS [ peak - 1 ] } USD { monthly [ hotel ] . max () : .0f } , low { MONTHS [ low - 1 ] } USD { monthly [ hotel ] . min () : .0f } " ) print () print ( f "Cancellation: online travel agency { cancel_by_channel [ 'Online travel agency' ] : .1% } , corporate { cancel_by_channel [ 'Corporate' ] : .1% } " ) suite_premium = rate_table [ "Suite" ] / rate_table [ "Standard" ] print ( "Suite rate ÷ standard rate:" , ", " . join ( f " { h } { suite_premium [ h ] : .2f } x" for h in HOTELS )) monthly = df.pivot_table(index="arrival_month", columns="hotel", values="adr", aggfunc="mean") for hotel in HOTELS: peak, low = monthly[hotel].idxmax(), monthly[hotel].idxmin() print(f"{hotel: < 13} peak {MONTHS[peak - 1]} USD {monthly[hotel].max():.0f}, low {MONTHS[low - 1]} USD {monthly[hotel].min():.0f}") print() print(f"Cancellation: online travel agency {cancel_by_channel['Online travel agency']:.1%}, corporate {cancel_by_channel['Corporate']:.1%}") suite_premium = rate_table["Suite"] / rate_table["Standard"] print("Suite rate ÷ standard rate:", ", ".join(f"{h} {suite_premium[h]:.2f}x" for h in HOTELS)) Santiago peak Oct USD 114, low Feb USD 76 Viña del Mar peak Jan USD 193, low Jun USD 85 Puerto Varas peak Jan USD 198, low May USD 99 Cancellation: online travel agency 42.2%, corporate 15.6% Suite rate ÷ standard rate: Santiago 1.82x, Viña del Mar 1.98x, Puerto Varas 1.93x Finding 1 · Every hotel has its own season. Viña del Mar's average rate goes from 193 USD in January to 85 USD in June; Santiago moves the other way, from 76 USD in February to 114 in October. For revenue management: one price calendar for the group would undercharge the beach in summer and overcharge the city. Next: a rate model must let each hotel have its own months. Finding 2 · Online travel agency bookings cancel most. 42.2% of them cancel, against 15.6% of corporate bookings. For operations: how many rooms we can oversell depends on the channel mix of each night. Next: week 4 predicts cancellations booking by booking. Finding 3 · Suites earn about twice a standard room. The suite rate is 1.8 to 2.0 times the standard rate at every hotel. For sales: upgrading even a few bookings is worth testing. Next: how many suites go unsold? Correlation is not causation. Finding 2 says OTA bookings cancel more ; it does not say the OTA makes guests cancel. Look again at the cancellation table by channel and customer type from section 06: In [25]: Copied! print ( "Cancellation rate by channel, for each type of customer (%):" ) ( cancel_table * 100 ) . round ( 1 )[[ "Business" , "Leisure" ]] print("Cancellation rate by channel, for each type of customer (%):") (cancel_table * 100).round(1)[["Business", "Leisure"]] Cancellation rate by channel, for each type of customer (%): Out[25]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_type Business Leisure channel Corporate 15.6 NaN Direct 14.8 33.3 Online travel agency 17.4 44.6 Travel agent NaN 31.0 Among business travellers the channel barely matters: 15 to 17% cancel whichever channel they use. Most of the OTA gap comes from who books there (leisure guests, planning months ahead), not from the channel itself. Closing the OTA channel would not make leisure guests more reliable. Before you recommend an action, ask: is it this factor, or something that travels with it? {"q": "Bookings with special requests cancel less. The marketing team proposes to ask every guest for a special request to reduce cancellations. What is the main problem?", "options": ["None: the data proves it works", "The pattern shows an association: committed guests make requests and also keep their bookings; asking for requests may not change commitment", "Special requests are too expensive", "The cancellation rate cannot be computed for special requests"], "answer": 1, "why": "Guests who already plan their stay in detail both ask for things and show up. The request is a sign of commitment, not necessarily its cause. Only a test (ask half the guests, compare) would tell whether asking changes behaviour.", "code": false}
docs.title: 08 From charts to findings

docs.text: This week's step of the applied case is today's session, done on your team's data. Open the case toolkit in Colab with your dataset and: Run section 02 Data quality audit. Read every count it prints and decide, as a team, what each problem would do to a decision. Run section 03 Cleaning , adjusting its ✏️ decisions, and keep its cleaning log : problem · decision · rows affected. Add one sentence of why to each line. Choose three charts from section 04 Exploration , one per pattern, with the question in the title and one sentence under each. Today with Altamar Your case 6,060 → 5,964 bookings, 9 problems logged Your cleaning log Rate by hotel and month; cancellation by channel Your target by its two most interesting columns Three findings for the general manager Three patterns, each with a chart and a "so what" Before next week: finish the lab and its graded quiz. In week 3 you will build Altamar's first rate model, and see how much of the seasons above a straight line can capture.

Why does the model underprice some of them and overprice others? Try TOP_N = 50 : does the pattern hold? Show the answer Almost all of them are **suites arriving in January or February**: peak summer. At **Viña del Mar and Puerto Varas** the model **underprices** them (guests paid USD 100 to 170 a night more than predicted), because suites go up *more* than other rooms in peak season, and the model only knows one fixed "+95" for a suite. At **Santiago** it **overprices** them, because it charges Santiago the January–February peak of the beach and the lake. Both are the same weakness: effects that depend on each other (room × season, hotel × month), which a model that adds one effect per input cannot draw. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. 04 Fewer inputs or more? ¶ Every input costs something: data to collect, a column to explain to the revenue team. Which single input brings the biggest drop in MAE? Then try the full list without "country" , "deposit" and "special_requests" : does the model get worse? Show the answer Hotel and room alone give a typical miss of about **USD 30** (R² ≈ 0.50). Adding **`arrival_month`** is by far the biggest single step: about **USD 23** (R² ≈ 0.68); no other input moves the MAE by more than a dollar on its own. `channel` and the guest counts then bring it down to about USD 21, and the rest to 20.5. Removing `country`, `deposit` and `special_requests` changes the MAE by only a few cents: they carry almost no information about the **rate** (they matter more for cancellations, next week). A simpler model that is just as accurate is easier to explain and to trust. 05 A note to the revenue manager ¶ The revenue manager will not read this notebook. docs.text: Altamar's revenue manager wants to use the model, not just admire it: type in a booking, get a rate, and know when to trust it. In this lab you turn the week's linear model into a rate simulator, test it one input at a time, hunt down its worst misses, and write the note that goes with it. ≈ 2 hours 5 tasks Runs in your browser Graded quiz Recap of the live session A model is a recipe learned from past bookings : it adds an intercept and one coefficient per input. Text columns become 0/1 columns, measured against a reference (Santiago, Standard, Direct, Leisure, January). We learn on 75% of the bookings and judge on the sealed 25% ( test set ). The linear model is typically off by about USD 20 per night (16% of the average rate), R² ≈ 0.74, far better than quoting each hotel's average. Its misses follow a pattern : one season shape for three hotels, and peaks it never reaches. Run this cell first. You don't need to read it. It loads the tools and the helpers of the live session, plus quote , which prices one booking and prints its recipe. In [1]: Copied! # Setup: tools for today. Run this cell first; you don't need to read it. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , r2_score DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/" MONTHS = [ "Jan" , "Feb" , "Mar" , "Apr" , "May" , "Jun" , "Jul" , "Aug" , "Sep" , "Oct" , "Nov" , "Dec" ] HOTELS = [ "Santiago" , "Viña del Mar" , "Puerto Varas" ] pd . set_option ( "display.width" , 120 ) sns . set_theme ( style = "whitegrid" ) # Every category of each text column. The FIRST one is the reference: its coefficient is 0, # and the model measures the others against it. LEVELS = { "hotel" : [ "Santiago" , "Viña del Mar" , "Puerto Varas" ], "room_type" : [ "Standard" , "Superior" , "Suite" ], "channel" : [ "Direct" , "Online travel agency" , "Corporate" , "Travel agent" ], "customer_type" : [ "Leisure" , "Business" , "Group" ], "deposit" : [ "No deposit" , "Non-refundable" ], "country" : [ "Chile" , "Argentina" , "Brazil" , "United States" , "Europe" , "Other" , "Unknown" ], "arrival_month" : list ( range ( 1 , 13 )), } def make_X ( data , features ): """Turn the chosen columns into numbers: one 0/1 column per category, minus the reference.""" parts = [] for col in features : if col in LEVELS : values = pd . Series ( pd . Categorical ( data [ col ], categories = LEVELS [ col ]), index = data . index ) parts . append ( pd . get_dummies ( values , prefix = col , drop_first = True , dtype = "int64" )) else : parts . append ( data [[ col ]]) return pd . concat ( parts , axis = 1 ) def scores ( name , actual , predicted ): """One row of a results table: the typical error in USD per night, and R².""" mae = mean_absolute_error ( actual , predicted ) return { "model" : name , "MAE (USD/night)" : round ( mae , 1 ), "MAE as % o f avg rate" : f " { mae / actual . mean () : .0% } " , "R²" : round ( r2_score ( actual , predicted ), 3 )} # A booking described in plain words. Anything you don't set takes these values. DEFAULTS = { "hotel" : "Santiago" , "arrival_month" : 1 , "room_type" : "Standard" , "channel" : "Direct" , "customer_type" : "Leisure" , "nights" : 3 , "weekend_nights" : 0 , "lead_time_days" : 30 , "adults" : 2 , "children" : 0 , "deposit" : "No deposit" , "repeat_guest" : 0 , "previous_cancellations" : 0 , "special_requests" : 0 , "parking" : 0 , "country" : "Chile" } def contributions ( model , features , booking ): """What each input adds to the predicted rate of one booking, in USD per night.""" row = pd . DataFrame ([{ ** DEFAULTS , ** booking }]) x = make_X ( row , features ) . iloc [ 0 ] parts = x * pd . Series ( model . coef_ , index = x . index ) owner = [ next ( f for f in features if c == f or c . startswith ( f + "_" )) for c in x . index ] return parts . groupby ( owner , sort = False ) . sum () . reindex ( features ), { ** DEFAULTS , ** booking } def quote ( model , features , show = True , ** booking ): """Price one booking. With show=True, print the recipe: intercept + one line per input.""" parts , full = contributions ( model , features , booking ) total = model . intercept_ + parts . sum () if show : keep = [ f for f in features if f in booking or abs ( parts [ f ]) >= 0.05 ] table = pd . DataFrame ({ "value" : [ full [ f ] for f in keep ], "adds (USD/night)" : parts [ keep ] . round ( 1 )}, index = keep ) table . loc [ "start (intercept)" ] = [ "Santiago · Jan · Standard · Direct" , round ( model . intercept_ , 1 )] table = table . loc [[ "start (intercept)" ] + keep ] print ( table . to_string ()) print ( f " { 'PREDICTED RATE' : <24 } USD { total : .1f } per night (inputs left at their reference add 0)" ) return total print ( "Ready: tools loaded." ) # Setup: tools for today. Run this cell first; you don't need to read it. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/" MONTHS = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"] HOTELS = ["Santiago", "Viña del Mar", "Puerto Varas"] pd.set_option("display.width", 120) sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid") # Every category of each text column. The FIRST one is the reference: its coefficient is 0, # and the model measures the others against it. LEVELS = { "hotel": ["Santiago", "Viña del Mar", "Puerto Varas"], "room_type": ["Standard", "Superior", "Suite"], "channel": ["Direct", "Online travel agency", "Corporate", "Travel agent"], "customer_type": ["Leisure", "Business", "Group"], "deposit": ["No deposit", "Non-refundable"], "country": ["Chile", "Argentina", "Brazil", "United States", "Europe", "Other", "Unknown"], "arrival_month": list(range(1, 13)), } def make_X(data, features): """Turn the chosen columns into numbers: one 0/1 column per category, minus the reference.""" parts = [] for col in features: if col in LEVELS: values = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(data[col], categories=LEVELS[col]), index=data.index) parts.append(pd.get_dummies(values, prefix=col, drop_first=True, dtype="int64")) else: parts.append(data[[col]]) return pd.concat(parts, axis=1) def scores(name, actual, predicted): """One row of a results table: the typical error in USD per night, and R².""" mae = mean_absolute_error(actual, predicted) return {"model": name, "MAE (USD/night)": round(mae, 1), "MAE as % of avg rate": f"{mae / actual.mean():.0%}", "R²": round(r2_score(actual, predicted), 3)} # A booking described in plain words. Anything you don't set takes these values. DEFAULTS = {"hotel": "Santiago", "arrival_month": 1, "room_type": "Standard", "channel": "Direct", "customer_type": "Leisure", "nights": 3, "weekend_nights": 0, "lead_time_days": 30, "adults": 2, "children": 0, "deposit": "No deposit", "repeat_guest": 0, "previous_cancellations": 0, "special_requests": 0, "parking": 0, "country": "Chile"} def contributions(model, features, booking): """What each input adds to the predicted rate of one booking, in USD per night.""" row = pd.DataFrame([{**DEFAULTS, **booking}]) x = make_X(row, features).iloc[0] parts = x * pd.Series(model.coef_, index=x.index) owner = [next(f for f in features if c == f or c.startswith(f + "_")) for c in x.index] return parts.groupby(owner, sort=False).sum().reindex(features), {**DEFAULTS, **booking} def quote(model, features, show=True, **booking): """Price one booking. With show=True, print the recipe: intercept + one line per input.""" parts, full = contributions(model, features, booking) total = model.intercept_ + parts.sum() if show: keep = [f for f in features if f in booking or abs(parts[f]) >= 0.05] table = pd.DataFrame({"value": [full[f] for f in keep], "adds (USD/night)": parts[keep].round(1)}, index=keep) table.loc["start (intercept)"] = ["Santiago · Jan · Standard · Direct", round(model.intercept_, 1)] table = table.loc[["start (intercept)"] + keep] print(table.to_string()) print(f"{'PREDICTED RATE': < 24} USD {total:.1f} per night (inputs left at their reference add 0)") return total print("Ready: tools loaded.") Ready: tools loaded. Load the clean bookings, split them as in class, and fit the full linear model from the live session (step 06). Check the test error: it should match the live session. DataFrame ([ scores ( "Full linear model, test set" , y_test , model . predict ( X_test ))]) . to_string ( index = False )) df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv") df["arrival_month"] = pd.to_datetime(df["arrival_date"]).dt.month train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.25, random_state=42) FEATURES = ["hotel", "arrival_month", "room_type", "channel", "customer_type", "nights", "weekend_nights", "lead_time_days", "adults", "children", "deposit", "repeat_guest", "previous_cancellations", "special_requests", "parking", "country"] X_train, X_test = make_X(train, FEATURES), make_X(test, FEATURES) y_train, y_test = train["adr"], test["adr"] model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train) print(pd.DataFrame([scores("Full linear model, test set", y_test, model.predict(X_test))]).to_string(index=False)) model MAE (USD/night) MAE as % of avg rate R² Full linear model, test set 20.5 16% 0.738

Guests: "Leisure" , "Business" , "Group" . Now quote the same booking in Santiago : by how much does the rate change, and which line of the recipe is the only one that moved? Show the answer For the Puerto Varas suite in July, the room adds the most (about **+95**), followed by the hotel (**+41**). July itself *subtracts* about 45 against January. Moving the booking to Santiago changes **only the hotel line**: from +41 to 0, so the rate drops by about USD 41. Every other line stays exactly the same, because a linear model adds each part on its own. The same recipe as a picture. The coefficients in the simulator are the ones your model just printed, rounded to one decimal. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.

docs.text: A revenue manager's favourite question: "what if?" Keep a booking fixed, change one input, and see how much the rate moves. In a linear model, the change is always the coefficient (for a category: the difference between two coefficients; for a number: the coefficient times the change). before : +.1f } = the { CHANGE_COLUMN } line going from { part_before : +.1f } to { part_after : +.1f } " ) # ✏️ Change these settings BOOKING = dict(hotel="Viña del Mar", arrival_month=2, room_type="Standard", channel="Direct", nights=4, lead_time_days=30) CHANGE_COLUMN = "room_type" # try "channel", "nights", "arrival_month", "hotel", "lead_time_days" NEW_VALUE = "Suite" # e.g. "Corporate", 5, 7, "Santiago", 120 after_booking = {**BOOKING, CHANGE_COLUMN: NEW_VALUE} before, after = quote(model, FEATURES, show=False, **BOOKING), quote(model, FEATURES, show=False, **after_booking) part_before = contributions(model, FEATURES, BOOKING)[0][CHANGE_COLUMN] part_after = contributions(model, FEATURES, after_booking)[0][CHANGE_COLUMN] old = {**DEFAULTS, **BOOKING}[CHANGE_COLUMN] print(f"Before: USD {before:.1f} per night ({CHANGE_COLUMN} = {old})") print(f"After: USD {after:.1f} per night ({CHANGE_COLUMN} = {NEW_VALUE})") print(f"Change: USD {after - before:+.1f} = the {CHANGE_COLUMN} line going from {part_before:+.1f} to {part_after:+.1f}") Before: USD 147.6 per night (room_type = Standard) After: USD 242.6 per night (room_type = Suite) Change: USD +95.0 = the room_type line going from +0.0 to +95.0 Think about it: Try three changes and explain each one with a coefficient. (1) channel from Direct to "Corporate" . (2) nights from 4 to 5, then from 6 to 7: is the discount the same? (3) hotel to "Santiago" for this February booking: does the change make sense, given what the heatmap in the live session showed for Santiago in February? Show the answer (1) Corporate is about **USD 14 cheaper** than Direct: the `channel_Corporate` coefficient. (2) Every extra night lowers the rate by the **same** USD 3.3, whether it is the 5th or the 7th. Altamar's real discounts come in steps at 5 and 7 nights; a straight line smooths them out. (3) The model moves the booking down by about **USD 21** (Viña's +20.8 disappears), in any month. But Santiago is *quiet* in February, while Viña is at its peak: the real gap is much larger (about USD 105 per night in February, in the live session's chart of rates by month). The model gets it wrong because it has one February effect for all hotels.

Why does the model underprice some of them and overprice others? Try TOP_N = 50 : does the pattern hold? Show the answer Almost all of them are **suites arriving in January or February**: peak summer. At **Viña del Mar and Puerto Varas** the model **underprices** them (guests paid USD 100 to 170 a night more than predicted), because suites go up *more* than other rooms in peak season, and the model only knows one fixed "+95" for a suite. At **Santiago** it **overprices** them, because it charges Santiago the January–February peak of the beach and the lake. Both are the same weakness: effects that depend on each other (room × season, hotel × month), which a model that adds one effect per input cannot draw. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.
docs.title: 03 The biggest misses

docs.text: Every input costs something: data to collect, a column to explain to the revenue team. Is it worth it? Fit a model with only the inputs in ✏️ FEATURES_SMALL and compare it with the full model on the same test set . Available inputs: hotel , arrival_month , room_type , channel , customer_type , nights , weekend_nights , lead_time_days , adults , children , deposit , repeat_guest , previous_cancellations , special_requests , parking , country . In [7]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings FEATURES_SMALL = [ "hotel" , "room_type" ] small = LinearRegression () . fit ( make_X ( train , FEATURES_SMALL ), y_train ) results = pd . DataFrame ([ scores ( f " { len ( FEATURES_SMALL ) } inputs: " + ", " . join ( FEATURES_SMALL ), y_test , small . predict ( make_X ( test , FEATURES_SMALL ))), scores ( f "Full model: { len ( FEATURES ) } inputs" , y_test , model . predict ( X_test )), ]) print ( results . to_string ( index = False )) # ✏️ Change these settings FEATURES_SMALL = ["hotel", "room_type"] small = LinearRegression().fit(make_X(train, FEATURES_SMALL), y_train) results = pd.DataFrame([ scores(f"{len(FEATURES_SMALL)} inputs: " + ", ".join(FEATURES_SMALL), y_test, small.predict(make_X(test, FEATURES_SMALL))), scores(f"Full model: {len(FEATURES)} inputs", y_test, model.predict(X_test)), ]) print(results.to_string(index=False)) model MAE (USD/night) MAE as % of avg rate R² 2 inputs: hotel, room_type 29.8 23% 0.505 Full model: 16 inputs 20.5 16% 0.738 Think about it: Start from ["hotel", "room_type"] and add one input at a time. Which single input brings the biggest drop in MAE? Then try the full list without "country" , "deposit" and "special_requests" : does the model get worse? Show the answer Hotel and room alone give a typical miss of about **USD 30** (R² ≈ 0.50). Adding **`arrival_month`** is by far the biggest single step: about **USD 23** (R² ≈ 0.68); no other input moves the MAE by more than a dollar on its own. `channel` and the guest counts then bring it down to about USD 21, and the rest to 20.5. Removing `country`, `deposit` and `special_requests` changes the MAE by only a few cents: they carry almost no information about the **rate** (they matter more for cancellations, next week). A simpler model that is just as accurate is easier to explain and to trust.

Show an example note *"The model suggests a starting rate for Standard and Superior rooms outside the summer peak that is typically within USD 20 of what guests pay, almost twice as accurate as quoting each hotel's average; use it to set a first quote and to flag quotes that look far off. Do not use it on its own for suites in January–February, or for Santiago in the summer and Puerto Varas in July, where it is off by USD 30 to 70 a night in a predictable direction, until we fit a model that learns each hotel's seasons (week 5)."* Notice: one use, one number, one comparison, and a limit that names **where**.

And the clean data told a story: the rate depends on the hotel, the season and the room , and each hotel has its own seasons. Now revenue management asks for more than a story. When a booking request comes in, they want an estimate of the right rate for it , one that combines everything we know about the booking at once. That estimate is a model . A good rate estimate has to weigh all of this at once, for every booking. That is the job of today's model. 02 A model is a recipe ¶ Remember week 1's picture: a model is a recipe that turns inputs into an answer. Today the answer is a number, the predicted rate , so this is regression . The recipe is not written by us: the model learns it from past bookings , where we know both the inputs and the rate the guest paid. Then it applies the recipe to a new request whose rate is still unknown. Which inputs? Only what we know when the guest asks for a price : hotel, arrival month, room, channel, nights, how far ahead they book, how many guests. Look at one past booking split into its two halves: what the model sees, and the answer it learns from. Not by asking it about bookings it learned from: that is an exam where the student has seen the answers. So before learning anything, we split the bookings. Three quarters go to the training set : the model learns from these. One quarter goes into a sealed envelope , the test set , which we open only once, at the end, to measure how wrong the model is on bookings it has never seen. Move the line yourself, then press Fit least squares . ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The same picture in code. LinearRegression finds the slope and intercept that the simulator found. (Here we use all bookings, because it only illustrates the idea; the real model in step 06 learns from train only.) In [8]: Copied! vina = df [ df [ "hotel" ] == "Viña del Mar" ] months = vina . groupby ( "arrival_month" ) . agg ( bookings = ( "adr" , "size" ), rate = ( "adr" , "mean" )) months [ "bookings" ] = months [ "bookings" ] / 2 # two years of data: bookings in a typical year line = LinearRegression () . fit ( months [[ "bookings" ]], months [ "rate" ]) print ( f "Slope: USD { line . coef_ [ 0 ] : .2f } per extra booking, so 10 more bookings in a month ≈ USD { 10 * line . coef_ [ 0 ] : .0f } higher rate" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax . scatter ( months [ "bookings" ], months [ "rate" ], color = "black" ) for m , row in months [ months [ "bookings" ] > 65 ] . iterrows (): # label the busy months ax . annotate ( MONTHS [ m - 1 ], ( row [ "bookings" ], row [ "rate" ]), xytext = ( 5 , 3 ), textcoords = "offset points" ) grid = pd . DataFrame ({ "bookings" : np . linspace ( 0 , 250 , 50 )}) ax . plot ( grid [ "bookings" ], line . predict ( grid ), label = "least-squares line" ) ax . set ( title = "Viña del Mar: busier months, higher rates" , xlabel = "bookings arriving in the month (typical year)" , ylabel = "average rate (USD per night)" ) ax . legend (); plt . show () vina = df[df["hotel"] == "Viña del Mar"] months = vina.groupby("arrival_month").agg(bookings=("adr", "size"), rate=("adr", "mean")) months["bookings"] = months["bookings"] / 2 # two years of data: bookings in a typical year line = LinearRegression().fit(months[["bookings"]], months["rate"]) print(f"Slope: USD {line.coef_[0]:.2f} per extra booking, so 10 more bookings in a month ≈ USD {10 * line.coef_[0]:.0f} higher rate") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5)) ax.scatter(months["bookings"], months["rate"], color="black") for m, row in months[months["bookings"] > 65].iterrows(): # label the busy months ax.annotate(MONTHS[m - 1], (row["bookings"], row["rate"]), xytext=(5, 3), textcoords="offset points") grid = pd.DataFrame({"bookings": np.linspace(0, 250, 50)}) ax.plot(grid["bookings"], line.predict(grid), label="least-squares line") ax.set(title="Viña del Mar: busier months, higher rates", xlabel="bookings arriving in the month (typical year)", ylabel="average rate (USD per night)") ax.legend(); plt.show() Slope: USD 0.61 per extra booking, so 10 more bookings in a month ≈ USD 6 higher rate Business takeaway: the slope is a sentence: every 10 extra bookings in a month go with about USD 6 more per night . The real model does exactly this, but with 36 inputs at once : it finds one number per input so that the total squared miss over 4,473 training bookings is as small as possible. ☕ Break (10 minutes). In the second block we build Altamar's rate model, read it like a revenue manager, measure its error in dollars, and find where it fails. 06 One model for every booking ¶ Now the full recipe. We give the model every input known when a guest asks for a price, with the month as twelve categories ( arrival_month ), because seasons do not go up in a straight line from January to December. Three steps, the same in every project: choose inputs → encode them → fit on the training set . Choose the inputs, encode training and test the same way, and fit LinearRegression on the training bookings only. In [9]: Copied! FEATURES = [ "hotel" , "arrival_month" , "room_type" , "channel" , "customer_type" , "nights" , "weekend_nights" , "lead_time_days" , "adults" , "children" , "deposit" , "repeat_guest" , "previous_cancellations" , "special_requests" , "parking" , "country" ] X_train , X_test = make_X ( train , FEATURES ), make_X ( test , FEATURES ) y_train , y_test = train [ "adr" ], test [ "adr" ] model = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_train , y_train ) print ( f " { len ( FEATURES ) } inputs became { X_train . shape [ 1 ] } number columns." ) print ( f "The model learned { X_train . shape [ 1 ] } coefficients and an intercept from { len ( X_train ) : , } bookings." ) FEATURES = ["hotel", "arrival_month", "room_type", "channel", "customer_type", "nights", "weekend_nights", "lead_time_days", "adults", "children", "deposit", "repeat_guest", "previous_cancellations", "special_requests", "parking", "country"] X_train, X_test = make_X(train, FEATURES), make_X(test, FEATURES) y_train, y_test = train["adr"], test["adr"] model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train) print(f"{len(FEATURES)} inputs became {X_train.shape[1]} number columns.") print(f"The model learned {X_train.shape[1]} coefficients and an intercept from {len(X_train):,} bookings.") 16 inputs became 36 number columns. The model learned 36 coefficients and an intercept from 4,473 bookings. Open the envelope a crack: predict six test bookings the model has never seen, next to the rate they actually paid. In [10]: Copied! compare = test [[ "hotel" , "arrival_month" , "room_type" , "channel" , "adr" ]] . head ( 6 ) . copy () compare [ "predicted" ] = model . predict ( X_test . head ( 6 )) . round ( 1 ) compare [ "miss (USD)" ] = ( compare [ "adr" ] - compare [ "predicted" ]) . round ( 1 ) print ( compare . to_string ( index = False )) compare = test[["hotel", "arrival_month", "room_type", "channel", "adr"]].head(6).copy() compare["predicted"] = model.predict(X_test.head(6)).round(1) compare["miss (USD)"] = (compare["adr"] - compare["predicted"]).round(1) print(compare.to_string(index=False)) hotel arrival_month room_type channel adr predicted miss (USD) Viña del Mar 11 Superior Direct 139.00 145.8 -6.8 Puerto Varas 11 Standard Corporate 108.58 109.4 -0.8 Viña del Mar 12 Standard Online travel agency 113.45 118.3 -4.8 Viña del Mar 5 Standard Direct 112.24 96.0 16.2 Puerto Varas 8 Superior Direct 135.34 148.8 -13.5 Puerto Varas 7 Standard Direct 153.98 139.7 14.3 Some predictions land within a dollar, others miss by USD 15 or more. A positive miss means the guest paid more than the model predicted: the model would have underpriced the room. Before asking how wrong it is on average (step 08), let's open the recipe. 07 Reading the coefficients like a revenue manager ¶ Each coefficient is in USD per night . For a category, it is the difference against the reference , everything else equal. For a number, it is the change per unit (per night, per day booked ahead, per adult). The intercept is the starting point: a Standard room booked direct at Santiago in January, before adding anything else. Print the intercept and the fifteen largest coefficients, biggest effect first. In [11]: Copied! coefs = pd . Series ( model . coef_ , index = X_train . columns ) . round ( 1 ) print ( f "Intercept: USD { model . intercept_ : .1f } \n " ) print ( coefs . sort_values ( key = abs , ascending = False ) . head ( 15 ) . to_string ()) coefs = pd.Series(model.coef_, index=X_train.columns).round(1) print(f"Intercept: USD {model.intercept_:.1f}\n") print(coefs.sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).head(15).to_string()) Intercept: USD 132.8 room_type_Suite 95.0 arrival_month_6 -69.9 arrival_month_5 -67.1 arrival_month_8 -65.8 arrival_month_4 -63.6 arrival_month_9 -59.7 arrival_month_10 -55.7 arrival_month_11 -53.0 arrival_month_3 -50.7 arrival_month_7 -45.3 arrival_month_12 -42.8 hotel_Puerto Varas 41.0 room_type_Superior 31.1 hotel_Viña del Mar 20.8 channel_Travel agent -19.5 The same coefficients as a picture, without the months (step 09 looks at them) and the countries (all small). Orange bars raise the rate, blue bars lower it. In [12]: Copied! show = coefs [ ~ coefs . index . str . startswith (( "arrival_month" , "country" ))] . sort_values () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) ax . barh ( show . index , show . values , color = np . where ( show . values > 0 , "tab:orange" , "tab:blue" )) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 1 ) ax . set ( title = "What each input adds to the nightly rate" , xlabel = "USD per night (vs the reference, or per unit)" ) plt . tight_layout (); plt . show () show = coefs[~coefs.index.str.startswith(("arrival_month", "country"))].sort_values() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6)) ax.barh(show.index, show.values, color=np.where(show.values > 0, "tab:orange", "tab:blue")) ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1) ax.set(title="What each input adds to the nightly rate", xlabel="USD per night (vs the reference, or per unit)") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() Translate them into sentences a revenue manager would use. In [13]: Copied! c = coefs print ( f "A suite adds about USD { c [ 'room_type_Suite' ] : .0f } per night over a Standard room; a Superior about USD { c [ 'room_type_Superior' ] : .0f } ." ) print ( f "Puerto Varas is about USD { c [ 'hotel_Puerto Varas' ] : .0f } above Santiago; Viña del Mar about USD { c [ 'hotel_Viña del Mar' ] : .0f } ." ) print ( f "Corporate rates are about USD { - c [ 'channel_Corporate' ] : .0f } lower than direct; travel agents about USD { - c [ 'channel_Travel agent' ] : .0f } lower." ) print ( f "Online travel agency bookings pay about USD { c [ 'channel_Online travel agency' ] : .0f } more than direct ones." ) print ( f "Each extra night lowers the nightly rate by about USD { - c [ 'nights' ] : .1f } ; each extra adult adds about USD { c [ 'adults' ] : .0f } ." ) print ( f "Each weekend night adds USD { c [ 'weekend_nights' ] : .1f } : almost nothing. Keep that in mind for step 09." ) c = coefs print(f"A suite adds about USD {c['room_type_Suite']:.0f} per night over a Standard room; a Superior about USD {c['room_type_Superior']:.0f}.") print(f"Puerto Varas is about USD {c['hotel_Puerto Varas']:.0f} above Santiago; Viña del Mar about USD {c['hotel_Viña del Mar']:.0f}.") print(f"Corporate rates are about USD {-c['channel_Corporate']:.0f} lower than direct; travel agents about USD {-c['channel_Travel agent']:.0f} lower.") print(f"Online travel agency bookings pay about USD {c['channel_Online travel agency']:.0f} more than direct ones.") print(f"Each extra night lowers the nightly rate by about USD {-c['nights']:.1f}; each extra adult adds about USD {c['adults']:.0f}.") print(f"Each weekend night adds USD {c['weekend_nights']:.1f}: almost nothing. Keep that in mind for step 09.") A suite adds about USD 95 per night over a Standard room; a Superior about USD 31. Puerto Varas is about USD 41 above Santiago; Viña del Mar about USD 21. Corporate rates are about USD 14 lower than direct; travel agents about USD 20 lower. Online travel agency bookings pay about USD 6 more than direct ones. Each extra night lowers the nightly rate by about USD 3.3; each extra adult adds about USD 9. Each weekend night adds USD 0.0: almost nothing. Keep that in mind for step 09. Watch out: average effects, not causes. "Corporate rates are USD 14 lower" describes the bookings we had, everything else equal. It does not promise that moving a corporate client to the direct channel earns USD 14 more: that client might not book at all. And "everything else equal" only covers the inputs we gave the model. Build a booking from these numbers yourself. The coefficients below are copied, rounded, from the model you just fitted. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. {"q": "The coefficient of <code>channel_Corporate</code> is about −14. The sales director says: “if we move every corporate client to direct booking, we earn USD 14 more per night from each.” What is the problem?", "options": ["Nothing: that is exactly what the coefficient means", "The coefficient describes an average difference in past bookings; it does not say what clients would do if we changed their channel", "The coefficient is in percent, not in dollars", "Coefficients only apply to the training set, never to new bookings"], "answer": 1, "why": "A regression coefficient is an association, everything else in the model being equal. Corporate clients get lower rates <em>because</em> of an agreement; without it, they might book elsewhere. Changing the channel is a business decision the data alone cannot price.", "code": false} 08 How wrong are we? ¶ Time to open the sealed envelope. Three numbers, all on the test set : MAE (mean absolute error): the typical miss, in USD per night . The number to give a manager. MAE as a % of the average rate : is USD 20 a lot? For a USD 127 room, yes and no. R² : the share of the differences between rates that the model explains. 1 is perfect; 0 is no better than quoting the average to everyone. Drag the misses below and watch the three numbers react. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Score the model on the training and the test set, next to a baseline that a person could compute in a spreadsheet: quote each hotel's average rate to every booking. A model is only worth using if it beats the baseline. In [14]: Copied! hotel_average = train . groupby ( "hotel" )[ "adr" ] . mean () predicted_test = model . predict ( X_test ) results = pd . DataFrame ([ scores ( "Baseline: the hotel's average rate (test)" , y_test , test [ "hotel" ] . map ( hotel_average )), scores ( "Linear model, training set" , y_train , model . predict ( X_train )), scores ( "Linear model, test set" , y_test , predicted_test ), ]) print ( results . to_string ( index = False )) mae = mean_absolute_error ( y_test , predicted_test ) print ( f " \n On bookings it has never seen, the model's rate is typically off by USD { mae : .0f } per night," ) print ( f "about { mae / y_test . mean () : .0% } of the average rate (USD { y_test . mean () : .0f } )." ) hotel_average = train.groupby("hotel")["adr"].mean() predicted_test = model.predict(X_test) results = pd.DataFrame([ scores("Baseline: the hotel's average rate (test)", y_test, test["hotel"].map(hotel_average)), scores("Linear model, training set", y_train, model.predict(X_train)), scores("Linear model, test set", y_test, predicted_test), ]) print(results.to_string(index=False)) mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, predicted_test) print(f"\nOn bookings it has never seen, the model's rate is typically off by USD {mae:.0f} per night,") print(f"about {mae / y_test.mean():.0%} of the average rate (USD {y_test.mean():.0f}).") model MAE (USD/night) MAE as % of avg rate R² Baseline: the hotel's average rate (test) 35.8 28% 0.197 Linear model, training set 20.1 16% 0.740 Linear model, test set 20.5 16% 0.738 On bookings it has never seen, the model's rate is typically off by USD 20 per night, about 16% of the average rate (USD 127). Reading the results: It beats the baseline clearly: a typical miss of USD 20 instead of USD 36, and R² 0.74 instead of 0.20. Training and test are almost the same (MAE 20.1 vs 20.5). The model did not memorize its training bookings; we can expect about the same error next month. But USD 20 is 16% of the average rate. Good enough to suggest a starting rate or to flag a quote that looks far off; not good enough to set peak-season suite prices on its own. {"q": "A colleague's model has a typical error (MAE) of USD 5 on the training set and USD 31 on the test set. Ours has USD 20 and USD 20. Which model should revenue management use?", "options": ["The colleague's: USD 5 is the best number in the table", "Ours: its test error is lower, and train ≈ test means it will behave the same on new bookings", "Either: the training error is what matters", "Neither: a model must have zero error on the training set"], "answer": 1, "why": "The test set is the only honest exam. USD 5 on training and USD 31 on test is the signature of <strong>overfitting</strong>: the model memorized its training bookings and is worse on new ones.", "code": false} 09 Where the line fails ¶ An average error hides where the model is wrong. If the misses were random, there would be nothing to fix. If they follow a pattern , the model is missing something a manager would recognise. Plot the actual rate of every test booking against the model's prediction. Points on the diagonal are perfect; look at the most expensive bookings, top right. In [15]: Copied! view = test . assign ( predicted = predicted_test , miss = y_test - predicted_test ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7.5 , 6 )) sns . scatterplot ( data = view , x = "predicted" , y = "adr" , hue = "hotel" , hue_order = HOTELS , alpha = 0.5 , s = 18 , ax = ax ) ax . plot ([ 0 , 450 ], [ 0 , 450 ], color = "black" , lw = 1 , label = "perfect prediction" ) ax . set ( title = "Actual vs predicted rate, test bookings" , xlabel = "predicted rate (USD per night)" , ylabel = "actual rate (USD per night)" ) ax . legend (); plt . show () print ( f "Test bookings that paid over USD 300 a night: { ( view [ 'adr' ] > 300 ) . sum () } ." ) print ( f "Test bookings the model priced over USD 300: { ( view [ 'predicted' ] > 300 ) . sum () } ." ) view = test.assign(predicted=predicted_test, miss=y_test - predicted_test) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6)) sns.scatterplot(data=view, x="predicted", y="adr", hue="hotel", hue_order=HOTELS, alpha=0.5, s=18, ax=ax) ax.plot([0, 450], [0, 450], color="black", lw=1, label="perfect prediction") ax.set(title="Actual vs predicted rate, test bookings", xlabel="predicted rate (USD per night)", ylabel="actual rate (USD per night)") ax.legend(); plt.show() print(f"Test bookings that paid over USD 300 a night: {(view['adr'] > 300).sum()}.") print(f"Test bookings the model priced over USD 300: {(view['predicted'] > 300).sum()}.") Test bookings that paid over USD 300 a night: 32. Test bookings the model priced over USD 300: 0. The model misses the peaks. The most expensive bookings sit far above the diagonal: a line that adds fixed amounts never reaches the top rates of peak-season suites. And there is a cloud of Santiago bookings priced too high. When and where? Average miss for each hotel and arrival month (actual − predicted). Red cells: the model underprices ; blue cells: it overprices . In [16]: Copied! heat = view . pivot_table ( index = "hotel" , columns = "arrival_month" , values = "miss" , aggfunc = "mean" ) . reindex ( HOTELS ) heat . columns = MONTHS fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 11 , 3.4 )) sns . heatmap ( heat , annot = True , fmt = ".0f" , cmap = "RdBu_r" , center = 0 , cbar_kws = { "label" : "USD per night" }, ax = ax ) ax . set ( title = "Average miss by hotel and month: red = priced too low, blue = priced too high" , xlabel = "arrival month" , ylabel = "" ) ax . tick_params ( axis = "y" , rotation = 0 ) plt . show () heat = view.pivot_table(index="hotel", columns="arrival_month", values="miss", aggfunc="mean").reindex(HOTELS) heat.columns = MONTHS fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.4)) sns.heatmap(heat, annot=True, fmt=".0f", cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, cbar_kws={"label": "USD per night"}, ax=ax) ax.set(title="Average miss by hotel and month: red = priced too low, blue = priced too high", xlabel="arrival month", ylabel="") ax.tick_params(axis="y", rotation=0) plt.show() A systematic pattern, not noise. The model has one January effect, one July effect, shared by all three hotels. It learned that January is expensive (true at the beach and the lake) and charges it to Santiago too, where January is quiet: about USD 70 too much per night. July is a peak only in Puerto Varas, so the model underprices it there and overprices it in Viña. Seasons differ by hotel , and a model that adds one month effect for everyone cannot draw that. Switch hotels below. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Does giving the model better inputs help? Compare the month as a single number (1 to 12, so the model can only draw a slope through the year) with the month as twelve categories . In [17]: Copied! features_num = [ f if f != "arrival_month" else "month_number" for f in FEATURES ] train_num , test_num = train . assign ( month_number = train [ "arrival_month" ]), test . assign ( month_number = test [ "arrival_month" ]) model_num = LinearRegression () . fit ( make_X ( train_num , features_num ), y_train ) results = pd . DataFrame ([ scores ( "Month as a number (1 to 12)" , y_test , model_num . predict ( make_X ( test_num , features_num ))), scores ( "Month as 12 categories" , y_test , predicted_test ), ]) print ( results . to_string ( index = False )) features_num = [f if f != "arrival_month" else "month_number" for f in FEATURES] train_num, test_num = train.assign(month_number=train["arrival_month"]), test.assign(month_number=test["arrival_month"]) model_num = LinearRegression().fit(make_X(train_num, features_num), y_train) results = pd.DataFrame([ scores("Month as a number (1 to 12)", y_test, model_num.predict(make_X(test_num, features_num))), scores("Month as 12 categories", y_test, predicted_test), ]) print(results.to_string(index=False)) model MAE (USD/night) MAE as % of avg rate R² Month as a number (1 to 12) 26.9 21% 0.621 Month as 12 categories 20.5 16% 0.738 Better inputs help, but a line has limits. Treating the month as categories lifts R² from about 0.62 to 0.74 and cuts the typical miss from USD 27 to USD 20. But no choice of inputs lets a model that adds one effect per input learn "January is peak at the beach and quiet in Santiago", or "suites go up more than other rooms in peak season". Those are interactions and curves . Coming in week 5: decision trees learn "Puerto Varas in July" on their own, and the typical miss drops well below USD 20. {"q": "In the heatmap, Santiago bookings in January are priced about USD 70 too high on average. What is the best explanation?", "options": ["Santiago guests in January negotiated discounts the data does not show", "The test set has too few Santiago bookings to say anything", "The model has one January effect for all hotels, learned mostly from the beach and the lake, where January is peak season", "Least squares always overprices the cheapest hotel"], "answer": 2, "why": "The month coefficients are shared by the three hotels. January is peak season in Viña and Puerto Varas, so the January effect is large, and the model applies it to Santiago, where January is quiet. The misses follow a pattern: the model is missing an interaction between hotel and month.", "code": false} 10 Case clinic: a first model ¶ This week's step of the applied case is a first model : a linear model evaluated on test data. In the next 40 minutes, with your team, in the case toolkit (in Colab): Run sections 05 Train/test split and baseline and 06 Linear model with your column to predict: linear regression for a number (TalentCo's salary), logistic regression for yes/no (FinTrust's default). Keep 25% of the rows as the sealed test set ( test_size=0.25 , random_state=42 ), as we did. Check what goes in. Remove IDs, raw dates and anything only known after the outcome (leakage). Read the error in business units: "our salary estimate is typically off by USD …, about …% of the average salary". For classification, write down the accuracy and compare it with the "predict the most common answer" baseline; week 4 gives you better metrics. Write three coefficient sentences like the ones in step 07, each with its reference category. What to bring next week: the test error of your first model next to a baseline, in one sentence a manager understands, and one place where you suspect the line is wrong (a group, a season, a range of values). Before next week: do the lab, A rate simulator , and its graded quiz. In week 4, Predicting cancellations , the answer becomes yes or no, and the question becomes how many rooms to oversell.
