docs.text: Altamar's revenue manager wants a number, not a hunch: the nightly rate a booking should carry, from its hotel, month, room and channel. Today you build that model with ready-made code, read its coefficients like a revenue manager, and say in dollars how wrong it is, and where it goes wrong. 4 hours 10 ideas Runs in your browser Case: a first model Before anything else: run the cell below. On this site, press its Run button (in Google Colab, the ▶ next to it, or Shift + Enter). It loads today's tools and two small helpers we use later. You don't need to read it. In [1]: Copied! # Setup: tools for today. Run this cell first; you don't need to read it. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , r2_score DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/" MONTHS = [ "Jan" , "Feb" , "Mar" , "Apr" , "May" , "Jun" , "Jul" , "Aug" , "Sep" , "Oct" , "Nov" , "Dec" ] HOTELS = [ "Santiago" , "Viña del Mar" , "Puerto Varas" ] pd . set_option ( "display.width" , 120 ) sns . set_theme ( style = "whitegrid" ) # Every category of each text column. The FIRST one is the reference: its coefficient is 0, # and the model measures the others against it. LEVELS = { "hotel" : [ "Santiago" , "Viña del Mar" , "Puerto Varas" ], "room_type" : [ "Standard" , "Superior" , "Suite" ], "channel" : [ "Direct" , "Online travel agency" , "Corporate" , "Travel agent" ], "customer_type" : [ "Leisure" , "Business" , "Group" ], "deposit" : [ "No deposit" , "Non-refundable" ], "country" : [ "Chile" , "Argentina" , "Brazil" , "United States" , "Europe" , "Other" , "Unknown" ], "arrival_month" : list ( range ( 1 , 13 )), } def make_X ( data , features ): """Turn the chosen columns into numbers: one 0/1 column per category, minus the reference.""" parts = [] for col in features : if col in LEVELS : values = pd . Series ( pd . Categorical ( data [ col ], categories = LEVELS [ col ]), index = data . index ) parts . append ( pd . get_dummies ( values , prefix = col , drop_first = True , dtype = "int64" )) else : parts . append ( data [[ col ]]) return pd . concat ( parts , axis = 1 ) def scores ( name , actual , predicted ): """One row of a results table: the typical error in USD per night, and R².""" mae = mean_absolute_error ( actual , predicted ) return { "model" : name , "MAE (USD/night)" : round ( mae , 1 ), "MAE as % o f avg rate" : f " { mae / actual . mean () : .0% } " , "R²" : round ( r2_score ( actual , predicted ), 3 )} print ( "Ready: tools loaded." ) # Setup: tools for today. Run this cell first; you don't need to read it. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/" MONTHS = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"] HOTELS = ["Santiago", "Viña del Mar", "Puerto Varas"] pd.set_option("display.width", 120) sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid") # Every category of each text column. The FIRST one is the reference: its coefficient is 0, # and the model measures the others against it. LEVELS = { "hotel": ["Santiago", "Viña del Mar", "Puerto Varas"], "room_type": ["Standard", "Superior", "Suite"], "channel": ["Direct", "Online travel agency", "Corporate", "Travel agent"], "customer_type": ["Leisure", "Business", "Group"], "deposit": ["No deposit", "Non-refundable"], "country": ["Chile", "Argentina", "Brazil", "United States", "Europe", "Other", "Unknown"], "arrival_month": list(range(1, 13)), } def make_X(data, features): """Turn the chosen columns into numbers: one 0/1 column per category, minus the reference.""" parts = [] for col in features: if col in LEVELS: values = pd.Series(pd.Categorical(data[col], categories=LEVELS[col]), index=data.index) parts.append(pd.get_dummies(values, prefix=col, drop_first=True, dtype="int64")) else: parts.append(data[[col]]) return pd.concat(parts, axis=1) def scores(name, actual, predicted): """One row of a results table: the typical error in USD per night, and R².""" mae = mean_absolute_error(actual, predicted) return {"model": name, "MAE (USD/night)": round(mae, 1), "MAE as % of avg rate": f"{mae / actual.mean():.0%}", "R²": round(r2_score(actual, predicted), 3)} print("Ready: tools loaded.") Ready: tools loaded.
docs.title: Pricing with regression

docs.text: In week 2 we cleaned the bookings: one spelling per hotel and channel, no free rooms or typed-in extra zeros, no impossible dates. And the clean data told a story: the rate depends on the hotel, the season and the room , and each hotel has its own seasons. Now revenue management asks for more than a story. When a booking request comes in, they want an estimate of the right rate for it , one that combines everything we know about the booking at once. That estimate is a model . Load the 5,964 clean bookings and print the average rate for each hotel and room type. Look at how far apart the cells are. In [2]: Copied! df = pd . read_csv ( DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv" ) df [ "arrival_month" ] = pd . to_datetime ( df [ "arrival_date" ]) . dt . month # 1 = January … 12 = December print ( f " { len ( df ) : , } bookings · average rate USD { df [ 'adr' ] . mean () : .0f } per night \n " ) table = df . pivot_table ( index = "hotel" , columns = "room_type" , values = "adr" , aggfunc = "mean" ) print ( table . reindex ( HOTELS )[[ "Standard" , "Superior" , "Suite" ]] . round ( 0 ) . to_string ()) df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv") df["arrival_month"] = pd.to_datetime(df["arrival_date"]).dt.month # 1 = January … 12 = December print(f"{len(df):,} bookings · average rate USD {df['adr'].mean():.0f} per night\n") table = df.pivot_table(index="hotel", columns="room_type", values="adr", aggfunc="mean") print(table.reindex(HOTELS)[["Standard", "Superior", "Suite"]].round(0).to_string()) 5,964 bookings · average rate USD 127 per night room_type Standard Superior Suite hotel Santiago 85.0 109.0 156.0 Viña del Mar 117.0 154.0 232.0 Puerto Varas 133.0 171.0 257.0 The same rates by arrival month, one line per hotel. Look for the months where the lines cross. In [3]: Copied! monthly = df . pivot_table ( index = "arrival_month" , columns = "hotel" , values = "adr" , aggfunc = "mean" )[ HOTELS ] ax = monthly . plot ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 ), marker = "o" ) ax . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 ), MONTHS ) ax . set ( title = "Average nightly rate by arrival month" , xlabel = "arrival month" , ylabel = "USD per night" ) plt . show () monthly = df.pivot_table(index="arrival_month", columns="hotel", values="adr", aggfunc="mean")[HOTELS] ax = monthly.plot(figsize=(8, 4.5), marker="o") ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13), MONTHS) ax.set(title="Average nightly rate by arrival month", xlabel="arrival month", ylabel="USD per night") plt.show() Business takeaway: a Suite costs about twice a Standard room, Puerto Varas and Viña charge more than Santiago, and summer (January and February) is peak season at the beach and the lake but the quiet season in Santiago. A good rate estimate has to weigh all of this at once, for every booking. That is the job of today's model.
docs.title: 01 Previously at Altamar

docs.text: Remember week 1's picture: a model is a recipe that turns inputs into an answer. Today the answer is a number, the predicted rate , so this is regression . The recipe is not written by us: the model learns it from past bookings , where we know both the inputs and the rate the guest paid. Then it applies the recipe to a new request whose rate is still unknown. Which inputs? Only what we know when the guest asks for a price : hotel, arrival month, room, channel, nights, how far ahead they book, how many guests. Look at one past booking split into its two halves: what the model sees, and the answer it learns from. In [4]: Copied! booking = df . iloc [ 0 ] inputs = [ "hotel" , "arrival_month" , "room_type" , "channel" , "nights" , "lead_time_days" , "adults" ] print ( "What the model sees (known when the guest asks for a price):" ) print ( booking [ inputs ] . to_string ()) print ( f " \n The answer it learns from: adr = USD { booking [ 'adr' ] : .2f } per night" ) booking = df.iloc[0] inputs = ["hotel", "arrival_month", "room_type", "channel", "nights", "lead_time_days", "adults"] print("What the model sees (known when the guest asks for a price):") print(booking[inputs].to_string()) print(f"\nThe answer it learns from: adr = USD {booking['adr']:.2f} per night") What the model sees (known when the guest asks for a price): hotel Viña del Mar arrival_month 1 room_type Superior channel Online travel agency nights 3 lead_time_days 92 adults 2 The answer it learns from: adr = USD 202.58 per night What we must not feed the recipe: Column Why not adr It is the answer. A model that sees it scores perfectly and is useless. booking_id A label, not a fact about the stay. Booking AH-200457 is not "bigger" than AH-200001. booking_date , arrival_date Text like "2025-02-14" is not a number. We keep what matters, the month ( arrival_month ). canceled We only know it after the booking. For a new request it does not exist yet. Watch out: an input that secretly contains the answer is called leakage . It makes a model look brilliant in testing and fail on the first real booking. {"q": "The revenue team wants to predict the rate of new booking requests. Which column should not be an input?", "options": ["room_type", "lead_time_days", "canceled", "arrival_month"], "answer": 2, "why": "Whether a booking is cancelled is only known later, so it does not exist when we quote a new request. Room, lead time and month are all known at the moment the guest asks for a price.", "code": false}
docs.title: 02 A model is a recipe

docs.text:
How do we know if the recipe is any good? Not by asking it about bookings it learned from: that is an exam where the student has seen the answers. So before learning anything, we split the bookings. Three quarters go to the training set : the model learns from these. One quarter goes into a sealed envelope , the test set , which we open only once, at the end, to measure how wrong the model is on bookings it has never seen. Press Play . ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Split the real bookings: 75% to learn from, 25% sealed ( test_size=0.25 ). random_state=42 makes the shuffle the same every time, for everyone in the class. Check that both parts look alike. In [5]: Copied! train , test = train_test_split ( df , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 42 ) print ( f "Training set: { len ( train ) : , } bookings · test set: { len ( test ) : , } bookings (sealed) 
 " ) mix = pd . DataFrame ({ "training set" : train [ "hotel" ] . value_counts ( normalize = True ), "test set" : test [ "hotel" ] . value_counts ( normalize = True )}) . reindex ( HOTELS ) print (( mix * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) . astype ( str ) . add ( " %" ) . to_string ()) print ( f " 
 Average rate: USD { train [ 'adr' ] . mean () : .1f } in training, USD { test [ 'adr' ] . mean () : .1f } in test" ) train, test = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.25, random_state=42) print(f"Training set: {len(train):,} bookings · test set: {len(test):,} bookings (sealed)
") mix = pd.DataFrame({"training set": train["hotel"].value_counts(normalize=True), "test set": test["hotel"].value_counts(normalize=True)}).reindex(HOTELS) print((mix * 100).round(1).astype(str).add(" %").to_string()) print(f"
Average rate: USD {train['adr'].mean():.1f} in training, USD {test['adr'].mean():.1f} in test") Training set: 4,473 bookings · test set: 1,491 bookings (sealed) training set test set hotel Santiago 41.4 % 40.0 % Viña del Mar 34.0 % 33.7 % Puerto Varas 24.6 % 26.4 % Average rate: USD 127.4 in training, USD 127.2 in test Business takeaway: the two sets have the same mix of hotels and almost the same average rate, so the test set is a fair stand-in for "next month's bookings". From now on, the model learns only from train ; test stays sealed until step 08.
docs.title: 03 Train and test: a sealed envelope

docs.text: A linear model can multiply nights by a number. It cannot multiply "Suite" . So each text column becomes a few 0/1 columns , one per category: room_type_Suite is 1 for suites and 0 otherwise. This is called one-hot encoding , or making dummies . One category per column gets no 0/1 column at all: the reference . A row of zeros means "reference", and every other category is measured against it . Encode the six bookings below, then try drop_first=True . ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. See it on six real bookings: the text column next to its 0/1 columns, first with all three, then without the reference. In [6]: Copied! sample = df [[ "hotel" , "room_type" , "adr" ]] . groupby ( "room_type" ) . head ( 2 ) . sort_index () # two of each room rooms = pd . get_dummies ( sample [ "room_type" ], prefix = "room_type" , dtype = "int64" ) print ( pd . concat ([ sample , rooms ], axis = 1 ) . to_string (), " \n " ) print ( "With drop_first=True, Standard (first alphabetically) becomes the reference:" ) print ( pd . get_dummies ( sample [ "room_type" ], prefix = "room_type" , drop_first = True , dtype = "int64" ) . to_string ()) sample = df[["hotel", "room_type", "adr"]].groupby("room_type").head(2).sort_index() # two of each room rooms = pd.get_dummies(sample["room_type"], prefix="room_type", dtype="int64") print(pd.concat([sample, rooms], axis=1).to_string(), "\n") print("With drop_first=True, Standard (first alphabetically) becomes the reference:") print(pd.get_dummies(sample["room_type"], prefix="room_type", drop_first=True, dtype="int64").to_string()) hotel room_type adr room_type_Standard room_type_Suite room_type_Superior 0 Viña del Mar Superior 202.58 0 0 1 1 Santiago Standard 115.22 1 0 0 2 Viña del Mar Standard 68.57 1 0 0 3 Viña del Mar Superior 133.13 0 0 1 9 Santiago Suite 177.19 0 1 0 10 Santiago Suite 167.53 0 1 0 With drop_first=True, Standard (first alphabetically) becomes the reference: room_type_Suite room_type_Superior 0 0 1 1 0 0 2 0 0 3 0 1 9 1 0 10 1 0 We choose the references so the coefficients read naturally for a revenue manager: "compared with a Standard room, booked direct, at Santiago, in January". Column Reference hotel Santiago room_type Standard channel Direct customer_type Leisure arrival_month 1 (January) deposit , country No deposit, Chile The Setup cell has a helper, make_X , that does the encoding for every text column with these references. Here it is on four bookings. In [7]: Copied! print ( make_X ( df . head ( 4 ), [ "hotel" , "room_type" , "nights" ]) . to_string ()) print(make_X(df.head(4), ["hotel", "room_type", "nights"]).to_string()) hotel_Viña del Mar hotel_Puerto Varas room_type_Superior room_type_Suite nights 0 1 0 1 0 3 1 0 0 0 0 2 2 1 0 0 0 5 3 1 0 1 0 6 Read the first row: a 0 in both hotel columns means Santiago ; a 0 in both room columns means Standard . Numbers like nights pass through unchanged. {"q": "With Standard as the reference room, how does the table show a booking for a Standard room?", "options": ["room_type_Standard = 1", "room_type_Superior = 0 and room_type_Suite = 0", "room_type_Superior = 1 and room_type_Suite = 1", "It is left out of the table"], "answer": 1, "why": "The reference has no column of its own: all zeros in the room columns means Standard. That is why every room coefficient reads as “USD more (or less) than a Standard room”.", "code": false}
docs.title: 04 Categories become numbers

docs.text: How does the model pick its numbers? Start with one input and one picture. At Viña del Mar, busy months charge more. Draw any line through the twelve months: each month misses it by some dollars (a residual ). Least squares squares every miss and picks the line with the smallest total . Squaring has a consequence a manager should know: a miss of USD 40 counts four times as much as a miss of USD 20. Move the line yourself, then press Fit least squares . ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The same picture in code. LinearRegression finds the slope and intercept that the simulator found. (Here we use all bookings, because it only illustrates the idea; the real model in step 06 learns from train only.) In [8]: Copied! vina = df [ df [ "hotel" ] == "Viña del Mar" ] months = vina . groupby ( "arrival_month" ) . agg ( bookings = ( "adr" , "size" ), rate = ( "adr" , "mean" )) months [ "bookings" ] = months [ "bookings" ] / 2 # two years of data: bookings in a typical year line = LinearRegression () . fit ( months [[ "bookings" ]], months [ "rate" ]) print ( f "Slope: USD { line . coef_ [ 0 ] : .2f } per extra booking, so 10 more bookings in a month ≈ USD { 10 * line . coef_ [ 0 ] : .0f } higher rate" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax . scatter ( months [ "bookings" ], months [ "rate" ], color = "black" ) for m , row in months [ months [ "bookings" ] > 65 ] . iterrows (): # label the busy months ax . annotate ( MONTHS [ m - 1 ], ( row [ "bookings" ], row [ "rate" ]), xytext = ( 5 , 3 ), textcoords = "offset points" ) grid = pd . DataFrame ({ "bookings" : np . linspace ( 0 , 250 , 50 )}) ax . plot ( grid [ "bookings" ], line . predict ( grid ), label = "least-squares line" ) ax . set ( title = "Viña del Mar: busier months, higher rates" , xlabel = "bookings arriving in the month (typical year)" , ylabel = "average rate (USD per night)" ) ax . legend (); plt . show () vina = df[df["hotel"] == "Viña del Mar"] months = vina.groupby("arrival_month").agg(bookings=("adr", "size"), rate=("adr", "mean")) months["bookings"] = months["bookings"] / 2 # two years of data: bookings in a typical year line = LinearRegression().fit(months[["bookings"]], months["rate"]) print(f"Slope: USD {line.coef_[0]:.2f} per extra booking, so 10 more bookings in a month ≈ USD {10 * line.coef_[0]:.0f} higher rate") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5)) ax.scatter(months["bookings"], months["rate"], color="black") for m, row in months[months["bookings"] > 65].iterrows(): # label the busy months ax.annotate(MONTHS[m - 1], (row["bookings"], row["rate"]), xytext=(5, 3), textcoords="offset points") grid = pd.DataFrame({"bookings": np.linspace(0, 250, 50)}) ax.plot(grid["bookings"], line.predict(grid), label="least-squares line") ax.set(title="Viña del Mar: busier months, higher rates", xlabel="bookings arriving in the month (typical year)", ylabel="average rate (USD per night)") ax.legend(); plt.show() Slope: USD 0.61 per extra booking, so 10 more bookings in a month ≈ USD 6 higher rate Business takeaway: the slope is a sentence: every 10 extra bookings in a month go with about USD 6 more per night . The real model does exactly this, but with 36 inputs at once : it finds one number per input so that the total squared miss over 4,473 training bookings is as small as possible. ☕ Break (10 minutes). In the second block we build Altamar's rate model, read it like a revenue manager, measure its error in dollars, and find where it fails.
docs.title: 05 The best line

docs.text: Now the full recipe. We give the model every input known when a guest asks for a price, with the month as twelve categories ( arrival_month ), because seasons do not go up in a straight line from January to December. Three steps, the same in every project: choose inputs → encode them → fit on the training set . Choose the inputs, encode training and test the same way, and fit LinearRegression on the training bookings only. In [9]: Copied! FEATURES = [ "hotel" , "arrival_month" , "room_type" , "channel" , "customer_type" , "nights" , "weekend_nights" , "lead_time_days" , "adults" , "children" , "deposit" , "repeat_guest" , "previous_cancellations" , "special_requests" , "parking" , "country" ] X_train , X_test = make_X ( train , FEATURES ), make_X ( test , FEATURES ) y_train , y_test = train [ "adr" ], test [ "adr" ] model = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_train , y_train ) print ( f " { len ( FEATURES ) } inputs became { X_train . shape [ 1 ] } number columns." ) print ( f "The model learned { X_train . shape [ 1 ] } coefficients and an intercept from { len ( X_train ) : , } bookings." ) FEATURES = ["hotel", "arrival_month", "room_type", "channel", "customer_type", "nights", "weekend_nights", "lead_time_days", "adults", "children", "deposit", "repeat_guest", "previous_cancellations", "special_requests", "parking", "country"] X_train, X_test = make_X(train, FEATURES), make_X(test, FEATURES) y_train, y_test = train["adr"], test["adr"] model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train) print(f"{len(FEATURES)} inputs became {X_train.shape[1]} number columns.") print(f"The model learned {X_train.shape[1]} coefficients and an intercept from {len(X_train):,} bookings.") 16 inputs became 36 number columns. The model learned 36 coefficients and an intercept from 4,473 bookings. Open the envelope a crack: predict six test bookings the model has never seen, next to the rate they actually paid. In [10]: Copied! compare = test [[ "hotel" , "arrival_month" , "room_type" , "channel" , "adr" ]] . head ( 6 ) . copy () compare [ "predicted" ] = model . predict ( X_test . head ( 6 )) . round ( 1 ) compare [ "miss (USD)" ] = ( compare [ "adr" ] - compare [ "predicted" ]) . round ( 1 ) print ( compare . to_string ( index = False )) compare = test[["hotel", "arrival_month", "room_type", "channel", "adr"]].head(6).copy() compare["predicted"] = model.predict(X_test.head(6)).round(1) compare["miss (USD)"] = (compare["adr"] - compare["predicted"]).round(1) print(compare.to_string(index=False)) hotel arrival_month room_type channel adr predicted miss (USD) Viña del Mar 11 Superior Direct 139.00 145.8 -6.8 Puerto Varas 11 Standard Corporate 108.58 109.4 -0.8 Viña del Mar 12 Standard Online travel agency 113.45 118.3 -4.8 Viña del Mar 5 Standard Direct 112.24 96.0 16.2 Puerto Varas 8 Superior Direct 135.34 148.8 -13.5 Puerto Varas 7 Standard Direct 153.98 139.7 14.3 Some predictions land within a dollar, others miss by USD 15 or more. A positive miss means the guest paid more than the model predicted: the model would have underpriced the room. Before asking how wrong it is on average (step 08), let's open the recipe.
docs.title: 06 One model for every booking

docs.text: Each coefficient is in USD per night . For a category, it is the difference against the reference , everything else equal. For a number, it is the change per unit (per night, per day booked ahead, per adult). The intercept is the starting point: a Standard room booked direct at Santiago in January, before adding anything else. Print the intercept and the fifteen largest coefficients, biggest effect first. In [11]: Copied! coefs = pd . Series ( model . coef_ , index = X_train . columns ) . round ( 1 ) print ( f "Intercept: USD { model . intercept_ : .1f } \n " ) print ( coefs . sort_values ( key = abs , ascending = False ) . head ( 15 ) . to_string ()) coefs = pd.Series(model.coef_, index=X_train.columns).round(1) print(f"Intercept: USD {model.intercept_:.1f}\n") print(coefs.sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False).head(15).to_string()) Intercept: USD 132.8 room_type_Suite 95.0 arrival_month_6 -69.9 arrival_month_5 -67.1 arrival_month_8 -65.8 arrival_month_4 -63.6 arrival_month_9 -59.7 arrival_month_10 -55.7 arrival_month_11 -53.0 arrival_month_3 -50.7 arrival_month_7 -45.3 arrival_month_12 -42.8 hotel_Puerto Varas 41.0 room_type_Superior 31.1 hotel_Viña del Mar 20.8 channel_Travel agent -19.5 The same coefficients as a picture, without the months (step 09 looks at them) and the countries (all small). Orange bars raise the rate, blue bars lower it. In [12]: Copied! show = coefs [ ~ coefs . index . str . startswith (( "arrival_month" , "country" ))] . sort_values () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) ax . barh ( show . index , show . values , color = np . where ( show . values > 0 , "tab:orange" , "tab:blue" )) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 1 ) ax . set ( title = "What each input adds to the nightly rate" , xlabel = "USD per night (vs the reference, or per unit)" ) plt . tight_layout (); plt . show () show = coefs[~coefs.index.str.startswith(("arrival_month", "country"))].sort_values() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6)) ax.barh(show.index, show.values, color=np.where(show.values > 0, "tab:orange", "tab:blue")) ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1) ax.set(title="What each input adds to the nightly rate", xlabel="USD per night (vs the reference, or per unit)") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() Translate them into sentences a revenue manager would use. In [13]: Copied! c = coefs print ( f "A suite adds about USD { c [ 'room_type_Suite' ] : .0f } per night over a Standard room; a Superior about USD { c [ 'room_type_Superior' ] : .0f } ." ) print ( f "Puerto Varas is about USD { c [ 'hotel_Puerto Varas' ] : .0f } above Santiago; Viña del Mar about USD { c [ 'hotel_Viña del Mar' ] : .0f } ." ) print ( f "Corporate rates are about USD { - c [ 'channel_Corporate' ] : .0f } lower than direct; travel agents about USD { - c [ 'channel_Travel agent' ] : .0f } lower." ) print ( f "Online travel agency bookings pay about USD { c [ 'channel_Online travel agency' ] : .0f } more than direct ones." ) print ( f "Each extra night lowers the nightly rate by about USD { - c [ 'nights' ] : .1f } ; each extra adult adds about USD { c [ 'adults' ] : .0f } ." ) print ( f "Each weekend night adds USD { c [ 'weekend_nights' ] : .1f } : almost nothing. Keep that in mind for step 09." ) c = coefs print(f"A suite adds about USD {c['room_type_Suite']:.0f} per night over a Standard room; a Superior about USD {c['room_type_Superior']:.0f}.") print(f"Puerto Varas is about USD {c['hotel_Puerto Varas']:.0f} above Santiago; Viña del Mar about USD {c['hotel_Viña del Mar']:.0f}.") print(f"Corporate rates are about USD {-c['channel_Corporate']:.0f} lower than direct; travel agents about USD {-c['channel_Travel agent']:.0f} lower.") print(f"Online travel agency bookings pay about USD {c['channel_Online travel agency']:.0f} more than direct ones.") print(f"Each extra night lowers the nightly rate by about USD {-c['nights']:.1f}; each extra adult adds about USD {c['adults']:.0f}.") print(f"Each weekend night adds USD {c['weekend_nights']:.1f}: almost nothing. Keep that in mind for step 09.") A suite adds about USD 95 per night over a Standard room; a Superior about USD 31. Puerto Varas is about USD 41 above Santiago; Viña del Mar about USD 21. Corporate rates are about USD 14 lower than direct; travel agents about USD 20 lower. Online travel agency bookings pay about USD 6 more than direct ones. Each extra night lowers the nightly rate by about USD 3.3; each extra adult adds about USD 9. Each weekend night adds USD 0.0: almost nothing. Keep that in mind for step 09. Watch out: average effects, not causes. "Corporate rates are USD 14 lower" describes the bookings we had, everything else equal. It does not promise that moving a corporate client to the direct channel earns USD 14 more: that client might not book at all. And "everything else equal" only covers the inputs we gave the model. Build a booking from these numbers yourself. Corporate clients get lower rates because of an agreement; without it, they might book elsewhere. Changing the channel is a business decision the data alone cannot price.", "code": false}
docs.title: 07 Reading the coefficients like a revenue manager

docs.text: Time to open the sealed envelope. Three numbers, all on the test set : MAE (mean absolute error): the typical miss, in USD per night . The number to give a manager. MAE as a % of the average rate : is USD 20 a lot? For a USD 127 room, yes and no. R² : the share of the differences between rates that the model explains. 1 is perfect; 0 is no better than quoting the average to everyone. Drag the misses below and watch the three numbers react. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Score the model on the training and the test set, next to a baseline that a person could compute in a spreadsheet: quote each hotel's average rate to every booking. A model is only worth using if it beats the baseline. In [14]: Copied! hotel_average = train . groupby ( "hotel" )[ "adr" ] . mean () predicted_test = model . predict ( X_test ) results = pd . DataFrame ([ scores ( "Baseline: the hotel's average rate (test)" , y_test , test [ "hotel" ] . map ( hotel_average )), scores ( "Linear model, training set" , y_train , model . predict ( X_train )), scores ( "Linear model, test set" , y_test , predicted_test ), ]) print ( results . to_string ( index = False )) mae = mean_absolute_error ( y_test , predicted_test ) print ( f " \n On bookings it has never seen, the model's rate is typically off by USD { mae : .0f } per night," ) print ( f "about { mae / y_test . mean () : .0% } of the average rate (USD { y_test . mean () : .0f } )." ) hotel_average = train.groupby("hotel")["adr"].mean() predicted_test = model.predict(X_test) results = pd.DataFrame([ scores("Baseline: the hotel's average rate (test)", y_test, test["hotel"].map(hotel_average)), scores("Linear model, training set", y_train, model.predict(X_train)), scores("Linear model, test set", y_test, predicted_test), ]) print(results.to_string(index=False)) mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, predicted_test) print(f"\nOn bookings it has never seen, the model's rate is typically off by USD {mae:.0f} per night,") print(f"about {mae / y_test.mean():.0%} of the average rate (USD {y_test.mean():.0f}).") model MAE (USD/night) MAE as % of avg rate R² Baseline: the hotel's average rate (test) 35.8 28% 0.197 Linear model, training set 20.1 16% 0.740 Linear model, test set 20.5 16% 0.738 On bookings it has never seen, the model's rate is typically off by USD 20 per night, about 16% of the average rate (USD 127). Reading the results: It beats the baseline clearly: a typical miss of USD 20 instead of USD 36, and R² 0.74 instead of 0.20. Training and test are almost the same (MAE 20.1 vs 20.5). The model did not memorize its training bookings; we can expect about the same error next month. But USD 20 is 16% of the average rate. Good enough to suggest a starting rate or to flag a quote that looks far off; not good enough to set peak-season suite prices on its own. {"q": "A colleague's model has a typical error (MAE) of USD 5 on the training set and USD 31 on the test set. Ours has USD 20 and USD 20. Which model should revenue management use?", "options": ["The colleague's: USD 5 is the best number in the table", "Ours: its test error is lower, and train ≈ test means it will behave the same on new bookings", "Either: the training error is what matters", "Neither: a model must have zero error on the training set"], "answer": 1, "why": "The test set is the only honest exam. USD 5 on training and USD 31 on test is the signature of overfitting: the model memorized its training bookings and is worse on new ones.", "code": false}
docs.title: 08 How wrong are we?

docs.text: An average error hides where the model is wrong. If the misses were random, there would be nothing to fix. If they follow a pattern , the model is missing something a manager would recognise. Plot the actual rate of every test booking against the model's prediction. Points on the diagonal are perfect; look at the most expensive bookings, top right. In [15]: Copied! view = test . assign ( predicted = predicted_test , miss = y_test - predicted_test ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7.5 , 6 )) sns . scatterplot ( data = view , x = "predicted" , y = "adr" , hue = "hotel" , hue_order = HOTELS , alpha = 0.5 , s = 18 , ax = ax ) ax . plot ([ 0 , 450 ], [ 0 , 450 ], color = "black" , lw = 1 , label = "perfect prediction" ) ax . set ( title = "Actual vs predicted rate, test bookings" , xlabel = "predicted rate (USD per night)" , ylabel = "actual rate (USD per night)" ) ax . legend (); plt . show () print ( f "Test bookings that paid over USD 300 a night: { ( view [ 'adr' ] > 300 ) . sum () } ." ) print ( f "Test bookings the model priced over USD 300: { ( view [ 'predicted' ] > 300 ) . sum () } ." ) view = test.assign(predicted=predicted_test, miss=y_test - predicted_test) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6)) sns.scatterplot(data=view, x="predicted", y="adr", hue="hotel", hue_order=HOTELS, alpha=0.5, s=18, ax=ax) ax.plot([0, 450], [0, 450], color="black", lw=1, label="perfect prediction") ax.set(title="Actual vs predicted rate, test bookings", xlabel="predicted rate (USD per night)", ylabel="actual rate (USD per night)") ax.legend(); plt.show() print(f"Test bookings that paid over USD 300 a night: {(view['adr'] > 300).sum()}.") print(f"Test bookings the model priced over USD 300: {(view['predicted'] > 300).sum()}.") Test bookings that paid over USD 300 a night: 32. Test bookings the model priced over USD 300: 0. The model misses the peaks. The most expensive bookings sit far above the diagonal: a line that adds fixed amounts never reaches the top rates of peak-season suites. And there is a cloud of Santiago bookings priced too high. When and where? Average miss for each hotel and arrival month (actual − predicted). Red cells: the model underprices ; blue cells: it overprices . In [16]: Copied! heat = view . pivot_table ( index = "hotel" , columns = "arrival_month" , values = "miss" , aggfunc = "mean" ) . reindex ( HOTELS ) heat . columns = MONTHS fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 11 , 3.4 )) sns . heatmap ( heat , annot = True , fmt = ".0f" , cmap = "RdBu_r" , center = 0 , cbar_kws = { "label" : "USD per night" }, ax = ax ) ax . set ( title = "Average miss by hotel and month: red = priced too low, blue = priced too high" , xlabel = "arrival month" , ylabel = "" ) ax . tick_params ( axis = "y" , rotation = 0 ) plt . show () heat = view.pivot_table(index="hotel", columns="arrival_month", values="miss", aggfunc="mean").reindex(HOTELS) heat.columns = MONTHS fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.4)) sns.heatmap(heat, annot=True, fmt=".0f", cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, cbar_kws={"label": "USD per night"}, ax=ax) ax.set(title="Average miss by hotel and month: red = priced too low, blue = priced too high", xlabel="arrival month", ylabel="") ax.tick_params(axis="y", rotation=0) plt.show() A systematic pattern, not noise. The model has one January effect, one July effect, shared by all three hotels. It learned that January is expensive (true at the beach and the lake) and charges it to Santiago too, where January is quiet: about USD 70 too much per night. July is a peak only in Puerto Varas, so the model underprices it there and overprices it in Viña. Seasons differ by hotel , and a model that adds one month effect for everyone cannot draw that. Switch hotels below. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Does giving the model better inputs help? Compare the month as a single number (1 to 12, so the model can only draw a slope through the year) with the month as twelve categories . In [17]: Copied! features_num = [ f if f != "arrival_month" else "month_number" for f in FEATURES ] train_num , test_num = train . assign ( month_number = train [ "arrival_month" ]), test . assign ( month_number = test [ "arrival_month" ]) model_num = LinearRegression () . fit ( make_X ( train_num , features_num ), y_train ) results = pd . DataFrame ([ scores ( "Month as a number (1 to 12)" , y_test , model_num . predict ( make_X ( test_num , features_num ))), scores ( "Month as 12 categories" , y_test , predicted_test ), ]) print ( results . to_string ( index = False )) features_num = [f if f != "arrival_month" else "month_number" for f in FEATURES] train_num, test_num = train.assign(month_number=train["arrival_month"]), test.assign(month_number=test["arrival_month"]) model_num = LinearRegression().fit(make_X(train_num, features_num), y_train) results = pd.DataFrame([ scores("Month as a number (1 to 12)", y_test, model_num.predict(make_X(test_num, features_num))), scores("Month as 12 categories", y_test, predicted_test), ]) print(results.to_string(index=False)) model MAE (USD/night) MAE as % of avg rate R² Month as a number (1 to 12) 26.9 21% 0.621 Month as 12 categories 20.5 16% 0.738 Better inputs help, but a line has limits. Treating the month as categories lifts R² from about 0.62 to 0.74 and cuts the typical miss from USD 27 to USD 20. But no choice of inputs lets a model that adds one effect per input learn "January is peak at the beach and quiet in Santiago", or "suites go up more than other rooms in peak season". Those are interactions and curves . Coming in week 5: decision trees learn "Puerto Varas in July" on their own, and the typical miss drops well below USD 20. {"q": "In the heatmap, Santiago bookings in January are priced about USD 70 too high on average. What is the best explanation?", "options": ["Santiago guests in January negotiated discounts the data does not show", "The test set has too few Santiago bookings to say anything", "The model has one January effect for all hotels, learned mostly from the beach and the lake, where January is peak season", "Least squares always overprices the cheapest hotel"], "answer": 2, "why": "The month coefficients are shared by the three hotels. January is peak season in Viña and Puerto Varas, so the January effect is large, and the model applies it to Santiago, where January is quiet. The misses follow a pattern: the model is missing an interaction between hotel and month.", "code": false}
docs.title: 09 Where the line fails

docs.text: This week's step of the applied case is a first model : a linear model evaluated on test data. In the next 40 minutes, with your team, in the case toolkit (in Colab): Run sections 05 Train/test split and baseline and 06 Linear model with your column to predict: linear regression for a number (TalentCo's salary), logistic regression for yes/no (FinTrust's default). Keep 25% of the rows as the sealed test set ( test_size=0.25 , random_state=42 ), as we did. Check what goes in. Remove IDs, raw dates and anything only known after the outcome (leakage). Read the error in business units: "our salary estimate is typically off by USD …, about …% of the average salary". For classification, write down the accuracy and compare it with the "predict the most common answer" baseline; week 4 gives you better metrics. Write three coefficient sentences like the ones in step 07, each with its reference category. What to bring next week: the test error of your first model next to a baseline, in one sentence a manager understands, and one place where you suspect the line is wrong (a group, a season, a range of values). Before next week: do the lab, A rate simulator , and its graded quiz. In week 4, Predicting cancellations , the answer becomes yes or no, and the question becomes how many rooms to oversell.

can defend: which rooms to resell, at which hotel, and how many rooms to oversell for a busy week. You will set it with this week's model and the costs of each mistake, then write her a short memo. ≈ 2 hours 5 tasks Runs in your browser Graded quiz What we saw in the live session A logistic regression gives every booking a probability of cancelling. On the test bookings it ranks cancellations above arrivals three times in four (AUC 0.74). A threshold turns the probability into a decision: resell the room or not. Lower thresholds catch more cancellations (recall) and walk more guests (lower precision). The cheapest threshold comes from the two costs : reselling pays off when p is above walk / (walk + empty room). Setup. Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the bookings, retrains the live session's model (same features, same stratified split) and defines two helpers, policy and cheapest , that count walked guests and empty rooms for a threshold. For Altamar's overbooking decision, which matters more, precision or recall? Does your answer depend on the hotel? What would make you change your mind? Show the answer Usually **precision**: every false flag is a guest turned away at the front desk, which costs more than money (reviews, loyalty). A missed cancellation only leaves a room empty, which is what happens today anyway. But the honest answer is "it depends on the costs". Where an empty room costs much more than a walk (Viña in high season), recall matters more and the threshold goes down; where walking a guest is hard (Puerto Varas), precision matters more and it goes up. You would change your mind if the costs changed, for example if a partner hotel next door made walks cheap. 05 A memo to the operations manager ¶ The cell drafts a memo with your numbers from tasks 1 to 3. docs.title: An overbooking policy

docs.text: The operations manager wants a rule for overbooking that she can defend: which rooms to resell, at which hotel, and how many rooms to oversell for a busy week. You will set it with this week's model and the costs of each mistake, then write her a short memo. ≈ 2 hours 5 tasks Runs in your browser Graded quiz What we saw in the live session A logistic regression gives every booking a probability of cancelling. On the test bookings it ranks cancellations above arrivals three times in four (AUC 0.74). A threshold turns the probability into a decision: resell the room or not. Lower thresholds catch more cancellations (recall) and walk more guests (lower precision). The cheapest threshold comes from the two costs : reselling pays off when p is above walk / (walk + empty room). Setup. Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the bookings, retrains the live session's model (same features, same stratified split) and defines two helpers, policy and cheapest , that count walked guests and empty rooms for a threshold. docs.text: Every policy has two mistakes: a cancellation we did not resell ( an empty room ) and a resold booking whose guest comes anyway ( a walked guest ). Start in the simulator: move both costs and the threshold, and watch the cheapest point move. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Now in code. ✏️ Set the two costs, run, and read the cheapest threshold, the bookings it flags, and what it saves against doing nothing. best_all['cost'])} saved ({(nothing_all - best_all['cost']) / nothing_all:.0%})") Cheapest threshold: 0.43 (break-even 0.43) Bookings flagged, rooms resold: 451 of 1,491 guests walked 189, rooms left empty 241 Expected cost USD 153,100 against USD 201,200 doing nothing: USD 48,100 saved (24%) Think about it. Guest relations says a walked guest also costs a bad review: set COST_WALK = 600 . Then go back to 300 and set COST_EMPTY_ROOM = 130 , a single night at the average rate. What happens to the threshold and to the savings each time? Why? Show the answer With a walk at USD 600 the break-even rises to 600 / 1,000 = 0.6 and the cheapest threshold moves to 0.54: only 260 rooms are resold and the saving falls from USD 48,100 to about USD 7,000. Dearer walks mean fewer, surer resales. With an empty room at only USD 130 the break-even is 300 / 430 ≈ 0.70, and the cheapest policy resells 2 rooms for a saving of USD 260: when an empty room is cheap, overbooking is not worth the risk. The model is the same every time; only the money changed, and with it the decision.
docs.title: 01 Your costs, your threshold

docs.text: The three hotels are different businesses. An empty room in Puerto Varas loses a long, expensive stay; in Santiago, a short business night. Walking a guest in Santiago is easy (dozens of hotels nearby); in Puerto Varas, in high season, it can mean a taxi to the next town. ✏️ Set the two costs for each hotel and compare the policies. DataFrame ( rows ) . round ( 2 ) by_hotel # ✏️ Change these settings: (empty room, walked guest) in USD COSTS = {"Santiago": (250, 200), # short business stays; many hotels nearby "Viña del Mar": (480, 300), "Puerto Varas": (560, 450)} # long, dear stays; few comparable hotels nearby rows = [] for hotel, (empty, walk) in COSTS.items(): h = test[test["hotel"] == hotel] b = cheapest(h["p_cancel"].values, h["canceled"].values, empty, walk) rows.append({"hotel": hotel, "test bookings": len(h), "cancel rate": h["canceled"].mean(), "break-even": walk / (walk + empty), "cheapest threshold": b["threshold"], "rooms resold": b["resold"], "guests walked": b["walked"], "saved vs doing nothing": empty * h["canceled"].sum() - b["cost"]}) by_hotel = pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2) by_hotel Out[3]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } hotel test bookings cancel rate break-even cheapest threshold rooms resold guests walked saved vs doing nothing 0 Santiago 591 0.25 0.44 0.43 85 40 3250 1 Viña del Mar 526 0.42 0.38 0.36 293 122 45480 2 Puerto Varas 374 0.36 0.45 0.49 99 38 17060 Think about it. Which hotel gains most from the policy, and why that one? Would you use a single company-wide threshold or one per hotel? What is the risk of setting a threshold on only a few hundred bookings? Show the answer **Viña del Mar** gains most, about USD 45,000: the highest cancellation rate (42%) and dear empty rooms give it the lowest threshold (0.36). **Santiago** saves only about USD 3,000: few cancellations, cheap rooms, and a walk costs almost as much as an empty room. Different costs justify **one threshold per hotel**. The risk: with a few hundred bookings, the cheapest threshold jumps around by chance (Viña's 0.36 versus its break-even of 0.38). Anchor each threshold on its break-even, and check it on fresh validation data before using it.
docs.title: 02 One policy per hotel

docs.text: Operations does not resell rooms one by one; it decides how many rooms to oversell for a week. The model helps: adding up the probabilities of all bookings for that week gives the expected number of cancellations , just as ten bookings with a 30% risk each should bring about three cancellations. ✏️ Choose a hotel and a week. In [4]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings HOTEL = "Viña del Mar" WEEK_START = "2025-02-10" # a Monday; the week runs to Sunday MAX_WALK_RISK = 0.10 # the highest chance of walking at least one guest we accept days_from_start = ( pd . to_datetime ( df [ "arrival_date" ]) - pd . Timestamp ( WEEK_START )) . dt . days week = ( df [ "hotel" ] == HOTEL ) & days_from_start . between ( 0 , 6 ) p_week = model . predict_proba ( X [ week ])[:, 1 ] expected = p_week . sum () print ( f " { week . sum () } bookings arrive at { HOTEL } in the week of { WEEK_START } " ) print ( f "Expected cancellations (sum of the probabilities): { expected : .1f } " ) print ( f "What really happened: { df . loc [ week , 'canceled' ] . sum () } cancellations" ) # ✏️ Change these settings HOTEL = "Viña del Mar" WEEK_START = "2025-02-10" # a Monday; the week runs to Sunday MAX_WALK_RISK = 0.10 # the highest chance of walking at least one guest we accept days_from_start = (pd.to_datetime(df["arrival_date"]) - pd.Timestamp(WEEK_START)).dt.days week = (df["hotel"] == HOTEL) & days_from_start.between(0, 6) p_week = model.predict_proba(X[week])[:, 1] expected = p_week.sum() print(f"{week.sum()} bookings arrive at {HOTEL} in the week of {WEEK_START}") print(f"Expected cancellations (sum of the probabilities): {expected:.1f}") print(f"What really happened: {df.loc[week, 'canceled'].sum()} cancellations") 54 bookings arrive at Viña del Mar in the week of 2025-02-10 Expected cancellations (sum of the probabilities): 24.2 What really happened: 24 cancellations Overselling as many rooms as the expected cancellations is a coin flip: in about half of the weeks fewer guests cancel and someone is walked. We simulate 10,000 versions of this week and, for each number of rooms oversold, count the chance of walking someone and the expected cost (with the costs of task 1). Watch out: most of these bookings helped train the model, so this is a demonstration; in real use you score the bookings on the books for next week. We also assume the hotel is full, so every oversold room is a walk if its guest comes. Why is the "safe" number lower than the expected cancellations? Try MAX_WALK_RISK = 0.02 and 0.30 . Then try a quiet week, WEEK_START = "2025-06-09" . Who in the company should choose MAX_WALK_RISK ? Show the answer Cancellations vary from week to week around their expected value (24 here). Overselling 24 rooms walks someone in about four weeks out of ten; to be 90% sure of walking nobody you oversell fewer, 20. With `0.02` you oversell 17; with `0.30`, 22. The cheapest on average (25) accepts a walk in half of the weeks, because an empty room costs more than a walk. A quiet June week has 11 bookings and 3.6 expected cancellations, and the hotel is probably not full: little reason to oversell. `MAX_WALK_RISK` is a guest-experience decision for the general manager, not for the analyst.
docs.title: 03 How many rooms for a busy week?

docs.text: For a resale decision, precision is the share of resold rooms whose guest really cancels (every miss is a walked guest), and recall is the share of cancellations whose room we resell (every miss is an empty room). The simulator shows the trade-off on 80 real test bookings. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. ✏️ Try thresholds between 0.3 and 0.7 and read both metrics, in rooms and guests. In [6]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings THRESHOLD = 0.43 flag = p >= THRESHOLD print ( f "Threshold { THRESHOLD : .2f } : { flag . sum () } of { len ( p ) : , } bookings flagged, their rooms resold" ) print ( f "Precision { precision_score ( cancelled , flag ) : .2f } : share of resold rooms whose guest really cancels" ) print ( f "Recall { recall_score ( cancelled , flag ) : .2f } : share of cancellations whose room we resell" ) print ( f "→ { ( flag & ( cancelled == 0 )) . sum () } guests walked, { ( ~ flag & ( cancelled == 1 )) . sum () } rooms left empty" ) # ✏️ Change these settings THRESHOLD = 0.43 flag = p >= THRESHOLD print(f"Threshold {THRESHOLD:.2f}: {flag.sum()} of {len(p):,} bookings flagged, their rooms resold") print(f"Precision {precision_score(cancelled, flag):.2f}: share of resold rooms whose guest really cancels") print(f"Recall {recall_score(cancelled, flag):.2f}: share of cancellations whose room we resell") print(f"→ {(flag & (cancelled == 0)).sum()} guests walked, {(~flag & (cancelled == 1)).sum()} rooms left empty") Threshold 0.43: 451 of 1,491 bookings flagged, their rooms resold Precision 0.58: share of resold rooms whose guest really cancels Recall 0.52: share of cancellations whose room we resell → 189 guests walked, 241 rooms left empty Think about it. For Altamar's overbooking decision, which matters more, precision or recall? Does your answer depend on the hotel? What would make you change your mind? Show the answer Usually **precision**: every false flag is a guest turned away at the front desk, which costs more than money (reviews, loyalty). A missed cancellation only leaves a room empty, which is what happens today anyway. But the honest answer is "it depends on the costs". Where an empty room costs much more than a walk (Viña in high season), recall matters more and the threshold goes down; where walking a guest is hard (Puerto Varas), precision matters more and it goes up. You would change your mind if the costs changed, for example if a partner hotel next door made walks cheap.

A straight line keeps going forever, so sooner or later it leaves the range 0 to 1. Logistic regression fixes this. It computes a score exactly like a line, then bends it through an S-curve (the sigmoid ) that always stays between 0 and 1: big scores become probabilities near 1, very negative ones near 0. In the simulator, switch between the two models, move the sliders and press Best fit . ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. For the curious: the score is z = b₀ + b₁·x₁ + b₂·x₂ + …, just as in a linear regression, and the probability is p = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). A score of 0 gives exactly 0.5. Watch out: the simulator stops at 120 days on purpose. Further out, the real risk of cancelling falls again, and an S-curve can only go one way. Keep that in mind; section 07 comes back to it. In the second block we turn the probabilities into an overbooking policy, read what drives cancellations, and find where the model goes wrong. 05 Choosing the threshold with money ¶ 0.5 is a habit, not a decision. The right threshold depends on what each mistake costs. Finance gives us two numbers: an empty room (a cancellation we did not resell) costs about USD 400 : an average stay is worth USD 510, and part of it gets resold anyway; a walked guest (a resold booking whose guest shows up) costs about USD 300 : another hotel, a taxi, a voucher. The overbooking policy : resell the room of every booking whose probability of cancelling is at least the threshold. The simulator shows its total cost for every threshold, on our real test bookings. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The same calculation in code. Change the two costs (✏️) and run the next three cells again. In [15]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings COST_EMPTY_ROOM = 400 # USD lost when a booking we kept is cancelled and the room stays empty COST_WALK = 300 # USD to walk a guest whose room we resold: another hotel, taxi, voucher def policy_cost ( threshold , p = p_test , y = y_test ): resold = p >= threshold walked = ( resold & ( y . values == 0 )) . sum () # we resold it and the guest came empty = ( ~ resold & ( y . values == 1 )) . sum () # we kept it and it was cancelled return COST_EMPTY_ROOM * empty + COST_WALK * walked print ( f "Do nothing (resell no room): { usd ( policy_cost ( 1.01 )) } " ) print ( f "Resell every room: { usd ( policy_cost ( 0 )) } " ) print ( f "Threshold 0.50: { usd ( policy_cost ( 0.5 )) } " ) # ✏️ Change these settings COST_EMPTY_ROOM = 400 # USD lost when a booking we kept is cancelled and the room stays empty COST_WALK = 300 # USD to walk a guest whose room we resold: another hotel, taxi, voucher def policy_cost(threshold, p=p_test, y=y_test): resold = p >= threshold walked = (resold & (y.values == 0)).sum() # we resold it and the guest came empty = (~resold & (y.values == 1)).sum() # we kept it and it was cancelled return COST_EMPTY_ROOM * empty + COST_WALK * walked print(f"Do nothing (resell no room): {usd(policy_cost(1.01))}") print(f"Resell every room: {usd(policy_cost(0))}") print(f"Threshold 0.50: {usd(policy_cost(0.5))}") Do nothing (resell no room): USD 201,200 Resell every room: USD 296,400 Threshold 0.50: USD 158,600 Now every threshold from 0 to 1, and the cheapest one. In [17]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) plt . plot ( costs [ "threshold" ], costs [ "total cost" ] / 1000 , lw = 2.5 , color = "#333333" ) plt . axhline ( policy_cost ( 1.01 ) / 1000 , ls = "--" , color = "grey" , label = "do nothing" ) plt . scatter ([ 0.5 ], [ policy_cost ( 0.5 ) / 1000 ], s = 70 , zorder = 3 , color = ARRIVE , label = "the habit: 0.50" ) plt . scatter ([ best [ "threshold" ]], [ best [ "total cost" ] / 1000 ], s = 70 , zorder = 3 , color = CANCEL , label = f "cheapest: { best [ 'threshold' ] : .2f } " ) plt . ylim ( 0 , policy_cost ( 1.01 ) / 1000 * 1.5 ) plt . title ( "Total cost of the overbooking policy, test bookings" ) plt . xlabel ( "threshold: resell the room if p(cancel) ≥ threshold" ) plt . ylabel ( "total cost (thousand USD)" ) plt . legend () plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.plot(costs["threshold"], costs["total cost"] / 1000, lw=2.5, color="#333333") plt.axhline(policy_cost(1.01) / 1000, ls="--", color="grey", label="do nothing") plt.scatter([0.5], [policy_cost(0.5) / 1000], s=70, zorder=3, color=ARRIVE, label="the habit: 0.50") plt.scatter([best["threshold"]], [best["total cost"] / 1000], s=70, zorder=3, color=CANCEL, label=f"cheapest: {best['threshold']:.2f}") plt.ylim(0, policy_cost(1.01) / 1000 * 1.5) plt.title("Total cost of the overbooking policy, test bookings") plt.xlabel("threshold: resell the room if p(cancel) ≥ threshold") plt.ylabel("total cost (thousand USD)") plt.legend() plt.show() The cheapest threshold is 0.43 : resell 451 rooms, for USD 48,100 less than doing nothing and USD 5,500 less than the habit of 0.5. Why 0.43? Reselling a booking with probability p costs on average (1 − p) × 300; keeping it costs p × 400. Reselling pays off when p × 400 > (1 − p) × 300, that is, when p > 300 / 700 ≈ 0.43. The break-even threshold comes from the two costs. Watch out: we chose the threshold on the test set, the same bookings we use to grade the model. In a real project you choose it on separate validation data and keep the test set for the final check. {"q": "Guest relations argues that a walked guest also writes a bad review, and puts the cost of a walk at USD 600 instead of 300. Because we scaled the features, the coefficients are comparable: each one says how strongly one standard step of that feature pushes the score up (towards cancelling) or down (towards arriving). Dummies compare against the baseline: a business guest booking direct for a Standard room in Santiago, with no deposit. In [18]: Copied! coefs = pd . Series ( model . named_steps [ "logit" ] . coef_ [ 0 ], index = X . columns ) top = coefs [ coefs . abs () . sort_values () . index [ - 12 :]] # the 12 strongest, weakest first plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) plt . barh ( top . index , top . values , color = [ CANCEL if c > 0 else ARRIVE for c in top ]) plt . axvline ( 0 , color = "grey" , lw = 0.8 ) plt . title ( "What pushes a booking towards cancelling (scaled coefficients)" ) plt . xlabel ( "← towards arriving towards cancelling →" ) plt . show () coefs = pd.Series(model.named_steps["logit"].coef_[0], index=X.columns) top = coefs[coefs.abs().sort_values().index[-12:]] # the 12 strongest, weakest first plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5)) plt.barh(top.index, top.values, color=[CANCEL if c > 0 else ARRIVE for c in top]) plt.axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8) plt.title("What pushes a booking towards cancelling (scaled coefficients)") plt.xlabel("← towards arriving towards cancelling →") plt.show() Reading the chart: lead time pushes hardest towards cancelling. So do leisure and group guests (compared with business travellers), guests who cancelled before , expensive bookings ( adr ) and the online travel agency channel. A non-refundable deposit pulls hardest towards arriving, followed by special requests and repeat guests . These are associations, not causes . The model says that guests with a deposit cancel less; it does not say that a deposit makes anyone keep a booking. Let's check a few of these stories against the raw cancellation rates. In [19]: Copied! print ( df . groupby ( "deposit" )[ "canceled" ] . mean () . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) . to_string (), " \n " ) print ( df . groupby ( df [ "previous_cancellations" ] > 0 )[ "canceled" ] . mean () . rename ({ False : "never cancelled before" , True : "cancelled before" }) . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) . to_string (), " \n " ) ota_far = ( df [ "channel" ] == "Online travel agency" ) & ( df [ "lead_time_days" ] > 45 ) print ( f "OTA bookings made more than 45 days ahead: { df . loc [ ota_far , 'canceled' ] . mean () : .0% } cancel ( { ota_far . sum () : , } bookings)" ) print ( f "All other bookings: { df . loc [ ~ ota_far , 'canceled' ] . mean () : .0% } cancel" ) print ( f "Special requests 0 / 1 / 2+: " + " / " . join ( f " { r : .0% } " for r in df . groupby ( df [ "special_requests" ] . clip ( upper = 2 ))[ "canceled" ] . mean ())) print(df.groupby("deposit")["canceled"].mean().map("{:.0%}".format).to_string(), "\n") print(df.groupby(df["previous_cancellations"] > 0)["canceled"].mean() .rename({False: "never cancelled before", True: "cancelled before"}).map("{:.0%}".format).to_string(), "\n") ota_far = (df["channel"] == "Online travel agency") & (df["lead_time_days"] > 45) print(f"OTA bookings made more than 45 days ahead: {df.loc[ota_far, 'canceled'].mean():.0%} cancel ({ota_far.sum():,} bookings)") print(f"All other bookings: {df.loc[~ota_far, 'canceled'].mean():.0%} cancel") print(f"Special requests 0 / 1 / 2+: " + " / ".join(f"{r:.0%}" for r in df.groupby(df["special_requests"].clip(upper=2))["canceled"].mean())) deposit No deposit 36% Non-refundable 19% previous_cancellations never cancelled before 31% cancelled before 55% OTA bookings made more than 45 days ahead: 73% cancel (1,032 bookings) All other bookings: 26% cancel Special requests 0 / 1 / 2+: 34% / 35% / 31% The raw rates back the deposit and history stories (19% against 36%, 55% against 31%), and OTA bookings made more than 45 days ahead cancel at 73%. Special requests look flat in the raw data, because leisure guests make more requests and cancel more; compared with similar bookings, the model finds that a guest who asked for something cancels less. That is what "other things equal" means. Three actions to test: (1) a deposit for OTA bookings made far ahead , the riskiest segment; (2) a confirmation email to high-risk bookings, inviting guests to confirm or release the room; (3) treat repeat guests and guests with requests as safe when overbooking. {"q": "The coefficient of <code>deposit_Non-refundable</code> is clearly negative. And lead time pushes even harder. The honest move is a test.", "code": false} 07 Where the line fails ¶ Lead time is the strongest driver. But is its effect really "the further ahead, the riskier", as a single coefficient says? We group the test bookings by lead time and compare the share that really cancelled with the model's average probability. In [20]: Copied! BUCKETS = [ 0 , 15 , 30 , 45 , 60 , 75 , 90 , 105 , 120 , 150 , 180 , 240 , 500 ] test [ "lead_bucket" ] = pd . cut ( test [ "lead_time_days" ], BUCKETS , right = False ) by_lead = test . groupby ( "lead_bucket" , observed = True ) . agg ( bookings = ( "canceled" , "size" ), really_cancelled = ( "canceled" , "mean" ), model_says = ( "p_cancel" , "mean" )) by_lead . round ( 2 ) BUCKETS = [0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90, 105, 120, 150, 180, 240, 500] test["lead_bucket"] = pd.cut(test["lead_time_days"], BUCKETS, right=False) by_lead = test.groupby("lead_bucket", observed=True).agg( bookings=("canceled", "size"), really_cancelled=("canceled", "mean"), model_says=("p_cancel", "mean")) by_lead.round(2) Out[20]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } bookings really_cancelled model_says lead_bucket [0, 15) 447 0.15 0.20 [15, 30) 307 0.23 0.30 [30, 45) 192 0.34 0.34 [45, 60) 139 0.48 0.38 [60, 75) 88 0.65 0.41 [75, 90) 67 0.70 0.43 [90, 105) 57 0.74 0.47 [105, 120) 44 0.59 0.49 [120, 150) 67 0.43 0.52 [150, 180) 24 0.33 0.59 [180, 240) 40 0.40 0.68 [240, 500) 19 0.32 0.76 The same table as a chart: bars for what really happened, the line for what the model predicts. In [21]: Copied! labels = [ f " { int ( b . left ) } – { int ( b . right ) - 1 } " for b in by_lead . index ] labels [ - 1 ] = "240+" plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) plt . bar ( labels , by_lead [ "really_cancelled" ], color = ARRIVE , alpha = 0.45 , label = "really cancelled" ) plt . plot ( labels , by_lead [ "model_says" ], marker = "o" , lw = 2.5 , color = CANCEL , label = "logistic model says" ) plt . title ( "Cancellation rate by lead time, test bookings" ) plt . xlabel ( "days booked ahead" ) plt . ylabel ( "share cancelled" ) plt . xticks ( rotation = 45 ) plt . legend () plt . show () labels = [f"{int(b.left)}–{int(b.right) - 1}" for b in by_lead.index] labels[-1] = "240+" plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.bar(labels, by_lead["really_cancelled"], color=ARRIVE, alpha=0.45, label="really cancelled") plt.plot(labels, by_lead["model_says"], marker="o", lw=2.5, color=CANCEL, label="logistic model says") plt.title("Cancellation rate by lead time, test bookings") plt.xlabel("days booked ahead") plt.ylabel("share cancelled") plt.xticks(rotation=45) plt.legend() plt.show() The real rate climbs from 15% for last-minute bookings to 74% for bookings made 90–104 days ahead , then falls back to about a third for bookings made half a year ahead. The model's line only climbs: it says 41–49% around the peak and 76% for bookings made 240 days ahead or more, which really cancel 32%. Step through the simulator to see why no S-curve can follow the bars. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Business takeaway: the model is wrong in the two places operations cares about most. Around three months out it underestimates the risk, so we leave rooms empty; for bookings made half a year ahead it overestimates it, so we would resell rooms and walk guests. A straight score, even bent into an S, can only rise. Next week we use models that can bend: curves and decision trees . 08 What we tell the operations manager ¶ Let's put the policies side by side, on the 1,491 test bookings the model never saw. In [22]: Copied! def policy ( name , resold ): resold = np . asarray ( resold , dtype = bool ) walked = ( resold & ( y_test . values == 0 )) . sum () empty = ( ~ resold & ( y_test . values == 1 )) . sum () return { "policy" : name , "rooms resold" : resold . sum (), "guests walked" : walked , "rooms left empty" : empty , "total cost" : COST_EMPTY_ROOM * empty + COST_WALK * walked } t_best = best [ "threshold" ] plan = pd . DataFrame ([ policy ( "Do nothing" , p_test > 1 ), policy ( "Model, threshold 0.50" , p_test >= 0.5 ), policy ( f "Model, threshold { t_best : .2f } " , p_test >= t_best )]) plan [ "saved vs doing nothing" ] = plan [ "total cost" ] . iloc [ 0 ] - plan [ "total cost" ] plan def policy(name, resold): resold = np.asarray(resold, dtype=bool) walked = (resold & (y_test.values == 0)).sum() empty = (~resold & (y_test.values == 1)).sum() return {"policy": name, "rooms resold": resold.sum(), "guests walked": walked, "rooms left empty": empty, "total cost": COST_EMPTY_ROOM * empty + COST_WALK * walked} t_best = best["threshold"] plan = pd.DataFrame([policy("Do nothing", p_test > 1), policy("Model, threshold 0.50", p_test >= 0.5), policy(f"Model, threshold {t_best:.2f}", p_test >= t_best)]) plan["saved vs doing nothing"] = plan["total cost"].iloc[0] - plan["total cost"] plan Out[22]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } policy rooms resold guests walked rooms left empty total cost saved vs doing nothing 0 Do nothing 0 0 503 201200 0 1 Model, threshold 0.50 327 126 302 158600 42600 2 Model, threshold 0.43 451 189 241 153100 48100 Doing nothing costs USD 201,200 in empty rooms on these bookings. The model at 0.43 saves USD 48,100 , about a quarter, or USD 32,000 per 1,000 bookings. Top of the pyramid: Resell the room of every booking whose predicted risk of cancelling is above 43%; on our test bookings it cuts the cost of cancellations by a quarter. Then the evidence: who is risky (far ahead, OTA, no deposit), how sure we are (AUC 0.74), and the honest caveats: 189 walked guests is a lot of apologies, and the model misjudges bookings made far ahead. 09 Case clinic: the right metric ¶ This week's step of the applied case is the right metric for your decision . Open the case toolkit with your team. Classification (FinTrust, most own datasets): compare with the baseline ("nobody defaults"), then read precision, recall and AUC on the test set. Set the two costs in section 00 Settings (approving a client who defaults, rejecting a good one), run section 07 Threshold by cost , read the cheapest threshold , and write where each cost comes from. Regression (TalentCo): choose between the typical error in dollars (MAE) and R², and say which mistake hurts more. Everyone: "we judge the model by … because the decision is …" . docs.text: One Altamar booking in three is cancelled, and every cancellation is either an empty room or, if we oversold it, a guest with nowhere to sleep. Today you build a model that gives each booking a probability of cancelling, judge it with the right metric, and set an overbooking policy with money, not habit. 4 hours 9 ideas Runs in your browser Case: the right metric Setup. Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the tools we use today and a small helper that writes dollars nicely.
