docs.title: Predicting cancellations

docs.text: Last week the revenue team got a linear model for the nightly rate. Today the operations team knocks on the door: one booking in three is cancelled . If we keep the room for a guest who cancels, it stays empty. If we resell it (we overbook ) and the guest does show up, we must walk them: pay for a room at another hotel, a taxi and an apology. So the question is: which bookings will cancel? The answer is not a number of dollars but yes or no , a classification problem. We load the clean bookings from week 2 and count the cancellations, overall and by hotel. In [2]: Copied! df = pd . read_csv ( DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv" ) cancelled = df [ df [ "canceled" ] == 1 ] print ( f " { len ( df ) : , } bookings, { len ( cancelled ) : , } cancelled ( { df [ 'canceled' ] . mean () : .1% } )" ) print ( f "Room revenue of the cancelled bookings: { usd (( cancelled [ 'adr' ] * cancelled [ 'nights' ]) . sum ()) } " ) print () print ( df . groupby ( "hotel" )[ "canceled" ] . mean () . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) . to_string ()) df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv") cancelled = df[df["canceled"] == 1] print(f"{len(df):,} bookings, {len(cancelled):,} cancelled ({df['canceled'].mean():.1%})") print(f"Room revenue of the cancelled bookings: {usd((cancelled['adr'] * cancelled['nights']).sum())}") print() print(df.groupby("hotel")["canceled"].mean().map("{:.1%}".format).to_string()) 5,964 bookings, 2,012 cancelled (33.7%) Room revenue of the cancelled bookings: USD 1,200,647 hotel Puerto Varas 37.5% Santiago 25.3% Viña del Mar 41.1% Business takeaway: about USD 1.2 million of room revenue was booked and then cancelled in two years. Viña del Mar loses four bookings in ten, Santiago one in four. If we knew which bookings will cancel, we could resell those rooms and keep most of that money.
docs.title: 01 Previously at Altamar

docs.text: How do we judge a model that says "cancels" or "shows up"? The obvious score is accuracy : the share of bookings it gets right. It sounds like exactly what we want. But think of the laziest possible model: it says "nobody cancels" for every booking. It needs no data at all. In the simulator, pick a model and slide the cancellation rate. Watch accuracy and the number of cancellations caught. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The same lazy model on the real Altamar bookings: what is its accuracy, and how many cancellations does it catch? In [3]: Copied! lazy = np . zeros ( len ( df ), dtype = "int64" ) # predicts 0, "shows up", for everyone print ( f "Accuracy of 'nobody cancels': { accuracy_score ( df [ 'canceled' ], lazy ) : .1% } " ) print ( f "Cancellations it catches (recall): { recall_score ( df [ 'canceled' ], lazy ) : .0% } " ) lazy = np.zeros(len(df), dtype="int64") # predicts 0, "shows up", for everyone print(f"Accuracy of 'nobody cancels': {accuracy_score(df['canceled'], lazy):.1%}") print(f"Cancellations it catches (recall): {recall_score(df['canceled'], lazy):.0%}") Accuracy of 'nobody cancels': 66.3% Cancellations it catches (recall): 0% Business takeaway: a model that never predicts a cancellation is right two times in three and resells exactly zero rooms. Accuracy mostly measures how common the bigger group is. From now on every cancellation model must beat 66% , and we will also look at the cancellations themselves. {"q": "A vendor offers Altamar a cancellation model with 67% accuracy. What do you ask first?", "options": ["Nothing: two thirds right is a good grade", "How many of the bookings that really cancelled does it catch?", "Whether it uses more than twenty features"], "answer": 1, "why": "Saying \"nobody cancels\" already scores about 66% on our bookings. Accuracy alone cannot tell a useful model from the lazy one; the share of real cancellations it catches can.", "code": false}
docs.title: 02 The accuracy trap

docs.text: Why not reuse last week's linear regression, with canceled (0 or 1) as the target? Its prediction would be a number we could read as a "chance of cancelling". Let's try it with one feature, the lead time (days between booking and arrival). In [4]: Copied! line = LinearRegression () . fit ( df [[ "lead_time_days" ]], df [ "canceled" ]) for days in [ 0 , 30 , 90 , 200 , 400 ]: guess = line . predict ( pd . DataFrame ({ "lead_time_days" : [ days ]}))[ 0 ] print ( f "Booked { days : 3d } days ahead → 'probability' { guess : .2f } " ) line = LinearRegression().fit(df[["lead_time_days"]], df["canceled"]) for days in [0, 30, 90, 200, 400]: guess = line.predict(pd.DataFrame({"lead_time_days": [days]}))[0] print(f"Booked {days:3d} days ahead → 'probability' {guess:.2f}") Booked 0 days ahead → 'probability' 0.23 Booked 30 days ahead → 'probability' 0.30 Booked 90 days ahead → 'probability' 0.42 Booked 200 days ahead → 'probability' 0.66 Booked 400 days ahead → 'probability' 1.08 A booking made 400 days ahead gets a "probability" of 1.08: more than certain. A straight line keeps going forever, so sooner or later it leaves the range 0 to 1. Logistic regression fixes this. It computes a score exactly like a line, then bends it through an S-curve (the sigmoid ) that always stays between 0 and 1: big scores become probabilities near 1, very negative ones near 0. In the simulator, switch between the two models, move the sliders and press Best fit . ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. For the curious: the score is z = b₀ + b₁·x₁ + b₂·x₂ + …, just as in a linear regression, and the probability is p = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). A score of 0 gives exactly 0.5. Watch out: the simulator stops at 120 days on purpose. Further out, the real risk of cancelling falls again, and an S-curve can only go one way. Keep that in mind; section 07 comes back to it.
docs.title: 03 From yes/no to a probability

docs.text: The recipe is last week's, with a new target. Out of the features: the booking id (a label), the two dates (we keep only the arrival month) and, of course, canceled . In: everything we know when the booking is made, including its rate adr . Text columns become 0/1 dummies ; the first category in each list below is the baseline the others are compared with. In [5]: Copied! y = df [ "canceled" ] X = df . drop ( columns = [ "booking_id" , "booking_date" , "arrival_date" , "canceled" ]) X [ "arrival_month" ] = pd . to_datetime ( df [ "arrival_date" ]) . dt . month BASELINE = { "hotel" : [ "Santiago" , "Viña del Mar" , "Puerto Varas" ], "room_type" : [ "Standard" , "Superior" , "Suite" ], "customer_type" : [ "Business" , "Leisure" , "Group" ], "deposit" : [ "No deposit" , "Non-refundable" ], "channel" : [ "Direct" , "Online travel agency" , "Corporate" , "Travel agent" ], "country" : [ "Chile" , "Argentina" , "Brazil" , "United States" , "Europe" , "Other" , "Unknown" ]} for col , order in BASELINE . items (): X [ col ] = pd . Categorical ( X [ col ], order ) X = pd . get_dummies ( X , columns = list ( BASELINE ), drop_first = True , dtype = "int64" ) print ( f " { X . shape [ 1 ] } features for { len ( X ) : , } bookings" ) y = df["canceled"] X = df.drop(columns=["booking_id", "booking_date", "arrival_date", "canceled"]) X["arrival_month"] = pd.to_datetime(df["arrival_date"]).dt.month BASELINE = {"hotel": ["Santiago", "Viña del Mar", "Puerto Varas"], "room_type": ["Standard", "Superior", "Suite"], "customer_type": ["Business", "Leisure", "Group"], "deposit": ["No deposit", "Non-refundable"], "channel": ["Direct", "Online travel agency", "Corporate", "Travel agent"], "country": ["Chile", "Argentina", "Brazil", "United States", "Europe", "Other", "Unknown"]} for col, order in BASELINE.items(): X[col] = pd.Categorical(X[col], order) X = pd.get_dummies(X, columns=list(BASELINE), drop_first=True, dtype="int64") print(f"{X.shape[1]} features for {len(X):,} bookings") 27 features for 5,964 bookings Now the train/test split, with one new argument: stratify=y . It keeps the same cancellation rate in the training and the test bookings, so the test set looks like the real business and no metric is distorted by a lucky cut. In [6]: Copied! X_train , X_test , y_train , y_test = train_test_split ( X , y , test_size = 0.25 , stratify = y , random_state = 42 ) print ( f "Train: { len ( X_train ) : , } bookings, { y_train . mean () : .1% } cancelled" ) print ( f "Test: { len ( X_test ) : , } bookings, { y_test . mean () : .1% } cancelled" ) X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=42) print(f"Train: {len(X_train):,} bookings, {y_train.mean():.1%} cancelled") print(f"Test: {len(X_test):,} bookings, {y_test.mean():.1%} cancelled") Train: 4,473 bookings, 33.7% cancelled Test: 1,491 bookings, 33.7% cancelled
docs.title: Preparing the data

docs.text: We put a StandardScaler in front of LogisticRegression , inside a Pipeline . Scaling puts every feature on the same ruler (lead time in days, the rate in dollars, special requests in units) so the model trains reliably and its coefficients can be compared. The pipeline learns the scaling from the training bookings only. In [7]: Copied! model = Pipeline ([( "scale" , StandardScaler ()), ( "logit" , LogisticRegression ( max_iter = 2000 ))]) model . fit ( X_train , y_train ) p_test = model . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ] # probability of cancelling, each test booking print ( f "Trained on { len ( X_train ) : , } bookings. Average predicted risk on the test set: { p_test . mean () : .1% } " ) model = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("logit", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))]) model.fit(X_train, y_train) p_test = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] # probability of cancelling, each test booking print(f"Trained on {len(X_train):,} bookings. Average predicted risk on the test set: {p_test.mean():.1%}") Trained on 4,473 bookings. Average predicted risk on the test set: 33.9% predict_proba gives each booking two numbers, the probability of showing up and of cancelling; we keep the second. Here are five test bookings, described in words. In [8]: Copied! test = df . loc [ X_test . index ] . assign ( p_cancel = p_test ) for _ , b in test . sample ( 5 , random_state = 3 ) . iterrows (): outcome = "cancelled" if b [ "canceled" ] else "arrived" print ( f " { b [ 'hotel' ] } , { b [ 'customer_type' ] . lower () } guest, { b [ 'lead_time_days' ] } days ahead, " f " { b [ 'channel' ] . lower () } , { b [ 'deposit' ] . lower () } : { b [ 'p_cancel' ] : .0% } risk → { outcome } " ) test = df.loc[X_test.index].assign(p_cancel=p_test) for _, b in test.sample(5, random_state=3).iterrows(): outcome = "cancelled" if b["canceled"] else "arrived" print(f"{b['hotel']}, {b['customer_type'].lower()} guest, {b['lead_time_days']} days ahead, " f"{b['channel'].lower()}, {b['deposit'].lower()}: {b['p_cancel']:.0%} risk → {outcome}") Viña del Mar, leisure guest, 90 days ahead, direct, no deposit: 40% risk → cancelled Santiago, business guest, 4 days ahead, corporate, no deposit: 15% risk → arrived Santiago, leisure guest, 12 days ahead, direct, no deposit: 18% risk → cancelled Viña del Mar, leisure guest, 18 days ahead, online travel agency, no deposit: 58% risk → arrived Viña del Mar, leisure guest, 20 days ahead, travel agent, no deposit: 54% risk → arrived Read them like a reservations manager. A leisure booking at Viña made 90 days ahead with no deposit: 40%. A business traveller booking Santiago four days ahead through the corporate channel: 15%. But the model is no crystal ball: the Santiago booking at 18% was cancelled, and two Viña bookings above 50% arrived. A probability is a risk, not a verdict. Across all 1,491 test bookings, do the ones that really cancelled get higher probabilities? In [9]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . histplot ( x = p_test , hue = y_test . map ({ 0 : "arrived" , 1 : "cancelled" }), hue_order = [ "arrived" , "cancelled" ], palette = { "arrived" : ARRIVE , "cancelled" : CANCEL }, bins = 30 , stat = "density" , common_norm = False , element = "step" ) plt . title ( "Predicted probability of cancelling, test bookings" ) plt . xlabel ( "predicted probability of cancelling" ) plt . ylabel ( "share of bookings (density)" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) sns.histplot(x=p_test, hue=y_test.map({0: "arrived", 1: "cancelled"}), hue_order=["arrived", "cancelled"], palette={"arrived": ARRIVE, "cancelled": CANCEL}, bins=30, stat="density", common_norm=False, element="step") plt.title("Predicted probability of cancelling, test bookings") plt.xlabel("predicted probability of cancelling") plt.ylabel("share of bookings (density)") plt.show() Cancelled bookings (orange) tend to sit further right, but the two groups overlap a lot. No single cut-off separates them perfectly, and that is why the next two sections exist.
docs.title: Training the model

docs.text: To act on a probability we need a threshold : flag the booking as "likely to cancel", and resell its room, if p ≥ threshold. The default of model.predict() is 0.5. Every test booking then lands in one of four cells: Flagged and cancelled: we resold a room that would have been empty. Revenue saved. Flagged but the guest came: we have to walk a guest. A false positive . Not flagged and cancelled: the room stays empty. A false negative . Not flagged and the guest came: a normal stay. In [10]: Copied! pred_05 = ( p_test >= 0.5 ) . astype ( "int64" ) # the same as model.predict(X_test) tn , fp , fn , tp = confusion_matrix ( y_test , pred_05 ) . ravel () print ( f "Flagged, cancelled (room resold): { tp } " ) print ( f "Flagged, guest came (guest walked): { fp } " ) print ( f "Not flagged, cancelled (empty room): { fn } " ) print ( f "Not flagged, guest came (normal stay): { tn } " ) pred_05 = (p_test >= 0.5).astype("int64") # the same as model.predict(X_test) tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred_05).ravel() print(f"Flagged, cancelled (room resold): {tp}") print(f"Flagged, guest came (guest walked): {fp}") print(f"Not flagged, cancelled (empty room): {fn}") print(f"Not flagged, guest came (normal stay): {tn}") Flagged, cancelled (room resold): 201 Flagged, guest came (guest walked): 126 Not flagged, cancelled (empty room): 302 Not flagged, guest came (normal stay): 862 The same four numbers as a picture: rows are what really happened, columns what the model predicted. In [11]: Copied! fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 5 , 4.5 )) ConfusionMatrixDisplay . from_predictions ( y_test , pred_05 , display_labels = [ "arrives" , "cancels" ], cmap = "Oranges" , colorbar = False , ax = ax ) ax . set_title ( "Threshold 0.5, test bookings" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "predicted" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "what really happened" ) plt . show () fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4.5)) ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, pred_05, display_labels=["arrives", "cancels"], cmap="Oranges", colorbar=False, ax=ax) ax.set_title("Threshold 0.5, test bookings") ax.set_xlabel("predicted") ax.set_ylabel("what really happened") plt.show() Two metrics read the matrix from the side of the cancellations: Precision : of the bookings we flag, how many really cancel? When we resell a room, how often are we right? Every miss is a walked guest. Recall : of the bookings that cancel, how many do we flag? How many empty rooms do we prevent? Both go from 0 to 1. One rises when the other falls, as we will see. In [12]: Copied! print ( f "Accuracy: { accuracy_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .1% } ('nobody cancels' scores { 1 - y_test . mean () : .1% } )" ) print ( f "Precision: { precision_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .2f } of the bookings we flag, the share that cancel" ) print ( f "Recall: { recall_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .2f } of the cancellations, the share we flag" ) print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test, pred_05):.1%} ('nobody cancels' scores {1 - y_test.mean():.1%})") print(f"Precision: {precision_score(y_test, pred_05):.2f} of the bookings we flag, the share that cancel") print(f"Recall: {recall_score(y_test, pred_05):.2f} of the cancellations, the share we flag") Accuracy: 71.3% ('nobody cancels' scores 66.3%) Precision: 0.61 of the bookings we flag, the share that cancel Recall: 0.40 of the cancellations, the share we flag Read it like the operations manager. At 0.5 we flag 327 bookings and 61% of them really cancel (precision 0.61): about four resales in ten end with a walked guest. And we flag only 201 of the 503 cancellations (recall 0.40), so 302 rooms stay empty. Accuracy, 71.3%, barely beats the lazy 66.3%. The threshold is a dial, not part of the model. In the simulator, each dot is a real test booking; drag the threshold and watch bookings move between the cells. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Now on all test bookings: how many we flag, and what happens to precision and recall, at five thresholds. In [13]: Copied! rows = [] for t in [ 0.3 , 0.4 , 0.5 , 0.6 , 0.7 ]: flag = p_test >= t rows . append ({ "threshold" : t , "bookings flagged" : flag . sum (), "precision" : precision_score ( y_test , flag ), "recall" : recall_score ( y_test , flag )}) pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . round ( 2 ) rows = [] for t in [0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7]: flag = p_test >= t rows.append({"threshold": t, "bookings flagged": flag.sum(), "precision": precision_score(y_test, flag), "recall": recall_score(y_test, flag)}) pd.DataFrame(rows).round(2) Out[13]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } threshold bookings flagged precision recall 0 0.3 750 0.50 0.74 1 0.4 524 0.56 0.58 2 0.5 327 0.61 0.40 3 0.6 180 0.62 0.22 4 0.7 97 0.60 0.12 Lower the threshold to 0.3 and we flag 750 bookings: recall jumps to 0.74, but precision falls to 0.50, so half the resales end with a walked guest. Raise it to 0.7 and the list shrinks to 97 bookings that catch only 12% of the cancellations. No row is "right": the best one depends on what an empty room and a walked guest cost. {"q": "Operations lowers the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3. What happens?", "options": ["More rooms are resold: recall goes up, precision goes down, more guests are walked", "Both precision and recall go up, because the model gets better", "Nothing changes: the threshold is part of the trained model"], "answer": 0, "why": "A lower bar flags more bookings. More of the real cancellations are among them (recall up), but so are more guests who will arrive (precision down). The model itself is untouched.", "code": false}
docs.title: 04 The confusion matrix

docs.text: Precision and recall depend on the threshold. The AUC does not: pick a random booking that cancelled and a random one that arrived; AUC is how often the model gives the cancelled one the higher probability. 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. The ROC curve behind it records every threshold at once. Press Sweep in the simulator. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Our model's ROC curve and AUC on the test bookings. In [14]: Copied! fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 5.5 , 5 )) RocCurveDisplay . from_predictions ( y_test , p_test , name = "logistic model" , ax = ax ) ax . plot ([ 0 , 1 ], [ 0 , 1 ], ls = "--" , color = "grey" , label = "coin flip (AUC 0.5)" ) ax . set_title ( "ROC curve, test bookings" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "share of arriving guests flagged (false positive rate)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "share of cancellations flagged (recall)" ) ax . legend ( loc = "lower right" ) plt . show () print ( f "AUC: { roc_auc_score ( y_test , p_test ) : .2f } " ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5)) RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, p_test, name="logistic model", ax=ax) ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ls="--", color="grey", label="coin flip (AUC 0.5)") ax.set_title("ROC curve, test bookings") ax.set_xlabel("share of arriving guests flagged (false positive rate)") ax.set_ylabel("share of cancellations flagged (recall)") ax.legend(loc="lower right") plt.show() print(f"AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, p_test):.2f}") AUC: 0.74 Business takeaway: an AUC of 0.74 means that three times in four the model ranks a booking that will cancel above one that will arrive. The ranking carries real signal; what we do with it depends on where we put the threshold, and that is a money question. ☕ Break. Ten minutes. In the second block we turn the probabilities into an overbooking policy, read what drives cancellations, and find where the model goes wrong.
docs.title: One number for the whole dial: AUC

docs.text: 0.5 is a habit, not a decision. The right threshold depends on what each mistake costs. Finance gives us two numbers: an empty room (a cancellation we did not resell) costs about USD 400 : an average stay is worth USD 510, and part of it gets resold anyway; a walked guest (a resold booking whose guest shows up) costs about USD 300 : another hotel, a taxi, a voucher. The overbooking policy : resell the room of every booking whose probability of cancelling is at least the threshold. The simulator shows its total cost for every threshold, on our real test bookings. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The same calculation in code. Change the two costs (✏️) and run the next three cells again. In [15]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings COST_EMPTY_ROOM = 400 # USD lost when a booking we kept is cancelled and the room stays empty COST_WALK = 300 # USD to walk a guest whose room we resold: another hotel, taxi, voucher def policy_cost ( threshold , p = p_test , y = y_test ): resold = p >= threshold walked = ( resold & ( y . values == 0 )) . sum () # we resold it and the guest came empty = ( ~ resold & ( y . values == 1 )) . sum () # we kept it and it was cancelled return COST_EMPTY_ROOM * empty + COST_WALK * walked print ( f "Do nothing (resell no room): { usd ( policy_cost ( 1.01 )) } " ) print ( f "Resell every room: { usd ( policy_cost ( 0 )) } " ) print ( f "Threshold 0.50: { usd ( policy_cost ( 0.5 )) } " ) # ✏️ Change these settings COST_EMPTY_ROOM = 400 # USD lost when a booking we kept is cancelled and the room stays empty COST_WALK = 300 # USD to walk a guest whose room we resold: another hotel, taxi, voucher def policy_cost(threshold, p=p_test, y=y_test): resold = p >= threshold walked = (resold & (y.values == 0)).sum() # we resold it and the guest came empty = (~resold & (y.values == 1)).sum() # we kept it and it was cancelled return COST_EMPTY_ROOM * empty + COST_WALK * walked print(f"Do nothing (resell no room): {usd(policy_cost(1.01))}") print(f"Resell every room: {usd(policy_cost(0))}") print(f"Threshold 0.50: {usd(policy_cost(0.5))}") Do nothing (resell no room): USD 201,200 Resell every room: USD 296,400 Threshold 0.50: USD 158,600 Now every threshold from 0 to 1, and the cheapest one. In [16]: Copied! thresholds = np . round ( np . arange ( 0 , 1.001 , 0.01 ), 2 ) costs = pd . DataFrame ({ "threshold" : thresholds , "rooms resold" : [( p_test >= t ) . sum () for t in thresholds ], "total cost" : [ policy_cost ( t ) for t in thresholds ]}) best = costs . loc [ costs [ "total cost" ] . idxmin ()] print ( f "Cheapest threshold { best [ 'threshold' ] : .2f } : resell { int ( best [ 'rooms resold' ]) } rooms, total { usd ( best [ 'total cost' ]) } " ) print ( f " { usd ( policy_cost ( 0.5 ) - best [ 'total cost' ]) } less than threshold 0.50" ) print ( f " { usd ( policy_cost ( 1.01 ) - best [ 'total cost' ]) } less than doing nothing" ) print ( f "Break-even probability: { COST_WALK } / ( { COST_WALK } + { COST_EMPTY_ROOM } ) = { COST_WALK / ( COST_WALK + COST_EMPTY_ROOM ) : .2f } " ) thresholds = np.round(np.arange(0, 1.001, 0.01), 2) costs = pd.DataFrame({"threshold": thresholds, "rooms resold": [(p_test >= t).sum() for t in thresholds], "total cost": [policy_cost(t) for t in thresholds]}) best = costs.loc[costs["total cost"].idxmin()] print(f"Cheapest threshold {best['threshold']:.2f}: resell {int(best['rooms resold'])} rooms, total {usd(best['total cost'])}") print(f" {usd(policy_cost(0.5) - best['total cost'])} less than threshold 0.50") print(f" {usd(policy_cost(1.01) - best['total cost'])} less than doing nothing") print(f"Break-even probability: {COST_WALK} / ({COST_WALK} + {COST_EMPTY_ROOM}) = {COST_WALK / (COST_WALK + COST_EMPTY_ROOM):.2f}") Cheapest threshold 0.43: resell 451 rooms, total USD 153,100 USD 5,500 less than threshold 0.50 USD 48,100 less than doing nothing Break-even probability: 300 / (300 + 400) = 0.43 The cost curve, with the habit of 0.5 and the cheapest threshold marked. In [17]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) plt . plot ( costs [ "threshold" ], costs [ "total cost" ] / 1000 , lw = 2.5 , color = "#333333" ) plt . axhline ( policy_cost ( 1.01 ) / 1000 , ls = "--" , color = "grey" , label = "do nothing" ) plt . scatter ([ 0.5 ], [ policy_cost ( 0.5 ) / 1000 ], s = 70 , zorder = 3 , color = ARRIVE , label = "the habit: 0.50" ) plt . scatter ([ best [ "threshold" ]], [ best [ "total cost" ] / 1000 ], s = 70 , zorder = 3 , color = CANCEL , label = f "cheapest: { best [ 'threshold' ] : .2f } " ) plt . ylim ( 0 , policy_cost ( 1.01 ) / 1000 * 1.5 ) plt . title ( "Total cost of the overbooking policy, test bookings" ) plt . xlabel ( "threshold: resell the room if p(cancel) ≥ threshold" ) plt . ylabel ( "total cost (thousand USD)" ) plt . legend () plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.plot(costs["threshold"], costs["total cost"] / 1000, lw=2.5, color="#333333") plt.axhline(policy_cost(1.01) / 1000, ls="--", color="grey", label="do nothing") plt.scatter([0.5], [policy_cost(0.5) / 1000], s=70, zorder=3, color=ARRIVE, label="the habit: 0.50") plt.scatter([best["threshold"]], [best["total cost"] / 1000], s=70, zorder=3, color=CANCEL, label=f"cheapest: {best['threshold']:.2f}") plt.ylim(0, policy_cost(1.01) / 1000 * 1.5) plt.title("Total cost of the overbooking policy, test bookings") plt.xlabel("threshold: resell the room if p(cancel) ≥ threshold") plt.ylabel("total cost (thousand USD)") plt.legend() plt.show() The cheapest threshold is 0.43 : resell 451 rooms, for USD 48,100 less than doing nothing and USD 5,500 less than the habit of 0.5. Why 0.43? Reselling a booking with probability p costs on average (1 − p) × 300; keeping it costs p × 400. Reselling pays off when p × 400 > (1 − p) × 300, that is, when p > 300 / 700 ≈ 0.43. The break-even threshold comes from the two costs. Watch out: we chose the threshold on the test set, the same bookings we use to grade the model. In a real project you choose it on separate validation data and keep the test set for the final check. {"q": "Guest relations argues that a walked guest also writes a bad review, and puts the cost of a walk at USD 600 instead of 300. The empty room still costs 400. Where does the best threshold move?", "options": ["Down, so that we resell more rooms", "Up, to about 600 / (600 + 400) = 0.6: we only resell rooms we are very sure about", "Nowhere: the model has not changed"], "answer": 1, "why": "Reselling pays off when p × 400 is larger than (1 − p) × 600, so the break-even moves to 0.6. Dearer walks mean fewer, surer resales. Try it with the preset in the simulator.", "code": false}
docs.title: 05 Choosing the threshold with money

docs.text: The operations manager will ask why a booking is risky. Because we scaled the features, the coefficients are comparable: each one says how strongly one standard step of that feature pushes the score up (towards cancelling) or down (towards arriving). Dummies compare against the baseline: a business guest booking direct for a Standard room in Santiago, with no deposit. In [18]: Copied! coefs = pd . Series ( model . named_steps [ "logit" ] . coef_ [ 0 ], index = X . columns ) top = coefs [ coefs . abs () . sort_values () . index [ - 12 :]] # the 12 strongest, weakest first plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) plt . barh ( top . index , top . values , color = [ CANCEL if c > 0 else ARRIVE for c in top ]) plt . axvline ( 0 , color = "grey" , lw = 0.8 ) plt . title ( "What pushes a booking towards cancelling (scaled coefficients)" ) plt . xlabel ( "← towards arriving towards cancelling →" ) plt . show () coefs = pd.Series(model.named_steps["logit"].coef_[0], index=X.columns) top = coefs[coefs.abs().sort_values().index[-12:]] # the 12 strongest, weakest first plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5)) plt.barh(top.index, top.values, color=[CANCEL if c > 0 else ARRIVE for c in top]) plt.axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8) plt.title("What pushes a booking towards cancelling (scaled coefficients)") plt.xlabel("← towards arriving towards cancelling →") plt.show() Reading the chart: lead time pushes hardest towards cancelling. So do leisure and group guests (compared with business travellers), guests who cancelled before , expensive bookings ( adr ) and the online travel agency channel. A non-refundable deposit pulls hardest towards arriving, followed by special requests and repeat guests . These are associations, not causes . The model says that guests with a deposit cancel less; it does not say that a deposit makes anyone keep a booking. Let's check a few of these stories against the raw cancellation rates. In [19]: Copied! print ( df . groupby ( "deposit" )[ "canceled" ] . mean () . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) . to_string (), " " ) print ( df . groupby ( df [ "previous_cancellations" ] > 0 )[ "canceled" ] . mean () . rename ({ False : "never cancelled before" , True : "cancelled before" }) . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) . to_string (), " " ) ota_far = ( df [ "channel" ] == "Online travel agency" ) & ( df [ "lead_time_days" ] > 45 ) print ( f "OTA bookings made more than 45 days ahead: { df . loc [ ota_far , 'canceled' ] . mean () : .0% } cancel ( { ota_far . sum () : , } bookings)" ) print ( f "All other bookings: { df . loc [ ~ ota_far , 'canceled' ] . mean () : .0% } cancel" ) print ( f "Special requests 0 / 1 / 2+: " + " / " . join ( f " { r : .0% } " for r in df . groupby ( df [ "special_requests" ] . clip ( upper = 2 ))[ "canceled" ] . mean ())) print(df.groupby("deposit")["canceled"].mean().map("{:.0%}".format).to_string(), " ") print(df.groupby(df["previous_cancellations"] > 0)["canceled"].mean() .rename({False: "never cancelled before", True: "cancelled before"}).map("{:.0%}".format).to_string(), " ") ota_far = (df["channel"] == "Online travel agency") & (df["lead_time_days"] > 45) print(f"OTA bookings made more than 45 days ahead: {df.loc[ota_far, 'canceled'].mean():.0%} cancel ({ota_far.sum():,} bookings)") print(f"All other bookings: {df.loc[~ota_far, 'canceled'].mean():.0%} cancel") print(f"Special requests 0 / 1 / 2+: " + " / ".join(f"{r:.0%}" for r in df.groupby(df["special_requests"].clip(upper=2))["canceled"].mean())) deposit No deposit 36% Non-refundable 19% previous_cancellations never cancelled before 31% cancelled before 55% OTA bookings made more than 45 days ahead: 73% cancel (1,032 bookings) All other bookings: 26% cancel Special requests 0 / 1 / 2+: 34% / 35% / 31% The raw rates back the deposit and history stories (19% against 36%, 55% against 31%), and OTA bookings made more than 45 days ahead cancel at 73%. Special requests look flat in the raw data, because leisure guests make more requests and cancel more; compared with similar bookings, the model finds that a guest who asked for something cancels less. That is what "other things equal" means. Three actions to test: (1) a deposit for OTA bookings made far ahead , the riskiest segment; (2) a confirmation email to high-risk bookings, inviting guests to confirm or release the room; (3) treat repeat guests and guests with requests as safe when overbooking. {"q": "The coefficient of deposit_Non-refundable is clearly negative. Which statement can you defend in front of the general manager?", "options": ["Asking every guest for a non-refundable deposit will cut cancellations in half", "Bookings with a non-refundable deposit cancel less, other things equal; it is worth testing a deposit policy on the riskiest segment", "The deposit is the only thing that matters for cancellations"], "answer": 1, "why": "A coefficient describes an association in past bookings, not a cause: guests who accept a non-refundable deposit may be the ones who were sure anyway. And lead time pushes even harder. The honest move is a test.", "code": false}
docs.title: 06 What drives cancellations

docs.text: Lead time is the strongest driver. But is its effect really "the further ahead, the riskier", as a single coefficient says? We group the test bookings by lead time and compare the share that really cancelled with the model's average probability. In [20]: Copied! The model's line only climbs: it says 41–49% around the peak and 76% for bookings made 240 days ahead or more, which really cancel 32%. Step through the simulator to see why no S-curve can follow the bars. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Business takeaway: the model is wrong in the two places operations cares about most. Around three months out it underestimates the risk, so we leave rooms empty; for bookings made half a year ahead it overestimates it, so we would resell rooms and walk guests. A straight score, even bent into an S, can only rise. Next week we use models that can bend: curves and decision trees .

The model at 0.43 saves USD 48,100 , about a quarter, or USD 32,000 per 1,000 bookings. Top of the pyramid: Resell the room of every booking whose predicted risk of cancelling is above 43%; on our test bookings it cuts the cost of cancellations by a quarter. Then the evidence: who is risky (far ahead, OTA, no deposit), how sure we are (AUC 0.74), and the honest caveats: 189 walked guests is a lot of apologies, and the model misjudges bookings made far ahead.
docs.title: 08 What we tell the operations manager

docs.text: This week's step of the applied case is the right metric for your decision . Open the case toolkit with your team. Classification (FinTrust, most own datasets): compare with the baseline ("nobody defaults"), then read precision, recall and AUC on the test set. Set the two costs in section 00 Settings (approving a client who defaults, rejecting a good one), run section 07 Threshold by cost , read the cheapest threshold , and write where each cost comes from. Regression (TalentCo): choose between the typical error in dollars (MAE) and R², and say which mistake hurts more. Everyone: "we judge the model by … because the decision is …" . Before next week: the lab , An overbooking policy, and its graded quiz. In week 5, When lines are not enough , we go after what both straight lines missed: the cancellation risk that peaks about three months out, and each hotel's own seasons. {"q": "FinTrust's risk team says: rejecting a good client loses USD 400 of interest, approving a client who defaults loses USD 4,000. docs.text: Altamar's management liked the trees but asked a fair question: how deep, and why should we trust it? In this lab you turn the dials of a decision tree yourself, choose its depth with cross-validation, and turn its rules into decisions for the hotels. ≈ 2 hours 5 tasks Runs in your browser Graded quiz Recap of the live session : A decision tree asks yes/no questions and answers with the average of a group of similar bookings (a rate, or a share that cancel). With no limit it memorizes : perfect on training bookings, much worse on new ones. Cross-validation compares settings on the training bookings only (5 folds, averaged) so the test set stays an honest final check. Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the clean bookings, makes the usual train/test splits (25% test, random_state=42 ) and defines the helpers from the live session. docs.text: max_depth is the most important dial of a tree: how many questions a booking answers at most. This cell fits a rate tree with your depth and adds the result to a chart of all your runs so far . What to do: run it with MAX_DEPTH = 3 , then change it to 6, 10, 15 and 25, running the cell after each change. Watch the two lines grow. In [2]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings MAX_DEPTH = 3 tree = DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = MAX_DEPTH , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) train_err = mean_absolute_error ( yr_train , tree . predict ( Xr_train )) test_err = mean_absolute_error ( yr_test , tree . predict ( Xr_test )) experiments . append ({ "depth" : tree . get_depth (), "train" : train_err , "test" : test_err }) print ( f "Depth { tree . get_depth () } , { tree . get_n_leaves () : , } groups: typical error USD { train_err : .1f } on training bookings, USD { test_err : .1f } on test bookings." ) log = pd . DataFrame ( experiments ) . drop_duplicates ( "depth" , keep = "last" ) . sort_values ( "depth" ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) plt . plot ( log [ "depth" ], log [ "train" ], "o-" , label = "training bookings" ) plt . plot ( log [ "depth" ], log [ "test" ], "o-" , label = "test bookings" ) plt . title ( "Your runs: typical rate error by tree depth" ) plt . xlabel ( "max_depth" ); plt . ylabel ( "typical error (USD per night)" ); plt . legend () plt . show () # ✏️ Change these settings MAX_DEPTH = 3 tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=MAX_DEPTH, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) train_err = mean_absolute_error(yr_train, tree.predict(Xr_train)) test_err = mean_absolute_error(yr_test, tree.predict(Xr_test)) experiments.append({"depth": tree.get_depth(), "train": train_err, "test": test_err}) print(f"Depth {tree.get_depth()}, {tree.get_n_leaves():,} groups: typical error USD {train_err:.1f} on training bookings, USD {test_err:.1f} on test bookings.") log = pd.DataFrame(experiments).drop_duplicates("depth", keep="last").sort_values("depth") plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.plot(log["depth"], log["train"], "o-", label="training bookings") plt.plot(log["depth"], log["test"], "o-", label="test bookings") plt.title("Your runs: typical rate error by tree depth") plt.xlabel("max_depth"); plt.ylabel("typical error (USD per night)"); plt.legend() plt.show() Depth 3, 8 groups: typical error USD 23.1 on training bookings, USD 22.7 on test bookings. Think about it: what happens to the training error as you raise MAX_DEPTH ? And to the test error? Where would you stop, and why? Show the answer The **training error always falls**, to USD 0 at depth 25: every booking gets its own group. The **test error falls until about depth 10–12** (about USD 13 a night), then creeps back up (about USD 14 at depth 15+). The growing gap is memorization. Stop where the test error stops improving: deeper buys nothing on new bookings. (Task 3 makes this choice without peeking at the test set.) The same idea on one hotel and one input. Turn the dial and compare the two errors with what you just saw. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it.
docs.title: 01 How deep? Train versus test error

docs.text: A second dial, min_samples_leaf , sets the smallest group the tree may use for an answer. In business terms: never quote a rate based on fewer than N bookings. This cell grows a tree with no depth limit but with your minimum group size. What to do: run it with MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF = 1 , then try 5, 10, 50 and 200. In [3]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF = 1 tree = DecisionTreeRegressor ( min_samples_leaf = MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) table ([ rate_scores ( f "no depth limit, min_samples_leaf= { MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF } " , tree , Xr_train , Xr_test )]) print ( f " { tree . get_n_leaves () : , } groups, up to { tree . get_depth () } questions deep." ) print ( f "Every predicted rate is the average of at least { MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF } training booking(s)." ) # ✏️ Change these settings MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF = 1 tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_leaf=MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) table([rate_scores(f"no depth limit, min_samples_leaf={MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF}", tree, Xr_train, Xr_test)]) print(f"{tree.get_n_leaves():,} groups, up to {tree.get_depth()} questions deep.") print(f"Every predicted rate is the average of at least {MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF} training booking(s).") R² train R² test typical error, test (USD) model no depth limit, min_samples_leaf=1 1.0 0.878 14.263 4,465 groups, up to 26 questions deep. Every predicted rate is the average of at least 1 training booking(s). Think about it: how do the number of groups and the gap between R² train and R² test change as you raise MIN_SAMPLES_LEAF ? Which value would you defend in front of the revenue manager? Show the answer With 1: about 4,465 groups for 4,473 bookings, R² train 1.00, test 0.88. With **5 to 10**: a few hundred groups and test R² *rises* to 0.90–0.91 (typical error about USD 12), because the tree can no longer chase single bookings. With 50 the gap almost closes but real patterns get missed (test 0.86); 200 is far too coarse (0.49). Around 10 is easy to defend: every quoted rate rests on at least ten real bookings, and it scores best on new ones.
docs.title: 02 The smallest group a tree may answer from

docs.text: In task 1 you looked at the test set to choose, which spends the honest final check. Now choose the depth of the cancellation tree the right way: 5-fold cross-validation on the training bookings only, scored with AUC. With 11 depths and 5 folds this is 55 fits; it takes a few seconds. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. This cell computes the average validation AUC (and its spread across the folds) for each depth and plots the curve. In [4]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings DEPTHS = range ( 2 , 13 ) FOLDS = 5 cv = StratifiedKFold ( n_splits = FOLDS , shuffle = True , random_state = 42 ) rows = [] for d in DEPTHS : s = cross_val_score ( DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = d , random_state = 42 ), Xc_train , yc_train , cv = cv , scoring = "roc_auc" ) rows . append ({ "depth" : d , "mean AUC" : s . mean (), "spread (std)" : s . std ()}) curve = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) plt . errorbar ( curve [ "depth" ], curve [ "mean AUC" ], yerr = curve [ "spread (std)" ], marker = "o" , capsize = 4 , color = "#c85a24" ) plt . title ( f "Cancellation tree: { FOLDS } -fold cross-validated AUC by depth" ) plt . xlabel ( "max_depth" ); plt . ylabel ( "average validation AUC" ) plt . show () print ( curve . round ( 3 ) . to_string ( index = False )) # ✏️ Change these settings DEPTHS = range(2, 13) FOLDS = 5 cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=FOLDS, shuffle=True, random_state=42) rows = [] for d in DEPTHS: s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=42), Xc_train, yc_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc") rows.append({"depth": d, "mean AUC": s.mean(), "spread (std)": s.std()}) curve = pd.DataFrame(rows) plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.errorbar(curve["depth"], curve["mean AUC"], yerr=curve["spread (std)"], marker="o", capsize=4, color="#c85a24") plt.title(f"Cancellation tree: {FOLDS}-fold cross-validated AUC by depth") plt.xlabel("max_depth"); plt.ylabel("average validation AUC") plt.show() print(curve.round(3).to_string(index=False)) depth mean AUC spread (std) 2 0.741 0.008 3 0.768 0.010 4 0.780 0.007 5 0.775 0.014 6 0.766 0.012 7 0.745 0.011 8 0.722 0.008 9 0.704 0.009 10 0.687 0.006 11 0.662 0.008 12 0.653 0.011 Think about it: which depth would you choose? Is the best average the only thing that matters? Look at the spread too. Show the answer The curve is an upside-down U: AUC rises from about 0.74 at depth 2 to its peak, **about 0.78 at depth 4**, then falls steadily (about 0.65 at depth 12). Depth 5 (0.775) is within the spread of depth 4, so the two are practically tied; when two settings tie, prefer the **simpler** one, which here is also the best: **depth 4**. A justification a manager accepts: "on bookings it had not seen, depth 4 ranked risky bookings best, and deeper trees got steadily worse because they memorize noise."
docs.title: 03 Choose the depth with cross-validation

docs.text: This cell fits the cancellation tree with your chosen depth, checks it once on the test set, and prints its riskiest and safest groups. Groups smaller than MIN_BOOKINGS are left out: too few bookings to build a policy on. In [5]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings CHOSEN_DEPTH = 4 MIN_BOOKINGS = 50 tree = DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = CHOSEN_DEPTH , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xc_train , yc_train ) print ( f "Test AUC with depth { CHOSEN_DEPTH } : { roc_auc_score ( yc_test , tree . predict_proba ( Xc_test )[:, 1 ]) : .3f } \n " ) rules = tree_rules ( tree , list ( Xc_train . columns )) rules = rules [ rules [ "bookings" ] >= MIN_BOOKINGS ] . sort_values ( "answer" , ascending = False ) for title , part in [( "Riskiest groups" , rules . head ( 3 )), ( "Safest groups" , rules . tail ( 3 ))]: print ( title ) for _ , r in part . iterrows (): print ( f " { r [ 'answer' ] : >4.0% } cancel ( { r [ 'bookings' ] : >4 } bookings) if { r [ 'rule' ] } " ) # ✏️ Change these settings CHOSEN_DEPTH = 4 MIN_BOOKINGS = 50 tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=CHOSEN_DEPTH, random_state=42).fit(Xc_train, yc_train) print(f"Test AUC with depth {CHOSEN_DEPTH}: {roc_auc_score(yc_test, tree.predict_proba(Xc_test)[:, 1]):.3f}\n") rules = tree_rules(tree, list(Xc_train.columns)) rules = rules[rules["bookings"] >= MIN_BOOKINGS].sort_values("answer", ascending=False) for title, part in [("Riskiest groups", rules.head(3)), ("Safest groups", rules.tail(3))]: print(title) for _, r in part.iterrows(): print(f" {r['answer']:>4.0%} cancel ({r['bookings']:>4} bookings) if {r['rule']}") Test AUC with depth 4: 0.752 Riskiest groups 81% cancel ( 607 bookings) if channel is Online travel agency and deposit is not Non-refundable and lead time 46–132 68% cancel ( 62 bookings) if lead time ≤ 45 and previous cancellations ≥ 1 and weekend nights ≥ 2 and rate > USD 124 55% cancel ( 521 bookings) if channel is not Online travel agency and deposit is not Non-refundable and lead time ≥ 61 Safest groups 13% cancel (1437 bookings) if deposit is not Non-refundable and lead time ≤ 45 and previous cancellations = 0 and rate ≤ USD 138 10% cancel ( 108 bookings) if deposit is Non-refundable and lead time ≤ 45 and previous cancellations = 0 and rate > USD 138 5% cancel ( 220 bookings) if deposit is Non-refundable and lead time ≤ 45 and previous cancellations = 0 and rate ≤ USD 138 Think about it: pick two of these rules and turn each one into an operational action for Altamar: who does what, for which bookings, and what you expect to change. Show the answer Two examples (yours may differ): 1. **About 81% of agency bookings made 46–132 days ahead without a deposit cancel.** Oversell more rooms on dates full of them, and ask these guests to reconfirm 30 days before arrival, releasing unconfirmed rooms early. 2. **Short-lead bookings with a non-refundable deposit and no previous cancellations almost never cancel (5–10%).** Treat them as firm: never count them as rooms to oversell. A small discount for paying a deposit moves more guests into this group. A good action names the segment, the decision and the number that should move.
docs.title: 04 From rules to operational actions

docs.text: This cell predicts the rate of the same typical booking (a leisure guest, 2 adults, 3 nights, booked 30 days ahead through an agency) for every hotel and every arrival month, once with the linear model of week 3 and once with a tree. Solid lines are the tree, dashed lines the linear model. In [6]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings RATE_DEPTH = 10 ROOM = "Standard" lin = LinearRegression () . fit ( Xl_train , yr_train ) tree = DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = RATE_DEPTH , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) grid = pd . DataFrame ([{ "hotel" : h , "arrival_month" : m } for h in [ "Santiago" , "Viña del Mar" , "Puerto Varas" ] for m in range ( 1 , 13 )]) grid = grid . assign ( lead_time_days = 30 , nights = 3 , weekend_nights = 1 , adults = 2 , children = 0 , repeat_guest = 0 , previous_cancellations = 0 , special_requests = 1 , parking = 0 , room_type = ROOM , customer_type = "Leisure" , channel = "Online travel agency" , deposit = "No deposit" , country = "Chile" ) grid [ "linear" ], grid [ "tree" ] = lin . predict ( rate_X ( grid , "dummies" )), tree . predict ( rate_X ( grid , "number" )) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) for ( hotel , g ), color in zip ( grid . groupby ( "hotel" , sort = False ), [ "#2b6f78" , "#c85a24" , "#7a4f8e" ]): ax . plot ( g [ "arrival_month" ], g [ "tree" ], "o-" , color = color , label = f " { hotel } · tree" ) ax . plot ( g [ "arrival_month" ], g [ "linear" ], "--" , color = color , alpha = 0.8 , label = f " { hotel } · linear" ) ax . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 ), MONTHS ); ax . legend ( ncol = 2 , fontsize = 8 ) ax . set_title ( f "Predicted rate of a typical { ROOM } booking by arrival month" ); ax . set_xlabel ( "arrival month" ); ax . set_ylabel ( "predicted rate (USD)" ) plt . show () # ✏️ Change these settings RATE_DEPTH = 10 ROOM = "Standard" lin = LinearRegression().fit(Xl_train, yr_train) tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=RATE_DEPTH, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) grid = pd.DataFrame([{"hotel": h, "arrival_month": m} for h in ["Santiago", "Viña del Mar", "Puerto Varas"] for m in range(1, 13)]) grid = grid.assign(lead_time_days=30, nights=3, weekend_nights=1, adults=2, children=0, repeat_guest=0, previous_cancellations=0, special_requests=1, parking=0, room_type=ROOM, customer_type="Leisure", channel="Online travel agency", deposit="No deposit", country="Chile") grid["linear"], grid["tree"] = lin.predict(rate_X(grid, "dummies")), tree.predict(rate_X(grid, "number")) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5)) for (hotel, g), color in zip(grid.groupby("hotel", sort=False), ["#2b6f78", "#c85a24", "#7a4f8e"]): ax.plot(g["arrival_month"], g["tree"], "o-", color=color, label=f"{hotel} · tree") ax.plot(g["arrival_month"], g["linear"], "--", color=color, alpha=0.8, label=f"{hotel} · linear") ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13), MONTHS); ax.legend(ncol=2, fontsize=8) ax.set_title(f"Predicted rate of a typical {ROOM} booking by arrival month"); ax.set_xlabel("arrival month"); ax.set_ylabel("predicted rate (USD)") plt.show() Think about it: compare the three dashed lines with each other, then the three solid lines. What can the tree say that the linear model cannot? Try ROOM = "Suite" . Show the answer The **dashed lines are parallel**: the linear model gives every hotel the same January bonus and the same July bonus, and only shifts each line up or down. So it predicts a summer peak for Santiago too, which is wrong. The **solid lines each have their own shape**: Santiago dips in January–February and rises from September; Viña del Mar peaks in summer; Puerto Varas in summer *and* July. The tree found these **interactions** (hotel × month) by itself. Its lines are also step-shaped: neighbouring months in the same group share one rate.
docs.title: 05 Does the model know each hotel's season?

Today's models are built to bend. 02 Curves: a line that bends ¶ The simplest way to bend a line is to add powers of the input: day, day², day³… A degree-2 polynomial is a U; each extra degree allows one more bend. For cancellations, "mixed" means a group with cancelled and kept bookings together. It is measured with the Gini impurity : 0 for a pure group, 0.5 for a 50/50 mix. For rates, "mixed" means rates that are far from their group's average. The tree keeps the question that most reduces that error, which is what you watched in the staircase. Try it with twenty bookings: drag the line, then let the tree try every split. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. For the curious: Gini of a group = 1 − (share cancelled)² − (share kept)². A question is scored by the Gini of its two sides, weighted by their size; the lowest score wins. For regression the score is the squared error around each side's average. The tree then repeats the same search inside each side, and again, level after level. Next: the lab lets you tune the tree yourself (depth, minimum group size, cross-validation) and ends with this week's graded quiz. Week 6 grows forests and boosting .

docs.text: Altamar's straight lines explain part of its rates and its cancellations, but the hotels' seasons and the risky bookings made three months ahead do not follow a line. Today you will fit models that bend, see how they can fool themselves, and tune them with cross-validation so they don't. 4 hours 8 ideas Runs in your browser Case: a nonlinear model Run this cell first. You don't need to read it: it loads the clean bookings, makes the same train/test splits as weeks 3 and 4 (25% test, random_state=42 ), and defines small helpers that print comparison tables and turn a tree into readable rules. docs.title: When lines are not enough

docs.text: In weeks 3 and 4 the management team got two straight-line models: Rates: a linear regression with one column per month explained about 74% of the variation in nightly rates (R² ≈ 0.74), with a typical error of about USD 20. Cancellations: a logistic regression ranked risky bookings with an AUC ≈ 0.74 . Both are useful, and both left money on the table. This cell refits them so we have a baseline to beat. In [2]: Copied! lin = LinearRegression () . fit ( Xl_train , yr_train ) logit = make_pipeline ( StandardScaler (), LogisticRegression ( max_iter = 1000 )) . fit ( Xc_train , yc_train ) table ([ rate_scores ( "linear regression (month dummies)" , lin , Xl_train , Xl_test )]) table ([ cancel_scores ( "logistic regression" , logit , Xc_train , Xc_test )]) lin = LinearRegression().fit(Xl_train, yr_train) logit = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(Xc_train, yc_train) table([rate_scores("linear regression (month dummies)", lin, Xl_train, Xl_test)]) table([cancel_scores("logistic regression", logit, Xc_train, Xc_test)]) R² train R² test typical error, test (USD) model linear regression (month dummies) 0.74 0.738 20.483 accuracy train accuracy test AUC test model logistic regression 0.725 0.713 0.739 Where do the lines fail? This chart shows the average nightly rate by arrival month, one line per hotel. Look at how differently the three seasons move. In [3]: Copied! season = df . groupby ([ "arrival_month" , "hotel" ])[ "adr" ] . mean () . unstack () ax = season . plot ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 ), marker = "o" ) ax . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 ), [ "Jan" , "Feb" , "Mar" , "Apr" , "May" , "Jun" , "Jul" , "Aug" , "Sep" , "Oct" , "Nov" , "Dec" ]) ax . set_title ( "Average nightly rate by arrival month" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "arrival month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "average rate (USD)" ) plt . show () season = df.groupby(["arrival_month", "hotel"])["adr"].mean().unstack() ax = season.plot(figsize=(8, 4.5), marker="o") ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13), ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]) ax.set_title("Average nightly rate by arrival month") ax.set_xlabel("arrival month") ax.set_ylabel("average rate (USD)") plt.show() Viña del Mar and Puerto Varas peak in the summer (January–February, and December), Puerto Varas again in the July winter holidays, while Santiago dips in summer and rises with the September–November conferences. The linear model gives each month one bonus that is the same for all three hotels , so it cannot draw three different seasons. Now cancellations. This chart shows the share of bookings that cancel, by how far ahead they were made. In [4]: Copied! bands = pd . cut ( df [ "lead_time_days" ], LEAD_BINS , labels = LEAD_LABELS , include_lowest = True ) share = df . groupby ( bands , observed = True )[ "canceled" ] . mean () ax = ( share * 100 ) . plot . bar ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 ), color = "#c85a24" ) ax . set_title ( "Share of bookings that cancel, by lead time" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "lead time (days between booking and arrival)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "cancelled (%)" ) plt . xticks ( rotation = 0 ) plt . show () bands = pd.cut(df["lead_time_days"], LEAD_BINS, labels=LEAD_LABELS, include_lowest=True) share = df.groupby(bands, observed=True)["canceled"].mean() ax = (share * 100).plot.bar(figsize=(8, 4.5), color="#c85a24") ax.set_title("Share of bookings that cancel, by lead time") ax.set_xlabel("lead time (days between booking and arrival)") ax.set_ylabel("cancelled (%)") plt.xticks(rotation=0) plt.show() Risk climbs from about 16% for last-minute bookings to about 70% for bookings made 61 to 120 days ahead , then falls back to about 40%. A logistic regression can only say "the further ahead, the riskier" (or the opposite): one direction, all the way. Business takeaway: both questions have shapes that bend: a peak, a dip, a hump. Today's models are built to bend.
