docs.text: The simplest way to bend a line is to add powers of the input: day, day², day³… A degree-2 polynomial is a U; each extra degree allows one more bend. The simulator uses 100 Standard-room bookings at Viña del Mar. Raise the degree slowly. Then press Draw other bookings at degree 12 to 15 and watch the ends of the year. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. This cell fits three curves to Viña del Mar's Standard-room rates by arrival date: a straight line, a U (degree 2) and the degree you choose. The faint band on each side is outside the year: watch what the curves do there. ✏️ Try DEGREE = 3 , 8 and 15 . In [5]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings HOTEL = "Viña del Mar" DEGREE = 12 h = df [( df [ "hotel" ] == HOTEL ) & ( df [ "room_type" ] == "Standard" )] day = pd . to_datetime ( h [ "arrival_date" ]) . dt . dayofyear / 365 * 12 # 0 = 1 Jan, 12 = 31 Dec d_tr , d_te , r_tr , r_te = train_test_split ( day , h [ "adr" ], test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 42 ) grid = np . linspace ( - 0.6 , 12.6 , 300 ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) plt . scatter ( d_tr , r_tr , s = 8 , alpha = 0.25 , color = "gray" , label = "bookings (train)" ) for deg in [ 1 , 2 , DEGREE ]: curve = np . polynomial . Polynomial . fit ( d_tr , r_tr , deg ) plt . plot ( grid , curve ( grid ), lw = 2 , label = f "degree { deg } : typical test error USD { mean_absolute_error ( r_te , curve ( d_te )) : .1f } " ) plt . axvspan ( - 0.6 , 0 , color = "gray" , alpha = 0.12 ); plt . axvspan ( 12 , 12.6 , color = "gray" , alpha = 0.12 ) plt . ylim ( 0 , 300 ); plt . legend (); plt . title ( f " { HOTEL } : polynomial curves for the season" ) plt . xlabel ( "arrival date (months into the year)" ); plt . ylabel ( "nightly rate (USD)" ) plt . show () # ✏️ Change these settings HOTEL = "Viña del Mar" DEGREE = 12 h = df[(df["hotel"] == HOTEL) & (df["room_type"] == "Standard")] day = pd.to_datetime(h["arrival_date"]).dt.dayofyear / 365 * 12 # 0 = 1 Jan, 12 = 31 Dec d_tr, d_te, r_tr, r_te = train_test_split(day, h["adr"], test_size=0.25, random_state=42) grid = np.linspace(-0.6, 12.6, 300) plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.scatter(d_tr, r_tr, s=8, alpha=0.25, color="gray", label="bookings (train)") for deg in [1, 2, DEGREE]: curve = np.polynomial.Polynomial.fit(d_tr, r_tr, deg) plt.plot(grid, curve(grid), lw=2, label=f"degree {deg}: typical test error USD {mean_absolute_error(r_te, curve(d_te)):.1f}") plt.axvspan(-0.6, 0, color="gray", alpha=0.12); plt.axvspan(12, 12.6, color="gray", alpha=0.12) plt.ylim(0, 300); plt.legend(); plt.title(f"{HOTEL}: polynomial curves for the season") plt.xlabel("arrival date (months into the year)"); plt.ylabel("nightly rate (USD)") plt.show() The U already beats the line clearly: the line has to slope one way through the year and misses the summer at one end. Higher degrees gain little on new bookings and become fragile at the edges : just outside the data, on the shaded bands, they swing wildly, so a booking on 31 December or 1 January can get an absurd rate. Watch out: a curve is chosen input by input and hotel by hotel. Altamar has a dozen inputs and three hotels with different seasons: hand-crafting curves and their combinations does not scale. We need a model that finds the bends by itself. {"q": "A revenue manager fits a degree-15 curve to rates by arrival date and it fits the training bookings almost perfectly. What is the main risk?", "options": ["None: a closer fit to the training bookings always means better prices", "It chases individual bookings and swings wildly near the ends of the year, so new bookings get unreliable rates", "It can only draw straight lines", "It will need more hotels to work"], "answer": 1, "why": "A very flexible curve bends to follow noise in the training data. It looks perfect on bookings it saw but is unreliable on new ones, especially at the edges where few bookings hold it in place.", "code": false}
docs.title: 02 Curves: a line that bends

docs.text: A decision tree does not draw a curve. It asks yes/no questions: does the guest arrive in January or February? Is it a suite? Each answer sends the booking down a branch, and at the end of the branch the prediction is simply the average rate of the training bookings that ended up there . So a tree answers with averages of groups of similar bookings. Along one input its answer is a staircase. Add depth in the simulator and watch the groups split. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Now the real thing: a regression tree on all the inputs, compared with last week's line on the same test bookings. max_depth is the number of questions a booking answers at most. ✏️ Try MAX_DEPTH = 3 , 6 and 10 . In [6]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings MAX_DEPTH = 6 tree = DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = MAX_DEPTH , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) table ([ rate_scores ( "linear regression (month dummies)" , lin , Xl_train , Xl_test ), rate_scores ( f "tree, max_depth= { MAX_DEPTH } " , tree , Xr_train , Xr_test )]) print ( f "The tree sorts the { len ( Xr_train ) : , } training bookings into { tree . get_n_leaves () } groups." ) # ✏️ Change these settings MAX_DEPTH = 6 tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=MAX_DEPTH, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) table([rate_scores("linear regression (month dummies)", lin, Xl_train, Xl_test), rate_scores(f"tree, max_depth={MAX_DEPTH}", tree, Xr_train, Xr_test)]) print(f"The tree sorts the {len(Xr_train):,} training bookings into {tree.get_n_leaves()} groups.") R² train R² test typical error, test (USD) model linear regression (month dummies) 0.740 0.738 20.483 tree, max_depth=6 0.857 0.845 16.740 The tree sorts the 4,473 training bookings into 62 groups. With MAX_DEPTH = 6 the tree explains about 85% of the variation (R² ≈ 0.85 against 0.74) and its typical error falls from about USD 20 to about USD 17 a night, about 15% of the average rate. It found the seasons of each hotel by itself: nobody told it that January means something different in Santiago and in Viña del Mar. To read a tree, keep it small. This cell draws a depth-3 tree for the rate. In [7]: Copied! small = DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = 3 , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 14 , 6 )) plot_tree ( small , feature_names = list ( Xr_train . columns ), filled = True , impurity = False , precision = 0 , fontsize = 9 ) plt . title ( "A depth-3 tree for the nightly rate: each box shows the question, the bookings and their average rate" ) plt . show () small = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6)) plot_tree(small, feature_names=list(Xr_train.columns), filled=True, impurity=False, precision=0, fontsize=9) plt.title("A depth-3 tree for the nightly rate: each box shows the question, the bookings and their average rate") plt.show() Read it top-down, like a pricing manual. Each box asks a question (left branch = yes, right = no), and value is the average rate of the bookings that reached it. The first question is the season : does the guest arrive in January or February? In summer the next question is the hotel (Santiago or not), the rest of the year it is the room. The bottom boxes are eight business rules , each an average rate for a group of similar bookings. This cell prints the same eight rules as plain sentences, from the most to the least expensive. In [8]: Copied! rules = tree_rules ( small , list ( Xr_train . columns )) . sort_values ( "answer" , ascending = False ) for _ , r in rules . iterrows (): print ( f "USD { r [ 'answer' ] : >4.0f } a night ( { r [ 'bookings' ] : >4 } bookings) if { r [ 'rule' ] } " ) rules = tree_rules(small, list(Xr_train.columns)).sort_values("answer", ascending=False) for _, r in rules.iterrows(): print(f"USD {r['answer']:>4.0f} a night ({r['bookings']:>4} bookings) if {r['rule']}") USD 341 a night ( 87 bookings) if hotel is not Santiago and room type is Suite and arrives in Jan–Feb USD 188 a night ( 169 bookings) if hotel is not Santiago and room type is Suite and arrives in Mar–Dec USD 176 a night ( 885 bookings) if hotel is not Santiago and room type is not Suite and arrives in Jan–Feb USD 161 a night ( 176 bookings) if hotel is Santiago and room type is Suite and arrives in Mar–Dec USD 122 a night ( 24 bookings) if hotel is Santiago and room type is Suite and arrives in Jan–Feb USD 122 a night ( 984 bookings) if room type is Superior and arrives in Mar–Dec USD 95 a night (1997 bookings) if room type is neither Suite nor Superior and arrives in Mar–Dec USD 72 a night ( 151 bookings) if hotel is Santiago and room type is not Suite and arrives in Jan–Feb
docs.title: 03 A tree asks questions

docs.text: At every step the tree tries every input and every cut point , and keeps the question that leaves the two groups least mixed . For cancellations, "mixed" means a group with cancelled and kept bookings together. It is measured with the Gini impurity : 0 for a pure group, 0.5 for a 50/50 mix. For rates, "mixed" means rates that are far from their group's average. The tree keeps the question that most reduces that error, which is what you watched in the staircase. Try it with twenty bookings: drag the line, then let the tree try every split. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. For the curious: Gini of a group = 1 − (share cancelled)² − (share kept)². A question is scored by the Gini of its two sides, weighted by their size; the lowest score wins. For regression the score is the squared error around each side's average. The tree then repeats the same search inside each side, and again, level after level. The next simulator grows a cancellation tree on two inputs, lead time and rate. Look at what the tree does with risk that rises and then falls. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Now on Altamar's full data. This cell fits a depth-3 classification tree for cancellations and prints its eight groups, from the riskiest to the safest. answer is the share of training bookings in that group that cancelled. In [9]: Copied! ctree = DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = 3 , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xc_train , yc_train ) crules = tree_rules ( ctree , list ( Xc_train . columns )) . sort_values ( "answer" , ascending = False ) for _ , r in crules . iterrows (): print ( f " { r [ 'answer' ] : >4.0% } cancel ( { r [ 'bookings' ] : >4 } bookings) if { r [ 'rule' ] } " ) table ([ cancel_scores ( "tree, max_depth=3" , ctree , Xc_train , Xc_test )]) ctree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42).fit(Xc_train, yc_train) crules = tree_rules(ctree, list(Xc_train.columns)).sort_values("answer", ascending=False) for _, r in crules.iterrows(): print(f"{r['answer']:>4.0%} cancel ({r['bookings']:>4} bookings) if {r['rule']}") table([cancel_scores("tree, max_depth=3", ctree, Xc_train, Xc_test)]) 77% cancel ( 695 bookings) if channel is Online travel agency and lead time 46–132 56% cancel ( 135 bookings) if lead time ≤ 45 and previous cancellations ≥ 1 and weekend nights ≥ 2 51% cancel ( 647 bookings) if channel is not Online travel agency and deposit is not Non-refundable and lead time ≥ 46 49% cancel ( 90 bookings) if channel is Online travel agency and lead time ≥ 133 29% cancel ( 147 bookings) if lead time ≤ 45 and previous cancellations ≥ 1 and weekend nights ≤ 1 26% cancel ( 848 bookings) if lead time ≤ 45 and previous cancellations = 0 and rate > USD 138 24% cancel ( 254 bookings) if channel is not Online travel agency and deposit is Non-refundable and lead time ≥ 46 12% cancel (1657 bookings) if lead time ≤ 45 and previous cancellations = 0 and rate ≤ USD 138 accuracy train accuracy test AUC test model tree, max_depth=3 0.751 0.737 0.741 The first question is lead time ≤ 45 days , the same cut the twenty bookings suggested. The riskiest group is bookings made 46 to 132 days ahead through an online travel agency (about 3 in 4 cancel): the three-months-out peak, found without anyone telling the tree. The safest are bookings made up to 45 days ahead by guests with no previous cancellations, at up to about USD 138 (12%). And for far-ahead bookings outside the agencies, a non-refundable deposit halves the risk (51% → 24%). Business takeaway: each rule is a segment the operations team can act on: a reminder, a deposit policy, how many rooms to oversell. {"q": "A tree considers two questions for 1,000 bookings. Question A gives groups with weighted Gini 0.31; question B gives 0.42. Before any question the Gini was 0.45. Which does the tree ask?", "options": ["B, because it is closer to the starting Gini", "A, because it leaves the two groups less mixed", "Neither: Gini must reach 0 before a tree can split", "Both at once, in the same box"], "answer": 1, "why": "A tree keeps the question with the lowest weighted impurity: the one that best separates cancellations from kept bookings. 0.31 is a bigger drop from 0.45 than 0.42.", "code": false} ☕ Break. Ten minutes. When we come back: what happens if we let the tree keep asking questions forever?
docs.title: 04 How a tree chooses a question

docs.text: Every extra level lets the tree carve smaller groups. With no limit it keeps going until every group is pure : often a single booking. It then knows the training bookings by heart, noise included, and that knowledge does not travel to new bookings. Turn the dial from 1 to 15 and watch the two errors on the right. Then switch to cross-validation. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. This cell grows both trees with no depth limit and compares training and test scores. Look at the gap between the two columns. In [10]: Copied! deep_rate = DecisionTreeRegressor ( random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) deep_cancel = DecisionTreeClassifier ( random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xc_train , yc_train ) table ([ rate_scores ( "rate tree, no limit" , deep_rate , Xr_train , Xr_test )]) table ([ cancel_scores ( "cancellation tree, no limit" , deep_cancel , Xc_train , Xc_test )]) print ( f "Groups: { deep_rate . get_n_leaves () : , } for the rate tree, { deep_cancel . get_n_leaves () : , } for the cancellation tree." ) print ( f "Accuracy of saying 'nobody cancels': { 1 - yc_test . mean () : .1% } " ) deep_rate = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) deep_cancel = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42).fit(Xc_train, yc_train) table([rate_scores("rate tree, no limit", deep_rate, Xr_train, Xr_test)]) table([cancel_scores("cancellation tree, no limit", deep_cancel, Xc_train, Xc_test)]) print(f"Groups: {deep_rate.get_n_leaves():,} for the rate tree, {deep_cancel.get_n_leaves():,} for the cancellation tree.") print(f"Accuracy of saying 'nobody cancels': {1 - yc_test.mean():.1%}") R² train R² test typical error, test (USD) model rate tree, no limit 1.0 0.878 14.263 accuracy train accuracy test AUC test model cancellation tree, no limit 1.0 0.655 0.624 Groups: 4,465 for the rate tree, 956 for the cancellation tree. Accuracy of saying 'nobody cancels': 66.3% The cancellation tree is 100% right on the bookings it learned from and about 66% right on new ones : no better than saying "nobody cancels". Its AUC drops to about 0.62, worse than the logistic regression. It memorized 4,473 bookings in almost a thousand tiny groups. The rate tree also gets a perfect training score (R² = 1.00) but about 0.88 on the test: a gap of 0.12. Rates follow strong rules, so memorizing hurts less, but the gap says the same thing: a training score is not evidence . The question is how deep to go. {"q": "A colleague reports a cancellation tree with 99% training accuracy and 67% test accuracy. 66% of test bookings do not cancel. What do you conclude?", "options": ["Excellent model: 99% accuracy", "The tree memorized the training bookings; on new bookings it is barely better than predicting that nobody cancels", "The test set must be wrong, because the training accuracy is high", "Accuracy is the wrong word; it should be called recall"], "answer": 1, "why": "A large gap between training and test scores is the signature of overfitting. The fair comparison is the test score against the 66% baseline, and 67% is almost nothing.", "code": false}
docs.title: 05 When trees memorize

docs.text: To pick the depth we must compare depths on bookings the tree did not learn from. But if we use the test set to choose, it is no longer an honest final check, and one test is just one opinion : a different split could favour a different depth. Cross-validation solves both problems: it cuts the training bookings into 5 folds, lets each fold be the validation set once, and averages the 5 scores. The test set stays locked until the very end. The scores in this simulator are real Altamar results. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. This cell runs 5-fold cross-validation for six depths of the rate tree (30 fits, a few seconds) and plots the average validation R² with its spread across folds. In [11]: Copied! DEPTHS = [ 2 , 4 , 6 , 8 , 10 , 12 ] cv = KFold ( n_splits = 5 , shuffle = True , random_state = 42 ) rows = [] for d in DEPTHS : s = cross_val_score ( DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = d , random_state = 42 ), Xr_train , yr_train , cv = cv , scoring = "r2" ) rows . append ({ "depth" : d , "mean" : s . mean (), "std" : s . std ()}) rate_cv = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) plt . errorbar ( rate_cv [ "depth" ], rate_cv [ "mean" ], yerr = rate_cv [ "std" ], marker = "o" , capsize = 4 ) plt . title ( "Rate tree: 5-fold cross-validated R² by depth" ) plt . xlabel ( "max_depth" ); plt . ylabel ( "average validation R²" ) plt . show () best_rate_depth = int ( rate_cv . loc [ rate_cv [ "mean" ] . idxmax (), "depth" ]) print ( f "Best depth for the rate: { best_rate_depth } (average R² { rate_cv [ 'mean' ] . max () : .3f } )" ) DEPTHS = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12] cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) rows = [] for d in DEPTHS: s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=d, random_state=42), Xr_train, yr_train, cv=cv, scoring="r2") rows.append({"depth": d, "mean": s.mean(), "std": s.std()}) rate_cv = pd.DataFrame(rows) plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.errorbar(rate_cv["depth"], rate_cv["mean"], yerr=rate_cv["std"], marker="o", capsize=4) plt.title("Rate tree: 5-fold cross-validated R² by depth") plt.xlabel("max_depth"); plt.ylabel("average validation R²") plt.show() best_rate_depth = int(rate_cv.loc[rate_cv["mean"].idxmax(), "depth"]) print(f"Best depth for the rate: {best_rate_depth} (average R² {rate_cv['mean'].max():.3f})") Best depth for the rate: 10 (average R² 0.866) For the rate, R² rises fast up to depth 8 and then flattens: depth 10 is the best average, with depth 8 practically tied. Rates follow many real rules (hotel × season × room × channel), so the tree can use many questions before it starts memorizing. The same search for cancellations , scored with AUC, the metric of week 4: In [12]: Copied! cv5 = StratifiedKFold ( n_splits = 5 , shuffle = True , random_state = 42 ) rows = [] for d in DEPTHS : s = cross_val_score ( DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = d , random_state = 42 ), Xc_train , yc_train , cv = cv5 , scoring = "roc_auc" ) rows . append ({ "depth" : d , "mean" : s . mean (), "std" : s . std ()}) cancel_cv = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) plt . errorbar ( cancel_cv [ "depth" ], cancel_cv [ "mean" ], yerr = cancel_cv [ "std" ], marker = "o" , capsize = 4 , color = "#c85a24" ) plt . title ( "Cancellation tree: 5-fold cross-validated AUC by depth" ) plt . xlabel ( "max_depth" ); plt . ylabel ( "average validation AUC" ) plt . show () best_cancel_depth = int ( cancel_cv . loc [ cancel_cv [ "mean" ] . idxmax (), "depth" ]) print ( f "Best depth for cancellations: { best_cancel_depth } (average AUC { cancel_cv [ 'mean' ] . max () : .3f } )" ) cv5 = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) rows = [] for d in DEPTHS: s = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=42), Xc_train, yc_train, cv=cv5, scoring="roc_auc") rows.append({"depth": d, "mean": s.mean(), "std": s.std()}) cancel_cv = pd.DataFrame(rows) plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.5)) plt.errorbar(cancel_cv["depth"], cancel_cv["mean"], yerr=cancel_cv["std"], marker="o", capsize=4, color="#c85a24") plt.title("Cancellation tree: 5-fold cross-validated AUC by depth") plt.xlabel("max_depth"); plt.ylabel("average validation AUC") plt.show() best_cancel_depth = int(cancel_cv.loc[cancel_cv["mean"].idxmax(), "depth"]) print(f"Best depth for cancellations: {best_cancel_depth} (average AUC {cancel_cv['mean'].max():.3f})") Best depth for cancellations: 4 (average AUC 0.780) Cancellations show the full U-shape : AUC peaks at depth 4 and falls steadily after it, because whether a guest cancels is far noisier than the rate. Different questions, different best depths: that is why we tune. Only now do we touch the test set, once , with the chosen depths retrained on all the training bookings. In [13]: Copied! rate_tree = DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = best_rate_depth , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) cancel_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = best_cancel_depth , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( Xc_train , yc_train ) table ([ rate_scores ( f "rate tree, depth { best_rate_depth } " , rate_tree , Xr_train , Xr_test )]) table ([ cancel_scores ( f "cancellation tree, depth { best_cancel_depth } " , cancel_tree , Xc_train , Xc_test )]) rate_tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=best_rate_depth, random_state=42).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) cancel_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=best_cancel_depth, random_state=42).fit(Xc_train, yc_train) table([rate_scores(f"rate tree, depth {best_rate_depth}", rate_tree, Xr_train, Xr_test)]) table([cancel_scores(f"cancellation tree, depth {best_cancel_depth}", cancel_tree, Xc_train, Xc_test)]) R² train R² test typical error, test (USD) model rate tree, depth 10 0.958 0.891 13.334 accuracy train accuracy test AUC test model cancellation tree, depth 4 0.767 0.742 0.752 The test scores land close to the cross-validated ones (rate R² ≈ 0.89, cancellation AUC ≈ 0.75): cross-validation told the truth about bookings it had not seen. That is the point of the method: you can trust the number before you deploy .
docs.title: 06 Cross-validation and tuning

docs.text: This cell puts the straight-line models and the tuned trees side by side, on the same test bookings. In [14]: Copied! table ([ rate_scores ( "rate: linear regression" , lin , Xl_train , Xl_test ), rate_scores ( f "rate: tuned tree (depth { best_rate_depth } )" , rate_tree , Xr_train , Xr_test )]) table ([ cancel_scores ( "cancellations: logistic regression" , logit , Xc_train , Xc_test ), cancel_scores ( f "cancellations: tuned tree (depth { best_cancel_depth } )" , cancel_tree , Xc_train , Xc_test )]) table([rate_scores("rate: linear regression", lin, Xl_train, Xl_test), rate_scores(f"rate: tuned tree (depth {best_rate_depth})", rate_tree, Xr_train, Xr_test)]) table([cancel_scores("cancellations: logistic regression", logit, Xc_train, Xc_test), cancel_scores(f"cancellations: tuned tree (depth {best_cancel_depth})", cancel_tree, Xc_train, Xc_test)]) R² train R² test typical error, test (USD) model rate: linear regression 0.740 0.738 20.483 rate: tuned tree (depth 10) 0.958 0.891 13.334 accuracy train accuracy test AUC test model cancellations: logistic regression 0.725 0.713 0.739 cancellations: tuned tree (depth 4) 0.767 0.742 0.752 Where does the cancellation tree win? This chart compares, for each lead-time band of the test bookings, the share that really cancelled with the average risk each model predicted. In [15]: Copied! test = df . loc [ Xc_test . index ] lead_band = pd . cut ( test [ "lead_time_days" ], LEAD_BINS , labels = LEAD_LABELS , include_lowest = True ) view = pd . DataFrame ({ "actual" : yc_test , "logistic" : logit . predict_proba ( Xc_test )[:, 1 ], "tree" : cancel_tree . predict_proba ( Xc_test )[:, 1 ]}) . groupby ( lead_band , observed = True ) . mean () ax = ( view * 100 ) . plot ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 ), marker = "o" , style = [ "k-" , "--" , "-" ]) ax . set_title ( "Test bookings: real and predicted cancellation risk by lead time" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "lead time band (days)" ); ax . set_ylabel ( "cancel (%)" ) plt . show () test = df.loc[Xc_test.index] lead_band = pd.cut(test["lead_time_days"], LEAD_BINS, labels=LEAD_LABELS, include_lowest=True) view = pd.DataFrame({"actual": yc_test, "logistic": logit.predict_proba(Xc_test)[:, 1], "tree": cancel_tree.predict_proba(Xc_test)[:, 1]}).groupby(lead_band, observed=True).mean() ax = (view * 100).plot(figsize=(8, 4.5), marker="o", style=["k-", "--", "-"]) ax.set_title("Test bookings: real and predicted cancellation risk by lead time") ax.set_xlabel("lead time band (days)"); ax.set_ylabel("cancel (%)") plt.show() Where the tree is better: it follows the hump (low risk last-minute, a peak two to four months out, lower again far ahead), while the logistic line keeps climbing and misses the peak. On rates it follows each hotel's own seasons and cuts the typical error by a third (USD 20 → 13). What it costs: Step-shaped answers: two bookings one day apart can get rates a full step apart. Less stable: a slightly different sample can change the first question and the rules. No extrapolation: beyond what it has seen, it repeats the last group's average. Next week: many trees voting together keep the strengths and soften these costs. {"q": "The tuned cancellation tree has a test AUC of 0.75 and the logistic regression 0.74, but the tree tracks the peak at 60–120 days much better. What is the best recommendation to the operations team?", "options": ["Use the tree's training accuracy to decide, because it is higher", "Adopt the tree's segments for overbooking decisions on mid-lead bookings, and check the result each season, since a single tree is less stable", "Keep the logistic regression forever: AUCs within 0.01 mean the shapes are identical", "Use the unlimited-depth tree: it scored 100% on training"], "answer": 1, "why": "Overall AUCs are close, but the tree gets the risky segment right, which is where overbooking money is made or lost. A single tree can change with new data, so it should be monitored.", "code": false}
docs.title: 07 What changed for the business

docs.text: This week's step for your team (see the applied case ): a decision tree, its depth chosen with cross-validation. Open the case toolkit with your data and settings from weeks 1–4. Run section 08 Decision tree with cross-validation (it tries depths 2 to 10 with 5 folds). Record the chosen depth , its cross-validated score (± spread) and its test score, next to your linear model from week 3. Print the tree's top rules and write two sentences: which rule surprises you, and what a manager would do with it. If the training score is far above the cross-validated score, say so: that is overfitting, and it belongs in your limitations. Next: the lab lets you tune the tree yourself (depth, minimum group size, cross-validation) and ends with this week's graded quiz. Week 6 grows forests and boosting .

" f "Best test error USD { min ( test_curve ) : .1f } at tree { best } ." ) # ✏️ Change these settings LEARNING_RATE = 0.1 MAX_ITER = 100 b = model(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE, max_iter=MAX_ITER, random_state=42)).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) train_curve = [mean_absolute_error(yr_train, p) for p in b[-1].staged_predict(b[:-1].transform(Xr_train))] test_curve = [mean_absolute_error(yr_test, p) for p in b[-1].staged_predict(b[:-1].transform(Xr_test))] best = int(np.argmin(test_curve)) + 1 plt.plot(range(1, len(test_curve) + 1), test_curve, lw=2.5, color="#c85a24", label="test bookings") plt.plot(range(1, len(train_curve) + 1), train_curve, lw=2.5, color="#2b6f78", label="training bookings") plt.axvline(best, color="grey", ls="--", label=f"lowest test error: tree {best}") plt.title(f"Boosting, learning rate {LEARNING_RATE}") plt.xlabel("Number of trees") plt.ylabel("Typical error (USD a night)") plt.ylim(0, 40) plt.legend() plt.show() print(f"After {len(test_curve)} trees: training USD {train_curve[-1]:.1f}, test USD {test_curve[-1]:.1f}. " f"Best test error USD {min(test_curve):.1f} at tree {best}.") After 100 trees: training USD 6.7, test USD 8.4. Best test error USD 8.4 at tree 100. Think about it. Try LEARNING_RATE = 0.5 with MAX_ITER = 300 , then 0.02 with 300 . Where is the best test error, and what does the training error do? Is "more trees" always better? Show the answer With **0.5** the training error keeps falling (to about USD 1.8) but the test error is lowest at tree 20 (USD 9.3) and then rises to USD 10.3: the later trees learn noise, which is overfitting. With **0.02** it is still improving after 300 trees (USD 8.9): steps too small. With **0.1** and 300 trees, the best is about USD 8.4 at tree 118, and it barely moves after that. Unlike in a forest, more trees is *not* always better in boosting. 03 Task 3 · Choose a model for each question ¶ The scoreboard is one input to the decision, not the decision. Weigh four criteria: Accuracy on the test bookings, in the metric that fits the decision. Stability: does the model change its answers when the history changes a little? Explainability: can you explain a single prediction to the person it affects? Cost of errors: what does one mistake cost Altamar, and how many decisions does the model make? The cell trains the four models for each question (the line and tree exactly as in week 5) on the same training bookings, and times them. In [5]: Copied! recipes = { "rate" : { "Linear" : model ( LinearRegression (), month_as_category = True ), "Tree" : model ( DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = 10 , random_state = 42 )), # week 5's tuned trees "Forest" : model ( RandomForestRegressor ( n_estimators = 200 , min_samples_leaf = 3 , random_state = 42 )), "Boosting" : model ( HistGradientBoostingRegressor ( random_state = 42 ))}, "cancel" : { "Linear" : model ( make_pipeline ( StandardScaler (), LogisticRegression ( max_iter = 1000 ))), "Tree" : model ( DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = 4 , random_state = 42 )), "Forest" : model ( RandomForestClassifier ( n_estimators = 200 , min_samples_leaf = 3 , random_state = 42 )), "Boosting" : model ( HistGradientBoostingClassifier ( random_state = 42 ))}, } board = [] for question , models in recipes . items (): X_tr , y_tr = ( Xr_train , yr_train ) if question == "rate" else ( Xc_train , yc_train ) for name , m in models . items (): start = time . time () m . fit ( X_tr , y_tr ) seconds = time . time () - start score = rate_scores ( name , m )[ "typical error (USD)" ] if question == "rate" else cancel_scores ( name , m )[ "AUC" ] board . append ({ "question" : question , "model" : name , "accuracy" : score , "seconds" : round ( seconds , 2 )}) board = pd . DataFrame ( board ) print ( board . to_string ( index = False , float_format = lambda v : f " { v : g } " )) print ( " \n Accuracy = typical error in USD for the rate (lower is better), AUC for cancellations (higher is better)." ) recipes = { "rate": {"Linear": model(LinearRegression(), month_as_category=True), "Tree": model(DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=10, random_state=42)), # week 5's tuned trees "Forest": model(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=3, random_state=42)), "Boosting": model(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=42))}, "cancel": {"Linear": model(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))), "Tree": model(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=42)), "Forest": model(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=3, random_state=42)), "Boosting": model(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42))}, } board = [] for question, models in recipes.items(): X_tr, y_tr = (Xr_train, yr_train) if question == "rate" else (Xc_train, yc_train) for name, m in models.items(): start = time.time() m.fit(X_tr, y_tr) seconds = time.time() - start score = rate_scores(name, m)["typical error (USD)"] if question == "rate" else cancel_scores(name, m)["AUC"] board.append({"question": question, "model": name, "accuracy": score, "seconds": round(seconds, 2)}) board = pd.DataFrame(board) print(board.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:g}")) print("\nAccuracy = typical error in USD for the rate (lower is better), AUC for cancellations (higher is better).") question model accuracy seconds rate Linear 20.5 0.01 rate Tree 13.3 0.02 rate Forest 10.3 1.6 rate Boosting 8.4 1.04 cancel Linear 0.739 0.01 cancel Tree 0.752 0.01 cancel Forest 0.771 0.55 cancel Boosting 0.77 0.69 Accuracy = typical error in USD for the rate (lower is better), AUC for cancellations (higher is better). Stability. The cell retrains each model on three different halves of the training bookings and measures how much their predictions for the same test bookings disagree (rate: USD; cancellations: percentage points). In [6]: Copied! halves = { "rate" : [ Xr_train . sample ( frac = 0.5 , random_state = s ) . index for s in [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]], "cancel" : [ Xc_train . sample ( frac = 0.5 , random_state = s ) . index for s in [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]]} spread = [] for question , models in recipes . items (): X_tr , y_tr , X_te = ( Xr_train , yr_train , Xr_test ) if question == "rate" else ( Xc_train , yc_train , Xc_test ) for name , m in models . items (): preds = [] for idx in halves [ question ]: copy = clone ( m ) . fit ( X_tr . loc [ idx ], y_tr . loc [ idx ]) # a fresh copy: the trained model stays as it is preds . append ( copy . predict ( X_te ) if question == "rate" else 100 * copy . predict_proba ( X_te )[:, 1 ]) spread . append ( np . ptp ( np . array ( preds ), axis = 0 ) . mean () . round ( 1 )) board [ "disagreement" ] = spread print ( board [[ "question" , "model" , "accuracy" , "disagreement" ]] . to_string ( index = False , float_format = lambda v : f " { v : g } " )) halves = {"rate": [Xr_train.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=s).index for s in [1, 2, 3]], "cancel": [Xc_train.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=s).index for s in [1, 2, 3]]} spread = [] for question, models in recipes.items(): X_tr, y_tr, X_te = (Xr_train, yr_train, Xr_test) if question == "rate" else (Xc_train, yc_train, Xc_test) for name, m in models.items(): preds = [] for idx in halves[question]: copy = clone(m).fit(X_tr.loc[idx], y_tr.loc[idx]) # a fresh copy: the trained model stays as it is preds.append(copy.predict(X_te) if question == "rate" else 100 * copy.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]) spread.append(np.ptp(np.array(preds), axis=0).mean().round(1)) board["disagreement"] = spread print(board[["question", "model", "accuracy", "disagreement"]].to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:g}")) question model accuracy disagreement rate Linear 20.5 4.1 rate Tree 13.3 19.9 rate Forest 10.3 8.4 rate Boosting 8.4 7.6 cancel Linear 0.739 5.4 cancel Tree 0.752 13.9 cancel Forest 0.771 8.4 cancel Boosting 0.77 17.6 A decision scorecard. Managers often compare options with weighted criteria. The cell turns each criterion into a score from 1 (worst of the four) to 5 (best), using the numbers above and a fixed explainability rating (line 5, tree 4, forest and boosting 2). Set the weights to what matters for your decision. In [7]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings QUESTION = "rate" # "rate" or "cancel" WEIGHTS = { "accuracy" : 0.5 , "stability" : 0.2 , "explainability" : 0.2 , "speed" : 0.1 } card = board [ board [ "question" ] == QUESTION ] . set_index ( "model" ) def to_1_5 ( values , higher_is_better ): v = values if higher_is_better else - values return ( 1 + 4 * ( v - v . min ()) / ( v . max () - v . min ())) . round ( 1 ) scores = pd . Series ({ "Linear" : 5 , "Tree" : 4 , "Forest" : 2 , "Boosting" : 2 }), "speed" : to_1_5 ( card [ "seconds" ], higher_is_better = False ), }) scores [ "weighted score" ] = sum ( scores [ k ] * w for k , w in WEIGHTS . items ()) . div ( sum ( WEIGHTS . values ())) . round ( 2 ) print ( scores . sort_values ( "weighted score" , ascending = False )) # ✏️ Change these settings QUESTION = "rate" # "rate" or "cancel" WEIGHTS = {"accuracy": 0.5, "stability": 0.2, "explainability": 0.2, "speed": 0.1} card = board[board["question"] == QUESTION].set_index("model") def to_1_5(values, higher_is_better): v = values if higher_is_better else -values return (1 + 4 * (v - v.min()) / (v.max() - v.min())).round(1) scores = pd.DataFrame({ "accuracy": to_1_5(card["accuracy"], higher_is_better=(QUESTION == "cancel")), "stability": to_1_5(card["disagreement"], higher_is_better=False), "explainability": pd.Series({"Linear": 5, "Tree": 4, "Forest": 2, "Boosting": 2}), "speed": to_1_5(card["seconds"], higher_is_better=False), }) scores["weighted score"] = sum(scores[k] * w for k, w in WEIGHTS.items()).div(sum(WEIGHTS.values())).round(2) print(scores.sort_values("weighted score", ascending=False)) accuracy stability explainability speed weighted score Boosting 5.0 4.1 2 2.4 3.96 Forest 4.4 3.9 2 1.0 3.48 Tree 3.4 1.0 4 5.0 3.20 Linear 1.0 5.0 5 5.0 3.00 Think about it. With the default weights, which model wins each question? What weights make the line win the rate question, and what decision would justify them? Then write two sentences per question ( "For the rate we choose … because …" ) covering all four criteria. Show the answer Boosting wins the rate: USD 8.4 vs 20.5 outweighs its lower explainability. The line wins only if explainability weighs far more, e.g. when each rate must be justified to a client. For cancellations the **forest** wins: as accurate as boosting, and much steadier (boosting's risks move about 18 points between samples, the forest's about 8). Example: *"For cancellations, the forest: AUC 0.77, 123 real cancellations among the 150 riskiest bookings (92 for the logistic model), and stable."* 04 Task 4 · Partial dependence for an input of your choice ¶ Partial dependence answers "how does the prediction change with this input, all else equal?". The simulator shows lead time and month; now pick another input. Some worth trying: nights , weekend_nights , adults and children for the rate; special_requests , adr (the rate itself) and previous_cancellations for cancellations; channel for either. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The cell draws the partial dependence of your input, one line per hotel, using the boosting models trained in Task 3. In [8]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings QUESTION = "rate" # "rate" or "cancel" INPUT = "nights" # any column except "hotel"; "adr" only for "cancel" m , X_test = ( recipes [ "rate" ][ "Boosting" ], Xr_test ) if QUESTION == "rate" else ( recipes [ "cancel" ][ "Boosting" ], Xc_test ) column = X_test [ INPUT ] if column . dtype == object or column . nunique () <= 15 : grid = sorted ( column . unique ()) else : grid = sorted ( set ( np . percentile ( column , np . linspace ( 1 , 99 , 20 )) . round ( 0 ))) for h in HOTELS : values = pd_curve ( m , X_test [ X_test [ "hotel" ] == h ], INPUT , grid , proba = ( QUESTION == "cancel" )) plt . plot ([ str ( g ) for g in grid ] if column . dtype == object else grid , values * ( 100 if QUESTION == "cancel" else 1 ), marker = "o" , color = COLORS [ h ], label = h ) plt . title ( f "Partial dependence of the { 'predicted rate' if QUESTION == 'rate' else 'cancellation risk' } on { INPUT } " ) plt . xlabel ( INPUT ) plt . ylabel ( "Predicted rate (USD a night)" if QUESTION == "rate" else "Predicted chance of cancelling (%)" ) plt . legend () plt . show () # ✏️ Change these settings QUESTION = "rate" # "rate" or "cancel" INPUT = "nights" # any column except "hotel"; "adr" only for "cancel" m, X_test = (recipes["rate"]["Boosting"], Xr_test) if QUESTION == "rate" else (recipes["cancel"]["Boosting"], Xc_test) column = X_test[INPUT] if column.dtype == object or column.nunique() < = 15: grid = sorted(column.unique()) else: grid = sorted(set(np.percentile(column, np.linspace(1, 99, 20)).round(0))) for h in HOTELS: values = pd_curve(m, X_test[X_test["hotel"] == h], INPUT, grid, proba=(QUESTION == "cancel")) plt.plot([str(g) for g in grid] if column.dtype == object else grid, values * (100 if QUESTION == "cancel" else 1), marker="o", color=COLORS[h], label=h) plt.title(f"Partial dependence of the {'predicted rate' if QUESTION == 'rate' else 'cancellation risk'} on {INPUT}") plt.xlabel(INPUT) plt.ylabel("Predicted rate (USD a night)" if QUESTION == "rate" else "Predicted chance of cancelling (%)") plt.legend() plt.show() Think about it. Describe the shape in one business sentence. A line, a step, a hump? Would a straight line capture it? Name one reason why it shows association, not cause . Show the answer For `nights` and the rate you should see **steps down** at 5 and 7 nights: Altamar's long-stay discounts, which a line would blur into a gentle slope. For `special_requests` and cancellations the risk **falls** with each request: guests who ask for a crib or a high floor are committed. Association, not cause: adding requests would not make a guest come. Requests reveal commitment; they do not create it. 05 Task 5 · Draft the pyramid for Altamar's management ¶ The general manager has ten minutes. Lead with the recommendation, support it with three arguments, and put one piece of evidence (a chart or a number) under each. Replay the pyramid in the simulator, then fix the weak draft in the next cell: it is written in report order, the way most first drafts are. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The cell checks your pyramid against five rules and prints it as an outline. Rewrite the three settings until every rule passes. ARGUMENTS = { "Methodology" : [ "Train/test split, 75% / 25%" ], "Gradient boosting has the best R²" : [ "R² 0.96 vs 0.74 for the line" ], "Lead time is the most important input for cancellations" : [], } ACTIONS = ( "use" , "price" , "oversell" , "review" , "raise" , "cut" , "adopt" , "set" , "launch" , "stop" , "start" , "invest" , "require" ) checks = [ ( "The key message is one short sentence (30 words or fewer)" , len ( KEY_MESSAGE . split ()) <= 30 ), ( "The key message recommends an action" , any ( w . strip ( ".,:;" ) . lower () in ACTIONS for w in KEY_MESSAGE . split ())), ( "The key message has a number" , any ( ch . isdigit () for ch in KEY_MESSAGE )), ( "There are exactly three arguments" , len ( ARGUMENTS ) == 3 ), ( "Every argument has 1 to 3 pieces of evidence, and none is about method" , all ( 1 <= len ( ev ) <= 3 for ev in ARGUMENTS . values ()) and not any ( "method" in a . lower () for a in ARGUMENTS )), ] for rule , ok in checks : print (( "✔ " if ok else "✘ " ) + rule ) print ( " \n " + KEY_MESSAGE ) for i , ( arg , evidence ) in enumerate ( ARGUMENTS . items (), start = 1 ): print ( f " { i } . { arg } " ) for ev in evidence : print ( f " – { ev } " ) # ✏️ Change these settings KEY_MESSAGE = "We tested four models on Altamar's bookings." ARGUMENTS = { "Methodology": ["Train/test split, 75% / 25%"], "Gradient boosting has the best R²": ["R² 0.96 vs 0.74 for the line"], "Lead time is the most important input for cancellations": [], } ACTIONS = ("use", "price", "oversell", "review", "raise", "cut", "adopt", "set", "launch", "stop", "start", "invest", "require") checks = [ ("The key message is one short sentence (30 words or fewer)", len(KEY_MESSAGE.split()) < = 30), ("The key message recommends an action", any(w.strip(".,:;").lower() in ACTIONS for w in KEY_MESSAGE.split())), ("The key message has a number", any(ch.isdigit() for ch in KEY_MESSAGE)), ("There are exactly three arguments", len(ARGUMENTS) == 3), ("Every argument has 1 to 3 pieces of evidence, and none is about method", all(1 < = len(ev) < = 3 for ev in ARGUMENTS.values()) and not any("method" in a.lower() for a in ARGUMENTS)), ] for rule, ok in checks: print(("✔ " if ok else "✘ ") + rule) print("\n" + KEY_MESSAGE) for i, (arg, evidence) in enumerate(ARGUMENTS.items(), start=1): print(f" {i}. {arg}") for ev in evidence: print(f" – {ev}") ✔ The key message is one short sentence (30 words or fewer) ✘ The key message recommends an action ✘ The key message has a number ✔ There are exactly three arguments ✘ Every argument has 1 to 3 pieces of evidence, and none is about method We tested four models on Altamar's bookings. 1. Methodology – Train/test split, 75% / 25% 2. Gradient boosting has the best R² – R² 0.96 vs 0.74 for the line 3. Lead time is the most important input for cancellations Think about it. Which rules did the draft break, and why does each matter to a manager with ten minutes? Rewrite it. Show the answer It opens with what *we did*, not what *they should do*; one argument is method (appendix material); one has no evidence. A passing version: - **Key message:** "Use gradient boosting to price: it cuts the typical pricing error from USD 20 to USD 8 a night." - **1. It prices like our best revenue manager:** R² 0.96 vs 0.74 for the line and 0.89 for week 5's tree. - **2. We know what drives it:** month, room and hotel; each hotel's own seasons. - **3. It pays off:** 11% of bookings sold more than 10% below similar ones, about USD 18,000 a year. Before the quiz. Your team now does the same for its case: run the comparison and explanation sections of the case toolkit , choose a model with reasons, and build the 10-slide pyramid described in the live session . docs.title: Choosing and explaining a model

docs.text: Altamar's management wants a decision, not a leaderboard. In this lab you tune a forest and a boosting model, choose a model for each question with reasons beyond accuracy, explain how one input drives it, and draft the pyramid you would present. ≈ 2 hours 5 tasks Runs in your browser Graded quiz Recap of the live session A random forest averages hundreds of trees, each grown on its own bootstrap sample with random inputs: steadier and more accurate than one tree. Gradient boosting adds small trees in a row, each fitted to the errors left by the previous ones. On the same test bookings, boosting cut the typical rate error from USD 20.5 (line) and USD 13.3 (week 5's tuned tree) to USD 8.4 a night; for cancellations the forest and boosting tie (AUC 0.77, against 0.74 and 0.75). Permutation importance says which inputs matter; partial dependence shows how; both describe patterns, not causes. Run this cell first. You don't need to read it. In [1]: Copied! # Run this cell first. You don't need to read it. import time import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.base import clone from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder , StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression , LogisticRegression from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor , DecisionTreeClassifier from sklearn.ensemble import ( RandomForestRegressor , RandomForestClassifier , GradientBoostingRegressor , HistGradientBoostingRegressor , HistGradientBoostingClassifier ) from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , r2_score , roc_auc_score , roc_curve from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/" df = pd . read_csv ( DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv" ) df [ "arrival_month" ] = pd . to_datetime ( df [ "arrival_date" ]) . dt . month HOTELS = [ "Santiago" , "Viña del Mar" , "Puerto Varas" ] TEXT = [ "hotel" , "room_type" , "customer_type" , "channel" , "deposit" , "country" ] NUMBERS = [ "lead_time_days" , "nights" , "weekend_nights" , "adults" , "children" , "repeat_guest" , "previous_cancellations" , "special_requests" , "parking" , "arrival_month" ] # The same inputs and train/test splits as in weeks 3 to 5 (25% of bookings kept aside for the test) X_rate , y_rate = df [ NUMBERS + TEXT ], df [ "adr" ] X_cancel , y_cancel = df [ NUMBERS + TEXT + [ "adr" ]], df [ "canceled" ] Xr_train , Xr_test , yr_train , yr_test = train_test_split ( X_rate , y_rate , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 42 ) Xc_train , Xc_test , yc_train , yc_test = train_test_split ( X_cancel , y_cancel , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 42 , stratify = y_cancel ) def model ( estimator , month_as_category = False ): """Turn the text columns into 0/1 columns (as pd.get_dummies(drop_first=True) did in week 5), then fit `estimator`.""" text = TEXT + ([ "arrival_month" ] if month_as_category else []) encode = make_column_transformer (( "passthrough" , lambda X : [ c for c in X . columns if c not in text ]), ( OneHotEncoder ( drop = "first" , handle_unknown = "ignore" , sparse_output = False ), text )) return make_pipeline ( encode , estimator ) def rate_scores ( name , m ): p = m . predict ( Xr_test ) return { "model" : name , "typical error (USD)" : round ( mean_absolute_error ( yr_test , p ), 1 ), "R²" : round ( r2_score ( yr_test , p ), 3 )} def cancel_scores ( name , m ): p = m . predict_proba ( Xc_test )[:, 1 ] top150 = np . argsort ( - p )[: 150 ] return { "model" : name , "AUC" : round ( roc_auc_score ( yc_test , p ), 3 ), "cancelled, of the 150 riskiest" : int ( yc_test . values [ top150 ] . sum ())} def pd_curve ( m , X , column , grid , proba = False ): """Partial dependence: give every booking in X the same value of `column`, average the predictions.""" out = [] for v in grid : X_v = X . assign ( ** { column : v }) out . append ( m . predict_proba ( X_v )[:, 1 ] . mean () if proba else m . predict ( X_v ) . mean ()) return np . array ( out ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4.5 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False }) COLORS = { "Santiago" : "#2b6f78" , "Viña del Mar" : "#c85a24" , "Puerto Varas" : "#7a4f8e" } print ( f " { len ( df ) : , } bookings loaded. Training: { len ( Xr_train ) : , } bookings · Test: { len ( Xr_test ) : , } bookings." ) # Run this cell first. You don't need to read it. import time import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.base import clone from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, DecisionTreeClassifier from sklearn.ensemble import (RandomForestRegressor, RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingRegressor, HistGradientBoostingRegressor, HistGradientBoostingClassifier) from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score, roc_auc_score, roc_curve from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance DATA = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/mba-business-analytics-1/main/docs/datasets/" df = pd.read_csv(DATA + "altamar_bookings_clean.csv") df["arrival_month"] = pd.to_datetime(df["arrival_date"]).dt.month HOTELS = ["Santiago", "Viña del Mar", "Puerto Varas"] TEXT = ["hotel", "room_type", "customer_type", "channel", "deposit", "country"] NUMBERS = ["lead_time_days", "nights", "weekend_nights", "adults", "children", "repeat_guest", "previous_cancellations", "special_requests", "parking", "arrival_month"] # The same inputs and train/test splits as in weeks 3 to 5 (25% of bookings kept aside for the test) X_rate, y_rate = df[NUMBERS + TEXT], df["adr"] X_cancel, y_cancel = df[NUMBERS + TEXT + ["adr"]], df["canceled"] Xr_train, Xr_test, yr_train, yr_test = train_test_split(X_rate, y_rate, test_size=0.25, random_state=42) Xc_train, Xc_test, yc_train, yc_test = train_test_split(X_cancel, y_cancel, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_cancel) def model(estimator, month_as_category=False): """Turn the text columns into 0/1 columns (as pd.get_dummies(drop_first=True) did in week 5), then fit `estimator`.""" text = TEXT + (["arrival_month"] if month_as_category else []) encode = make_column_transformer(("passthrough", lambda X: [c for c in X.columns if c not in text]), (OneHotEncoder(drop="first", handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), text)) return make_pipeline(encode, estimator) def rate_scores(name, m): p = m.predict(Xr_test) return {"model": name, "typical error (USD)": round(mean_absolute_error(yr_test, p), 1), "R²": round(r2_score(yr_test, p), 3)} def cancel_scores(name, m): p = m.predict_proba(Xc_test)[:, 1] top150 = np.argsort(-p)[:150] return {"model": name, "AUC": round(roc_auc_score(yc_test, p), 3), "cancelled, of the 150 riskiest": int(yc_test.values[top150].sum())} def pd_curve(m, X, column, grid, proba=False): """Partial dependence: give every booking in X the same value of `column`, average the predictions.""" out = [] for v in grid: X_v = X.assign(**{column: v}) out.append(m.predict_proba(X_v)[:, 1].mean() if proba else m.predict(X_v).mean()) return np.array(out) plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (8, 4.5), "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False}) COLORS = {"Santiago": "#2b6f78", "Viña del Mar": "#c85a24", "Puerto Varas": "#7a4f8e"} print(f"{len(df):,} bookings loaded. Training: {len(Xr_train):,} bookings · Test: {len(Xr_test):,} bookings.") 5,964 bookings loaded. Training: 4,473 bookings · Test: 1,491 bookings.
docs.title: Choosing and explaining a model

docs.text: A forest has two settings that matter most: the number of trees (more trees, a steadier average, but slower) and the minimum bookings per leaf (small leaves let each tree memorize single bookings; big leaves force broad rules). The cell trains one forest for the nightly rate with your settings and reports its typical error on the training bookings and on the test bookings. In [2]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings N_TREES = 100 MIN_LEAF = 3 f = model ( RandomForestRegressor ( n_estimators = N_TREES , min_samples_leaf = MIN_LEAF , random_state = 42 )) start = time . time () f . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) print ( f " { N_TREES } trees, at least { MIN_LEAF } bookings per leaf, trained in { time . time () - start : .1f } seconds" ) print ( f "Typical error on training bookings: USD { mean_absolute_error ( yr_train , f . predict ( Xr_train )) : .1f } " ) print ( f "Typical error on test bookings: USD { mean_absolute_error ( yr_test , f . predict ( Xr_test )) : .1f } " " (the line: USD 20.5; week 5's tuned tree: USD 13.3)" ) # ✏️ Change these settings N_TREES = 100 MIN_LEAF = 3 f = model(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=N_TREES, min_samples_leaf=MIN_LEAF, random_state=42)) start = time.time() f.fit(Xr_train, yr_train) print(f"{N_TREES} trees, at least {MIN_LEAF} bookings per leaf, trained in {time.time() - start:.1f} seconds") print(f"Typical error on training bookings: USD {mean_absolute_error(yr_train, f.predict(Xr_train)):.1f}") print(f"Typical error on test bookings: USD {mean_absolute_error(yr_test, f.predict(Xr_test)):.1f}" " (the line: USD 20.5; week 5's tuned tree: USD 13.3)") 100 trees, at least 3 bookings per leaf, trained in 0.8 seconds Typical error on training bookings: USD 6.3 Typical error on test bookings: USD 10.4 (the line: USD 20.5; week 5's tuned tree: USD 13.3) The cell trains forests of 1, 5, 20, 50 and 100 trees with your MIN_LEAF and plots their typical error on training and test bookings. In [3]: Copied! sizes = [ 1 , 5 , 20 , 50 , 100 ] train_err , test_err = [], [] for n in sizes : f = model ( RandomForestRegressor ( n_estimators = n , min_samples_leaf = MIN_LEAF , random_state = 42 )) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) train_err . append ( mean_absolute_error ( yr_train , f . predict ( Xr_train ))) test_err . append ( mean_absolute_error ( yr_test , f . predict ( Xr_test ))) plt . plot ( sizes , test_err , marker = "o" , lw = 2.5 , color = "#c85a24" , label = "test bookings" ) plt . plot ( sizes , train_err , marker = "o" , lw = 2.5 , color = "#2b6f78" , label = "training bookings" ) plt . title ( f "Random forest for the nightly rate (at least { MIN_LEAF } bookings per leaf)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Number of trees" ) plt . ylabel ( "Typical error (USD a night)" ) plt . ylim ( 0 , None ) plt . legend () plt . show () sizes = [1, 5, 20, 50, 100] train_err, test_err = [], [] for n in sizes: f = model(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=n, min_samples_leaf=MIN_LEAF, random_state=42)).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) train_err.append(mean_absolute_error(yr_train, f.predict(Xr_train))) test_err.append(mean_absolute_error(yr_test, f.predict(Xr_test))) plt.plot(sizes, test_err, marker="o", lw=2.5, color="#c85a24", label="test bookings") plt.plot(sizes, train_err, marker="o", lw=2.5, color="#2b6f78", label="training bookings") plt.title(f"Random forest for the nightly rate (at least {MIN_LEAF} bookings per leaf)") plt.xlabel("Number of trees") plt.ylabel("Typical error (USD a night)") plt.ylim(0, None) plt.legend() plt.show() Think about it. As you add trees, does the test error ever go up? Now try MIN_LEAF = 1 , then 20 , and rerun both cells. What happens to the gap between training and test error? Show the answer With 3 bookings per leaf the test error falls from about USD 13.8 (one tree) to USD 10.5 (20 trees), then **flattens**: more trees never make a forest overfit, they only cost time. With `MIN_LEAF = 1` trees memorize bookings: training error drops to about USD 4, test stays at USD 10.4, a gap that buys nothing. With `20` the rules get too broad and both errors rise (test about USD 12.9). A leaf of about 3 and 100–200 trees is sensible.
docs.title: 01 Task 1 · How many trees, how big the leaves

docs.text: Boosting's two key settings work together: the learning rate (how much of each tree's correction is added) and the number of trees ( MAX_ITER ). Replay the idea in the simulator first, then try it on all bookings. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The cell trains boosting with your settings and draws its typical error on training and test bookings after each tree. In [4]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings LEARNING_RATE = 0.1 MAX_ITER = 100 b = model ( HistGradientBoostingRegressor ( learning_rate = LEARNING_RATE , max_iter = MAX_ITER , random_state = 42 )) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) train_curve = [ mean_absolute_error ( yr_train , p ) for p in b [ - 1 ] . staged_predict ( b [: - 1 ] . transform ( Xr_train ))] test_curve = [ mean_absolute_error ( yr_test , p ) for p in b [ - 1 ] . staged_predict ( b [: - 1 ] . transform ( Xr_test ))] best = int ( np . argmin ( test_curve )) + 1 plt . plot ( range ( 1 , len ( test_curve ) + 1 ), test_curve , lw = 2.5 , color = "#c85a24" , label = "test bookings" ) plt . plot ( range ( 1 , len ( train_curve ) + 1 ), train_curve , lw = 2.5 , color = "#2b6f78" , label = "training bookings" ) plt . axvline ( best , color = "grey" , ls = "--" , label = f "lowest test error: tree { best } " ) plt . title ( f "Boosting, learning rate { LEARNING_RATE } " ) plt . xlabel ( "Number of trees" ) plt . ylabel ( "Typical error (USD a night)" ) plt . ylim ( 0 , 40 ) plt . legend () plt . show () print ( f "After { len ( test_curve ) } trees: training USD { train_curve [ - 1 ] : .1f } , test USD { test_curve [ - 1 ] : .1f } . " f "Best test error USD { min ( test_curve ) : .1f } at tree { best } ." ) # ✏️ Change these settings LEARNING_RATE = 0.1 MAX_ITER = 100 b = model(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE, max_iter=MAX_ITER, random_state=42)).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) train_curve = [mean_absolute_error(yr_train, p) for p in b[-1].staged_predict(b[:-1].transform(Xr_train))] test_curve = [mean_absolute_error(yr_test, p) for p in b[-1].staged_predict(b[:-1].transform(Xr_test))] best = int(np.argmin(test_curve)) + 1 plt.plot(range(1, len(test_curve) + 1), test_curve, lw=2.5, color="#c85a24", label="test bookings") plt.plot(range(1, len(train_curve) + 1), train_curve, lw=2.5, color="#2b6f78", label="training bookings") plt.axvline(best, color="grey", ls="--", label=f"lowest test error: tree {best}") plt.title(f"Boosting, learning rate {LEARNING_RATE}") plt.xlabel("Number of trees") plt.ylabel("Typical error (USD a night)") plt.ylim(0, 40) plt.legend() plt.show() print(f"After {len(test_curve)} trees: training USD {train_curve[-1]:.1f}, test USD {test_curve[-1]:.1f}. " f"Best test error USD {min(test_curve):.1f} at tree {best}.") After 100 trees: training USD 6.7, test USD 8.4. Best test error USD 8.4 at tree 100. Think about it. Try LEARNING_RATE = 0.5 with MAX_ITER = 300 , then 0.02 with 300 . Where is the best test error, and what does the training error do? Is "more trees" always better? Show the answer With **0.5** the training error keeps falling (to about USD 1.8) but the test error is lowest at tree 20 (USD 9.3) and then rises to USD 10.3: the later trees learn noise, which is overfitting. With **0.02** it is still improving after 300 trees (USD 8.9): steps too small. With **0.1** and 300 trees, the best is about USD 8.4 at tree 118, and it barely moves after that. Unlike in a forest, more trees is *not* always better in boosting.
docs.title: 02 Task 2 · Boosting: learning rate and number of trees

docs.text: The scoreboard is one input to the decision, not the decision. Weigh four criteria: Accuracy on the test bookings, in the metric that fits the decision. Stability: does the model change its answers when the history changes a little? Explainability: can you explain a single prediction to the person it affects? Cost of errors: what does one mistake cost Altamar, and how many decisions does the model make? The cell trains the four models for each question (the line and tree exactly as in week 5) on the same training bookings, and times them. In [5]: Copied! recipes = { "rate" : { "Linear" : model ( LinearRegression (), month_as_category = True ), "Tree" : model ( DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = 10 , random_state = 42 )), # week 5's tuned trees "Forest" : model ( RandomForestRegressor ( n_estimators = 200 , min_samples_leaf = 3 , random_state = 42 )), "Boosting" : model ( HistGradientBoostingRegressor ( random_state = 42 ))}, "cancel" : { "Linear" : model ( make_pipeline ( StandardScaler (), LogisticRegression ( max_iter = 1000 ))), "Tree" : model ( DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = 4 , random_state = 42 )), "Forest" : model ( RandomForestClassifier ( n_estimators = 200 , min_samples_leaf = 3 , random_state = 42 )), "Boosting" : model ( HistGradientBoostingClassifier ( random_state = 42 ))}, } board = [] for question , models in recipes . items (): X_tr , y_tr = ( Xr_train , yr_train ) if question == "rate" else ( Xc_train , yc_train ) for name , m in models . items (): start = time . time () m . fit ( X_tr , y_tr ) seconds = time . time () - start score = rate_scores ( name , m )[ "typical error (USD)" ] if question == "rate" else cancel_scores ( name , m )[ "AUC" ] board . append ({ "question" : question , "model" : name , "accuracy" : score , "seconds" : round ( seconds , 2 )}) board = pd . DataFrame ( board ) print ( board . to_string ( index = False , float_format = lambda v : f " { v : g } " )) print ( " \n Accuracy = typical error in USD for the rate (lower is better), AUC for cancellations (higher is better)." ) recipes = { "rate": {"Linear": model(LinearRegression(), month_as_category=True), "Tree": model(DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=10, random_state=42)), # week 5's tuned trees "Forest": model(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=3, random_state=42)), "Boosting": model(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=42))}, "cancel": {"Linear": model(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))), "Tree": model(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=42)), "Forest": model(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=3, random_state=42)), "Boosting": model(HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42))}, } board = [] for question, models in recipes.items(): X_tr, y_tr = (Xr_train, yr_train) if question == "rate" else (Xc_train, yc_train) for name, m in models.items(): start = time.time() m.fit(X_tr, y_tr) seconds = time.time() - start score = rate_scores(name, m)["typical error (USD)"] if question == "rate" else cancel_scores(name, m)["AUC"] board.append({"question": question, "model": name, "accuracy": score, "seconds": round(seconds, 2)}) board = pd.DataFrame(board) print(board.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:g}")) print("\nAccuracy = typical error in USD for the rate (lower is better), AUC for cancellations (higher is better).") question model accuracy seconds rate Linear 20.5 0.01 rate Tree 13.3 0.02 rate Forest 10.3 1.6 rate Boosting 8.4 1.04 cancel Linear 0.739 0.01 cancel Tree 0.752 0.01 cancel Forest 0.771 0.55 cancel Boosting 0.77 0.69 Accuracy = typical error in USD for the rate (lower is better), AUC for cancellations (higher is better). Stability. The cell retrains each model on three different halves of the training bookings and measures how much their predictions for the same test bookings disagree (rate: USD; cancellations: percentage points). In [6]: Copied! halves = { "rate" : [ Xr_train . sample ( frac = 0.5 , random_state = s ) . index for s in [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]], "cancel" : [ Xc_train . sample ( frac = 0.5 , random_state = s ) . index for s in [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]]} spread = [] for question , models in recipes . items (): X_tr , y_tr , X_te = ( Xr_train , yr_train , Xr_test ) if question == "rate" else ( Xc_train , yc_train , Xc_test ) for name , m in models . items (): preds = [] for idx in halves [ question ]: copy = clone ( m ) . fit ( X_tr . loc [ idx ], y_tr . loc [ idx ]) # a fresh copy: the trained model stays as it is preds . append ( copy . predict ( X_te ) if question == "rate" else 100 * copy . predict_proba ( X_te )[:, 1 ]) spread . append ( np . ptp ( np . array ( preds ), axis = 0 ) . mean () . round ( 1 )) board [ "disagreement" ] = spread print ( board [[ "question" , "model" , "accuracy" , "disagreement" ]] . to_string ( index = False , float_format = lambda v : f " { v : g } " )) halves = {"rate": [Xr_train.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=s).index for s in [1, 2, 3]], "cancel": [Xc_train.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=s).index for s in [1, 2, 3]]} spread = [] for question, models in recipes.items(): X_tr, y_tr, X_te = (Xr_train, yr_train, Xr_test) if question == "rate" else (Xc_train, yc_train, Xc_test) for name, m in models.items(): preds = [] for idx in halves[question]: copy = clone(m).fit(X_tr.loc[idx], y_tr.loc[idx]) # a fresh copy: the trained model stays as it is preds.append(copy.predict(X_te) if question == "rate" else 100 * copy.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]) spread.append(np.ptp(np.array(preds), axis=0).mean().round(1)) board["disagreement"] = spread print(board[["question", "model", "accuracy", "disagreement"]].to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:g}")) question model accuracy disagreement rate Linear 20.5 4.1 rate Tree 13.3 19.9 rate Forest 10.3 8.4 rate Boosting 8.4 7.6 cancel Linear 0.739 5.4 cancel Tree 0.752 13.9 cancel Forest 0.771 8.4 cancel Boosting 0.77 17.6 A decision scorecard. Managers often compare options with weighted criteria. The cell turns each criterion into a score from 1 (worst of the four) to 5 (best), using the numbers above and a fixed explainability rating (line 5, tree 4, forest and boosting 2). Set the weights to what matters for your decision. In [7]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings QUESTION = "rate" # "rate" or "cancel" WEIGHTS = { "accuracy" : 0.5 , "stability" : 0.2 , "explainability" : 0.2 , "speed" : 0.1 } card = board [ board [ "question" ] == QUESTION ] . set_index ( "model" ) def to_1_5 ( values , higher_is_better ): v = values if higher_is_better else - values return ( 1 + 4 * ( v - v . min ()) / ( v . max () - v . min ())) . round ( 1 ) scores = pd . DataFrame ({ "accuracy" : to_1_5 ( card [ "accuracy" ], higher_is_better = ( QUESTION == "cancel" )), "stability" : to_1_5 ( card [ "disagreement" ], higher_is_better = False ), "explainability" : pd . Series ({ "Linear" : 5 , "Tree" : 4 , "Forest" : 2 , "Boosting" : 2 }), "speed" : to_1_5 ( card [ "seconds" ], higher_is_better = False ), }) scores [ "weighted score" ] = sum ( scores [ k ] * w for k , w in WEIGHTS . items ()) . div ( sum ( WEIGHTS . values ())) . round ( 2 ) print ( scores . sort_values ( "weighted score" , ascending = False )) # ✏️ Change these settings QUESTION = "rate" # "rate" or "cancel" WEIGHTS = {"accuracy": 0.5, "stability": 0.2, "explainability": 0.2, "speed": 0.1} card = board[board["question"] == QUESTION].set_index("model") def to_1_5(values, higher_is_better): v = values if higher_is_better else -values return (1 + 4 * (v - v.min()) / (v.max() - v.min())).round(1) scores = pd.DataFrame({ "accuracy": to_1_5(card["accuracy"], higher_is_better=(QUESTION == "cancel")), "stability": to_1_5(card["disagreement"], higher_is_better=False), "explainability": pd.Series({"Linear": 5, "Tree": 4, "Forest": 2, "Boosting": 2}), "speed": to_1_5(card["seconds"], higher_is_better=False), }) scores["weighted score"] = sum(scores[k] * w for k, w in WEIGHTS.items()).div(sum(WEIGHTS.values())).round(2) print(scores.sort_values("weighted score", ascending=False)) accuracy stability explainability speed weighted score Boosting 5.0 4.1 2 2.4 3.96 Forest 4.4 3.9 2 1.0 3.48 Tree 3.4 1.0 4 5.0 3.20 Linear 1.0 5.0 5 5.0 3.00 Think about it. With the default weights, which model wins each question? What weights make the line win the rate question, and what decision would justify them? Then write two sentences per question ( "For the rate we choose … because …" ) covering all four criteria. Show the answer Boosting wins the rate: USD 8.4 vs 20.5 outweighs its lower explainability. The line wins only if explainability weighs far more, e.g. when each rate must be justified to a client. For cancellations the **forest** wins: as accurate as boosting, and much steadier (boosting's risks move about 18 points between samples, the forest's about 8). Example: *"For cancellations, the forest: AUC 0.77, 123 real cancellations among the 150 riskiest bookings (92 for the logistic model), and stable."*
docs.title: 03 Task 3 · Choose a model for each question

docs.text: Partial dependence answers "how does the prediction change with this input, all else equal?". The simulator shows lead time and month; now pick another input. Some worth trying: nights , weekend_nights , adults and children for the rate; special_requests , adr (the rate itself) and previous_cancellations for cancellations; channel for either. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The cell draws the partial dependence of your input, one line per hotel, using the boosting models trained in Task 3. In [8]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings QUESTION = "rate" # "rate" or "cancel" INPUT = "nights" # any column except "hotel"; "adr" only for "cancel" m , X_test = ( recipes [ "rate" ][ "Boosting" ], Xr_test ) if QUESTION == "rate" else ( recipes [ "cancel" ][ "Boosting" ], Xc_test ) column = X_test [ INPUT ] if column . dtype == object or column . nunique () <= 15 : grid = sorted ( column . unique ()) else : grid = sorted ( set ( np . percentile ( column , np . linspace ( 1 , 99 , 20 )) . round ( 0 ))) for h in HOTELS : values = pd_curve ( m , X_test [ X_test [ "hotel" ] == h ], INPUT , grid , proba = ( QUESTION == "cancel" )) plt . plot ([ str ( g ) for g in grid ] if column . dtype == object else grid , values * ( 100 if QUESTION == "cancel" else 1 ), marker = "o" , color = COLORS [ h ], label = h ) plt . title ( f "Partial dependence of the { 'predicted rate' if QUESTION == 'rate' else 'cancellation risk' } on { INPUT } " ) plt . xlabel ( INPUT ) plt . ylabel ( "Predicted rate (USD a night)" if QUESTION == "rate" else "Predicted chance of cancelling (%)" ) plt . legend () plt . show () # ✏️ Change these settings QUESTION = "rate" # "rate" or "cancel" INPUT = "nights" # any column except "hotel"; "adr" only for "cancel" m, X_test = (recipes["rate"]["Boosting"], Xr_test) if QUESTION == "rate" else (recipes["cancel"]["Boosting"], Xc_test) column = X_test[INPUT] if column.dtype == object or column.nunique() < = 15: grid = sorted(column.unique()) else: grid = sorted(set(np.percentile(column, np.linspace(1, 99, 20)).round(0))) for h in HOTELS: values = pd_curve(m, X_test[X_test["hotel"] == h], INPUT, grid, proba=(QUESTION == "cancel")) plt.plot([str(g) for g in grid] if column.dtype == object else grid, values * (100 if QUESTION == "cancel" else 1), marker="o", color=COLORS[h], label=h) plt.title(f"Partial dependence of the {'predicted rate' if QUESTION == 'rate' else 'cancellation risk'} on {INPUT}") plt.xlabel(INPUT) plt.ylabel("Predicted rate (USD a night)" if QUESTION == "rate" else "Predicted chance of cancelling (%)") plt.legend() plt.show() Think about it. Describe the shape in one business sentence. A line, a step, a hump? Would a straight line capture it? Name one reason why it shows association, not cause . Show the answer For `nights` and the rate you should see **steps down** at 5 and 7 nights: Altamar's long-stay discounts, which a line would blur into a gentle slope. For `special_requests` and cancellations the risk **falls** with each request: guests who ask for a crib or a high floor are committed. Association, not cause: adding requests would not make a guest come. Requests reveal commitment; they do not create it.
docs.title: 04 Task 4 · Partial dependence for an input of your choice

docs.text: The general manager has ten minutes. Lead with the recommendation, support it with three arguments, and put one piece of evidence (a chart or a number) under each. Replay the pyramid in the simulator, then fix the weak draft in the next cell: it is written in report order, the way most first drafts are. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. The cell checks your pyramid against five rules and prints it as an outline. Rewrite the three settings until every rule passes. On the test bookings the rate tree took R² from 0.74 (the line, month as a category) to 0.89 , and the typical error from USD 20.5 to USD 13.3 ; the cancellation tree took AUC from 0.74 (logistic) to 0.75 . But a single tree is jumpy . Its first question decides every question below it, so a slightly different sample of bookings can grow a quite different tree, and quote a different price for the same room. No revenue manager would trust such a colleague. The fix sounds like management common sense: don't ask one expert, ask a panel, and combine their answers. 02 Random forests: many trees voting ¶ A random forest grows hundreds of trees and averages them. Three ideas make the trees different from each other, so that their mistakes cancel out: Bootstrap samples. Each tree learns from its own sample of bookings, drawn at random with replacement : some bookings appear twice, about a third not at all. Random inputs. At each question a tree may only choose among a random subset of the inputs, so one strong input cannot dominate every tree. Averaging. For the rate, the forest's quote is the average of the trees' quotes. For cancellations, it is the share of trees that vote "cancel". ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Try it: press Run the forest for each booking. Gradient boosting grows them in a row , like a team where each member reviews the previous one's work: Start with the simplest prediction: the average rate. Look at the errors. A small tree learns where the prediction is too low and where it is too high. Add a damped copy of that correction (the learning rate , say 10% of it). Repeat with the errors that are left. Each tree is small and weak on its own; a hundred of them, each fixing what the others missed, make a strong model. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. One booking in nine sold more than 10% below similar ones; week 4's overbooking rule costs USD 140,000 instead of 153,100. 08 What's next: Business Analytics II ¶ Our best rate model still misses by USD 8 a night, and the best cancellation model is far from perfect. Some of what moves a guest is not in the booking form at all. It is in what guests write . Altamar has thousands of guest reviews: "the volcano view was worth every peso", "the corporate floor was noisy". Ratings and reviews explain what our columns cannot: why a hotel can charge more, why a guest does not come back. Business Analytics II · Text, NLP and LLMs starts there: turning text into numbers, finding topics and sentiment in reviews, and using large language models to read thousands of them for you. 09 Case clinic: comparison and presentation ¶ This is the last step of the applied case . In your team, with the case toolkit : Compare models. Run sections 09 Random forest and gradient boosting and 10 Scoreboard : linear model, tuned tree, random forest and gradient boosting, on the same test data , with the metric you chose in week 4. Explain the best one. Run section 11 What drives the predictions : permutation importance, then partial dependence for your top two or three inputs. One sentence per chart: what it means for the business. Decide. Choose a model: accuracy, stability, explainability, cost of errors. Write three recommendations someone could act on next week. Build the 10-slide pyramid. A skeleton that works: Slide Content 1 The key message: recommendation + the number that justifies it 2 The business question and who decides 3–4 Argument 1 and its evidence (e.g. the scoreboard) 5–6 Argument 2 and its evidence (e.g. importance, one partial dependence chart) 7–8 Argument 3 and its evidence (e.g. money or a decision rule) 9 Limitations and what you would test next 10 The three recommendations, with an owner each Check the rubric before you hand in: the notebook runs top to bottom, and every chart supports an argument.

docs.title: Forests, boosting, and decisions

docs.text: Week 5 ended with two tuned trees , their depth chosen by cross-validation: depth 10 for the rate and depth 4 for cancellations. On the test bookings the rate tree took R² from 0.74 (the line, month as a category) to 0.89 , and the typical error from USD 20.5 to USD 13.3 ; the cancellation tree took AUC from 0.74 (logistic) to 0.75 . But a single tree is jumpy . Its first question decides every question below it, so a slightly different sample of bookings can grow a quite different tree, and quote a different price for the same room. No revenue manager would trust such a colleague. The cell grows week 5's tuned rate tree (depth 10) three times, each on a different random half of the training bookings, and prices the same three test bookings. Look at the spread column: how far apart the three quotes are. In [2]: Copied! halves = [ Xr_train . sample ( frac = 0.5 , random_state = s ) . index for s in [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]] three = Xr_test . iloc [[ 0 , 5 , 8 ]] # three test bookings to follow names = [ f " { h } , { r } , month { m } " for h , r , m in zip ( three [ "hotel" ], three [ "room_type" ], three [ "arrival_month" ])] tree_quotes , quotes = [], {} for i , idx in enumerate ( halves , start = 1 ): tree = model ( DecisionTreeRegressor ( max_depth = 10 , random_state = 42 )) . fit ( Xr_train . loc [ idx ], yr_train . loc [ idx ]) tree_quotes . append ( tree . predict ( Xr_test )) quotes [ f "tree { i } " ] = tree . predict ( three ) . round ( 0 ) table = pd .
