Business takeaway: each of these rooms gets three quotes more than USD 30 apart, depending only on which half of the history the tree happened to see; across all test bookings, about USD 20. The fix sounds like management common sense: don't ask one expert, ask a panel, and combine their answers.
docs.title: 01 Previously: one tree is jumpy

docs.text: A random forest grows hundreds of trees and averages them. Three ideas make the trees different from each other, so that their mistakes cancel out: Bootstrap samples. Each tree learns from its own sample of bookings, drawn at random with replacement : some bookings appear twice, about a third not at all. Random inputs. At each question a tree may only choose among a random subset of the inputs, so one strong input cannot dominate every tree. Averaging. For the rate, the forest's quote is the average of the trees' quotes. For cancellations, it is the share of trees that vote "cancel". ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Try it: press Run the forest for each booking. Booking A gets a unanimous vote; Booking E splits the trees almost in half. Then press One tree at a time and read why each tree votes as it does: they disagree because each one saw different bookings and different inputs. The cell grows a forest of 200 trees for the nightly rate (every leaf keeps at least 3 bookings) and asks each of its trees to price the same three bookings. docs.title: 02 Random forests: many trees voting

docs.text: A forest grows its trees side by side , independently. Gradient boosting grows them in a row , like a team where each member reviews the previous one's work: Start with the simplest prediction: the average rate. Look at the errors. A small tree learns where the prediction is too low and where it is too high. Add a damped copy of that correction (the learning rate , say 10% of it). Repeat with the errors that are left. Each tree is small and weak on its own; a hundred of them, each fixing what the others missed, make a strong model. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Try it: press Play with the learning rate at 0.3 and watch the error bars shrink, January first, then the July holidays. Then try 1.0 and 0.1. How many trees does each need before the typical error stops falling? The same thing in code: scikit-learn's GradientBoostingRegressor on the simulator's 60 bookings, with the month as the only input. Change the learning rate and compare with the simulator. In [6]: Copied! # ✏️ Change these settings LEARNING_RATE = 0.3 pv = df [( df [ "hotel" ] == "Puerto Varas" ) & ( df [ "room_type" ] == "Standard" )] sample = pv . groupby ( "arrival_month" ) . sample ( 5 , random_state = 42 ) # the simulator's 60 bookings gb = GradientBoostingRegressor ( max_depth = 2 , min_samples_leaf = 5 , learning_rate = LEARNING_RATE , n_estimators = 40 , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( sample [[ "arrival_month" ]], sample [ "adr" ]) errors = [ mean_absolute_error ( sample [ "adr" ], p ) for p in gb . staged_predict ( sample [[ "arrival_month" ]])] print ( f "Average only: typical error USD { ( sample [ 'adr' ] - sample [ 'adr' ] . mean ()) . abs () . mean () : .0f } " ) for k in [ 1 , 2 , 5 , 10 , 20 , 40 ]: print ( f "After { k : >2 } trees: USD { errors [ k - 1 ] : .0f } " ) # ✏️ Change these settings LEARNING_RATE = 0.3 pv = df[(df["hotel"] == "Puerto Varas") & (df["room_type"] == "Standard")] sample = pv.groupby("arrival_month").sample(5, random_state=42) # the simulator's 60 bookings gb = GradientBoostingRegressor(max_depth=2, min_samples_leaf=5, learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE, n_estimators=40, random_state=42).fit(sample[["arrival_month"]], sample["adr"]) errors = [mean_absolute_error(sample["adr"], p) for p in gb.staged_predict(sample[["arrival_month"]])] print(f"Average only: typical error USD {(sample['adr'] - sample['adr'].mean()).abs().mean():.0f}") for k in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40]: print(f"After {k:>2} trees: USD {errors[k - 1]:.0f}") Average only: typical error USD 30 After 1 trees: USD 25 After 2 trees: USD 22 After 5 trees: USD 17 After 10 trees: USD 15 After 20 trees: USD 14 After 40 trees: USD 14 Now the real problem: all inputs, all bookings. HistGradientBoostingRegressor is scikit-learn's fast boosting (by default 100 small trees, learning rate 0.1). The cell trains it with three learning rates and records the test error after each tree. In [7]: Copied! curves = {} for lr in [ 0.03 , 0.1 , 0.5 ]: m = model ( HistGradientBoostingRegressor ( learning_rate = lr , random_state = 42 )) . fit ( Xr_train , yr_train ) test_encoded = m [: - 1 ] . transform ( Xr_test ) curves [ lr ] = [ mean_absolute_error ( yr_test , p ) for p in m [ - 1 ] . staged_predict ( test_encoded )] if lr == 0.1 : boost = m # the default: our boosting model best = int ( np . argmin ( curves [ lr ])) + 1 print ( f "Learning rate { lr } : after 100 trees USD { curves [ lr ][ - 1 ] : .1f } ; best USD { min ( curves [ lr ]) : .1f } at tree { best } " ) curves = {} for lr in [0.03, 0.1, 0.5]: m = model(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(learning_rate=lr, random_state=42)).fit(Xr_train, yr_train) test_encoded = m[:-1].transform(Xr_test) curves[lr] = [mean_absolute_error(yr_test, p) for p in m[-1].staged_predict(test_encoded)] if lr == 0.1: boost = m # the default: our boosting model best = int(np.argmin(curves[lr])) + 1 print(f"Learning rate {lr}: after 100 trees USD {curves[lr][-1]:.1f}; best USD {min(curves[lr]):.1f} at tree {best}") Learning rate 0.03: after 100 trees USD 11.4; best USD 11.4 at tree 100 Learning rate 0.1: after 100 trees USD 8.4; best USD 8.4 at tree 100 Learning rate 0.5: after 100 trees USD 9.8; best USD 9.3 at tree 20 The chart draws the three curves: typical test error against the number of trees. In [8]: Copied! for lr , c in curves . items (): plt . plot ( range ( 1 , len ( c ) + 1 ), c , lw = 2.5 , label = f "learning rate { lr } " ) plt . title ( "Boosting on all bookings: the test error falls tree by tree" ) plt . xlabel ( "Number of trees" ) plt . ylabel ( "Typical error on test bookings (USD)" ) plt . ylim ( 0 , 45 ) plt . legend () plt . show () for lr, c in curves.items(): plt.plot(range(1, len(c) + 1), c, lw=2.5, label=f"learning rate {lr}") plt.title("Boosting on all bookings: the test error falls tree by tree") plt.xlabel("Number of trees") plt.ylabel("Typical error on test bookings (USD)") plt.ylim(0, 45) plt.legend() plt.show() Reading the chart. With learning rate 0.03 the model is still learning after 100 trees (USD 11.4): steps too small. With 0.5 it is fastest, reaches USD 9.3 at tree 20, then gets slightly worse (USD 9.8): big steps start copying noise from the training bookings, the overfitting you met in week 5. The default 0.1 ends best here, at USD 8.4 . Rule of thumb: a smaller learning rate needs more trees, and is usually safer. {"q": "In gradient boosting, what does tree number 50 learn from?", "options": ["The original nightly rates, exactly like tree 1", "The errors that are still left after the first 49 trees", "A random half of the bookings, independently of the other trees"], "answer": 1, "why": "Each new tree is fitted to the current errors, so it fixes what the previous trees got wrong. Independent trees on random samples is the forest's recipe, not boosting's.", "code": false}
docs.title: 03 Gradient boosting: trees that fix each other's mistakes

docs.text: A fair comparison has three rules: the same training bookings , the same test bookings , and a metric that fits the decision . For the rate: the typical error in USD (MAE) and R². For cancellations: AUC, and a business number, how many real cancellations each model puts among the 150 bookings it flags as riskiest (about the top 10% of the test bookings). The cell retrains week 5's line and tuned tree for the rate (the forest and boosting are already trained) and prints one row per model. docs.title: 04 The scoreboard

docs.text: A tree you can read like a flowchart; 200 trees, you cannot. Management will still ask two questions, and both have answers: Which inputs matter? Permutation importance : shuffle one column of the test bookings (breaking its link with the outcome while keeping its values) and measure how much worse the model gets. Big damage, important input. How do they matter? Partial dependence : change one input for every booking, keep everything else as it was, and watch the average prediction move. The cell shuffles each input of the test bookings five times and records how many USD the boosting model's typical error grows. In [13]: Copied! imp = permutation_importance ( boost , Xr_test , yr_test , scoring = "neg_mean_absolute_error" , n_repeats = 5 , random_state = 42 ) rate_imp = pd . Series ( imp . importances_mean , index = Xr_test . columns ) . sort_values () rate_imp . tail ( 9 ) . plot . barh ( color = "#c85a24" ) plt . title ( "What drives the predicted rate? (gradient boosting)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Extra typical error when the input is shuffled (USD a night)" ) plt . show () imp = permutation_importance(boost, Xr_test, yr_test, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error", n_repeats=5, random_state=42) rate_imp = pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=Xr_test.columns).sort_values() rate_imp.tail(9).plot.barh(color="#c85a24") plt.title("What drives the predicted rate? (gradient boosting)") plt.xlabel("Extra typical error when the input is shuffled (USD a night)") plt.show() Reading it. Shuffle the arrival month and the typical error grows by about USD 24 a night; room type and hotel , about USD 21 each. Channel, length of stay, weekend nights, lead time and party size add a few USD each. Deposit, country or special requests: about zero. They do not move the price. The same for cancellations, now measured as AUC lost when each input is shuffled. In [14]: Copied! cancel_boost = cancel_models [ "Gradient boosting" ] imp = permutation_importance ( cancel_boost , Xc_test , yc_test , scoring = "roc_auc" , n_repeats = 5 , random_state = 42 ) cancel_imp = pd . Series ( imp . importances_mean , index = Xc_test . columns ) . sort_values () cancel_imp . tail ( 9 ) . plot . barh ( color = "#2b6f78" ) plt . title ( "What drives the predicted cancellation risk? (gradient boosting)" ) plt . xlabel ( "AUC lost when the input is shuffled" ) plt . show () cancel_boost = cancel_models["Gradient boosting"] imp = permutation_importance(cancel_boost, Xc_test, yc_test, scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=5, random_state=42) cancel_imp = pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=Xc_test.columns).sort_values() cancel_imp.tail(9).plot.barh(color="#2b6f78") plt.title("What drives the predicted cancellation risk? (gradient boosting)") plt.xlabel("AUC lost when the input is shuffled") plt.show() Reading it. One input dominates: lead time (shuffle it and AUC drops by 0.18, from 0.77 to about 0.60). Far behind come the deposit, previous cancellations, the rate and the channel. The hotel and the month barely matter for cancellations, although they matter a lot for price. Importance says which . It does not say in which direction , or whether the effect is a line, a step or a hump. For that, partial dependence. The cell computes its curves for each hotel: the boosting models' average prediction for that hotel's test bookings, as lead time or month changes and nothing else does. In [15]: Copied! In [16]: Copied! fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 4.2 ), sharey = True ) for h in HOTELS : left . plot ( LEAD_GRID , pdp [( "rate" , "lead" , h )], marker = "o" , ms = 3 , color = COLORS [ h ], label = h ) right . plot ( MONTH_GRID , pdp [( "rate" , "month" , h )], marker = "o" , ms = 4 , color = COLORS [ h ], label = h ) left . set ( title = "Rate vs lead time, all else equal" , xlabel = "Days booked ahead" , ylabel = "Predicted nightly rate (USD)" ) right . set ( title = "Rate vs arrival month, all else equal" , xlabel = "Arrival month" , xticks = MONTH_GRID ) right . legend () plt . show () fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), sharey=True) for h in HOTELS: left.plot(LEAD_GRID, pdp[("rate", "lead", h)], marker="o", ms=3, color=COLORS[h], label=h) right.plot(MONTH_GRID, pdp[("rate", "month", h)], marker="o", ms=4, color=COLORS[h], label=h) left.set(title="Rate vs lead time, all else equal", xlabel="Days booked ahead", ylabel="Predicted nightly rate (USD)") right.set(title="Rate vs arrival month, all else equal", xlabel="Arrival month", xticks=MONTH_GRID) right.legend() plt.show() Reading it. Lead time: a last-minute premium (bookings made 0–2 days ahead pay USD 6–15 more), a flat middle, then early-bird discounts stepping the rate down after 45 and 90 days. Month: each hotel has its own seasons . Viña del Mar and Puerto Varas peak in January–February, Puerto Varas again in the July winter holidays; Santiago dips in summer and peaks September–November with conferences. A straight line in month could draw none of these; one line per hotel would still miss Puerto Varas's two peaks. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Try it: drag the probe along the lead-time curve for Santiago, then switch on what a straight line would say . Where is the line most wrong? Then switch the question to cancellation risk . The chart below shows predicted cancellation risk against lead time, one line per hotel. In [17]: Copied! for h in HOTELS : plt . plot ( LEAD_GRID , pdp [( "cancel" , "lead" , h )], marker = "o" , ms = 3 , color = COLORS [ h ], label = h ) plt . title ( "Cancellation risk vs lead time, all else equal" ) plt . xlabel ( "Days booked ahead" ) plt . ylabel ( "Predicted chance of cancelling (%)" ) plt . legend () plt . show () for h in HOTELS: plt.plot(LEAD_GRID, pdp[("cancel", "lead", h)], marker="o", ms=3, color=COLORS[h], label=h) plt.title("Cancellation risk vs lead time, all else equal") plt.xlabel("Days booked ahead") plt.ylabel("Predicted chance of cancelling (%)") plt.legend() plt.show() Reading it. Risk is a hump : about 15–20% for last-minute bookings, rising to about 65–75% for bookings made two to four months ahead, then settling at 35–45%. A logistic regression has one coefficient for lead time, so it can only say "the earlier, the riskier" (or the opposite). That is why the trees win on cancellations. Watch out: association, not cause. The curve says bookings made 90 days ahead tend to cancel; it does not say that booking early makes guests cancel, or that banning early bookings would cut cancellations. Policies need a test. {"q": "Partial dependence shows a cancellation risk of about 70% for bookings made 90 days ahead and about 20% for bookings made a week ahead. A model is only worth what the decisions it improves are worth. Two decisions Altamar takes every day: (a) Revenue management: what rate to quote for an upcoming booking, and where today's prices are out of line. (b) Operations: how many rooms to oversell for a busy week. (a) A rate card. The cell describes four upcoming bookings and asks the boosting model for the rate that similar bookings have paid. On week 4's busy week the three models agree: about 24–25 cancellations, oversell 20–21 rooms. Watch out , as in week 4: 37 of these 54 bookings helped train the models, and forests and boosting partly remember their training bookings, so this week flatters them. In real use you score the bookings on the books for next week. Where the better models pay is in which rooms to resell. In week 4 we chose a policy with money: an empty room costs USD 400, a walked guest USD 300, so resell every booking with a risk of 0.43 or more. docs.title: 06 From model to decision

docs.text: Altamar's general manager has ten minutes and one question: what should we do? The pyramid principle answers it top-down: The recommendation first , in one sentence, with a number. Three arguments , each answering "why should I believe that?". Evidence under each argument: one chart or one number per box. We usually tell a story in the order we did the analysis: data, models, results, and the recommendation at the end. If the meeting runs late, the recommendation is what gets cut. ▶ Interactive simulator: open this session on the course website to use it. Altamar's pyramid, from today's numbers. Key message: price with gradient boosting and feed its cancellation risks into week 4's overbooking rule: the typical pricing error falls from USD 20 to USD 8 a night. 1. The model prices like our best revenue manager. R² 0.74 (line) → 0.89 (week 5's tree) → 0.96 on bookings it never saw. 2. We know what drives price and cancellations. Month, room and hotel set the price; each hotel has its own seasons; risk peaks 2–4 months out. 3. It pays off in two decisions. One booking in nine sold more than 10% below similar ones; week 4's overbooking rule costs USD 140,000 instead of 153,100.
docs.title: 07 Presenting to management

docs.text: Our best rate model still misses by USD 8 a night, and the best cancellation model is far from perfect. Some of what moves a guest is not in the booking form at all. It is in what guests write . Altamar has thousands of guest reviews: "the volcano view was worth every peso", "the corporate floor was noisy". Ratings and reviews explain what our columns cannot: why a hotel can charge more, why a guest does not come back. Business Analytics II · Text, NLP and LLMs starts there: turning text into numbers, finding topics and sentiment in reviews, and using large language models to read thousands of them for you.
docs.title: 08 What's next: Business Analytics II

docs.text: This is the last step of the applied case . In your team, with the case toolkit : Compare models. Run sections 09 Random forest and gradient boosting and 10 Scoreboard : linear model, tuned tree, random forest and gradient boosting, on the same test data , with the metric you chose in week 4. Explain the best one. Run section 11 What drives the predictions : permutation importance, then partial dependence for your top two or three inputs. One sentence per chart: what it means for the business. Decide. Choose a model: accuracy, stability, explainability, cost of errors. Write three recommendations someone could act on next week. Build the 10-slide pyramid. A skeleton that works: Slide Content 1 The key message: recommendation + the number that justifies it 2 The business question and who decides 3–4 Argument 1 and its evidence (e.g. the scoreboard) 5–6 Argument 2 and its evidence (e.g. importance, one partial dependence chart) 7–8 Argument 3 and its evidence (e.g. money or a decision rule) 9 Limitations and what you would test next 10 The three recommendations, with an owner each Check the rubric before you hand in: the notebook runs top to bottom, and every chart supports an argument.
docs.title: 09 Case clinic: comparison and presentation

docs.text: The six sessions All six sessions follow Altamar Hotels : a business hotel in Santiago, a beach hotel in Viña del Mar, and a lake hotel in Puerto Varas. Its management team asks two questions. What rate can we charge for a room-night? and which bookings will cancel? Each week takes the analysis one step further, and each step is the one your team then takes with its applied case. Every week has two parts: the live session , which you follow in class, and the lab , a self-paced notebook that ends with the week's graded quiz. Week 1 Reading data like a manager What a notebook is, the Python you need to read code, and a first look at 6,060 bookings. Live session · Lab: First look at Altamar → Case: choose your dataset and write the business question Week 2 From raw data to insight Finding and fixing problems in the data, summary tables, and charts that answer a question. Every hotel has its own seasons. Live session · Lab: Seasons by hotel → Case: clean your data and find three patterns Week 3 Pricing with regression A model for the nightly rate: train and test, coefficients a revenue manager can read, and errors in dollars. Live session · Lab: A rate simulator → Case: your first model Week 4 Predicting cancellations From a yes/no question to a probability; the confusion matrix; and how many rooms to oversell, decided with money. Live session · Lab: An overbooking policy → Case: the right metric for your decision Week 5 When lines are not enough Seasons, early-bird discounts, and last-minute premiums bend the line. Curves, decision trees, overfitting, and cross-validation. Live session · Lab: Tuning a tree → Case: a nonlinear model Week 6 Forests, boosting, and decisions Many trees are better than one. What drives each prediction, which model to trust, and how to present the recommendation. Live session · Lab: Choosing and explaining a model → Case: final comparison and executive presentation The story in numbers Each week's model starts from the last week's result and has to beat it on the same test bookings. This is where Altamar ends up: Week 3–4 · a straight line Week 5 · a tuned tree Week 6 · random forest Week 6 · gradient boosting Nightly rate: typical error per night USD 20.5 USD 13.3 USD 10.3 USD 8.4 Nightly rate: share of the variation explained (R²) 0.74 0.89 0.94 0.96 Cancellations: how well risky bookings are ranked (AUC) 0.74 0.75 0.77 0.77 Overbooking: cost of cancellations on the test bookings (doing nothing: USD 201,200) USD 153,100 — USD 136,100 USD 139,200 The pattern is the lesson of the module: better inputs and nonlinear models cut the pricing error by more than half, while cancellations are harder to predict and gain less. Knowing where a model helps, and by how much, is what you present to management in week 6. How to use a session Every page runs in your browser . Press ▶ next to a cell (or Shift + Enter ) to run it; cells share their results, so run them from top to bottom. Cells marked ✏️ have settings you are invited to change: change them, run again, and see what happens. The interactive simulators respond when you drag, slide, or press play, and the Check yourself questions tell you right away whether you got the idea. Browser or Colab? The browser is the quickest way to follow a session: nothing to install, and the first run takes a few seconds while Python downloads. For the applied case , use Google Colab, where your notebook is saved and shared with your team ( Colab guide ). Every session has an Open in Colab button at the top. The data is in Datasets .
